# Front Cover of the Volume

The manuscript is encased in a **half-leather binding**, a style common for durable scholarly or ledger-style books. The spine and the corners are reinforced with a dark red leather, while the main surfaces of the front and back boards are covered in a mottled, tan-colored paper.

->[Physical Description]<-

The paper on the boards shows significant signs of age and handling, with a marbled or discolored appearance. There are noticeable patches of wear in the upper and lower right-hand corners where the decorative paper has been rubbed away, likely from centuries of being pulled from a shelf or handled by readers. <note>The absence of a title on the front cover suggests that the identification of the work was likely gold-tooled onto the spine, which is a standard practice for library bindings of the 18th and 19th centuries.</note>

<summary>This page describes the physical exterior of the manuscript, which features a red half-leather binding and mottled paper boards showing signs of historical wear.</summary>

### [Decorative Endpaper]

The page displays a vibrant **marbled pattern**, a traditional artistic technique frequently used in historical bookbinding. The design features organic, swirling shapes in shades of **peach and soft pink**, separated by intricate veins of **black** and **light blue-grey**.

<note>Paper marbling is a method of aqueous surface design. Pigments are floated on a liquid "size" and manipulated with tools to create patterns similar to stone or marble before being transferred onto a sheet of paper. These papers were used as "endpapers" to line the inside of the book covers, providing a decorative finish while concealing the structural elements of the binding.</note>

Along the left-hand edge, the dark brown binding strip is visible, indicating where the paper is joined to the book's spine.

<summary>This page consists of a decorative marbled endpaper featuring peach, pink, black, and blue-grey swirling patterns, used to line the interior of the manuscript's cover.</summary>
<keywords>bookbinding, marbling, endpaper, decorative arts, manuscript anatomy</keywords>

<meta>This page serves as a preface or "Advertisement" to the reader, following the title page by Arnaud de Bruxelles. It describes the physical and thematic organization of the two-volume manuscript and provides historical provenance involving a 17th-century owner or editor.</meta>

# Notice to those who shall see this Manuscript

I have divided the book into two tomes or volumes —

The first of which begins at page One [and continues] until after the table [of contents], and ends at page 153.

The second begins at page 154 and continues — until the end.

In the First volume are contained several Treatises on the <term>Philosopher’s Stone</term> <note>The "Philosopher's Stone" was the central goal of alchemy, believed to be a substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and acting as an elixir of life.</note> which are excellent and orthodox within their genre. The theory and the principles are as true and solid as [any], but as for the rules of practice and the preparations for the operations, there is almost nothing else like them in the world. Inasmuch as among these manuscript treatises some are [also] printed—and being from antiquity they are very significant in this regard—[they] <unclear>can</unclear> serve to correct the errors of the Printed [works] by [means of] <unclear>one</unclear> <note>Likely referring to a specific master copy or source manuscript.</note> which, being very ancient, was not subsequently seen by the Printers.

The second volume contains several Treatises and mysterious treatises of the Stone, most of which have not been printed since the composition of the said manuscript, which was in 1438, and until the month of May 1653, [belonging to] Master — Jean De La Font of L.S.B. Myhumelicros <note>Original: "Myhumelicros." This may be an alchemical pseudonym or a Greek-inflected title used by the owner.</note>.

<summary>This preface outlines the division of the manuscript into two volumes and asserts the superior accuracy of these handwritten alchemical texts over contemporary printed versions. It provides a chronological link between the original 1438 composition and a 1653 owner, Jean De La Font.</summary>
<keywords>Philosopher's Stone, alchemy, manuscript history, printing vs manuscript, Jean De La Font, 1438, 1653, practical alchemy</keywords>

### The Straight Path

->Here begins the book composed by Albertus Magnus, called The Straight Path in alchemy.<-

<margin>
<insert>
This book is recorded in the medium-sized book of alchemy printed at Basel in the 2nd volume of the *Theatrum Chemicum* <note>The *Theatrum Chemicum* was a massive and influential compendium of alchemical writings first published in the early 17th century.</note>.
</insert>

> **A**ll wisdom is from the Lord God: and it has always been with Him and exists before time. Therefore, whoever loves wisdom should seek it from Him; and from Him, namely the one who gives to all abundantly and does not reproach. For He is the breadth and depth of all the treasures of wisdom, since from Him, and in Him, and through Him all things are: and without His will, nothing can be done. Therefore, at the beginning of my discourse, I announce His help, who is the fountain and origin of all good things. May He, through His benevolence and piety, deign to supplement the smallness of my knowledge through the grace of the Holy Spirit, so that through my teaching I may be able to manifest the light which lies hidden in the darkness, and lead those who wander into the way of truth. May He deign to grant this, He who sits in the highest and disposes and rules all things for ages of ages, amen.

#### Preface.

**S**ince I have traveled through many regions and very many provinces, and even cities and fortresses, for the sake of the science called <term>alchemy|The medieval precursor to chemistry, focused on the transformation of matter, particularly the turning of base metals into gold.</term> with great labor; and have inquired most diligently about this art from various men and wise people; and have investigated it most fully; and have scrutinized the writings of all; and have very often studied and sweated over their works: I did not find anything true in those things which the books affirm. I looked at

<column-break/>

the books, therefore, as <term>Avicenna|A Latinized name for Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose medical and philosophical works were foundational in medieval Europe.</term> says, of those who contradict and those who affirm, and I found them empty of all perfect work and foreign to every good thing. I also found many prudent and blessed men who, for the sake of this same art, incurred great expenses and labors, and finally failed. I, however, not despairing, though I undertook infinite expenses and labors, moving from place to place, watchful at all times, as <note>original: "sicut dicit Amos" (as Amos says). This paradoxical riddle is frequently found in alchemical texts but does not appear in the biblical Book of Amos.</note> Amos says: "If this thing is, how is it not? And if it is not, how is it?" Finally, persevering through studying, meditating, and working in its operations until I found what I was seeking: not from my own wisdom, but from the supernal grace of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, when I wisely understood that art overcomes nature, I began to watch more diligently in the <term>decoctions|The process of boiling or heating substances to extract their essence.</term> of alchemy, and the <term>sublimations|The alchemical process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used for purification.</term>, solutions, distillations, calcinations, coagulations, and in many other labors, until I found it possible for there to be a <term>transubstantiation|The conversion of one substance into another; here, the changing of base metals into precious ones.</term> into gold and silver <note>original: "solem et lunam" (literally: the sun and the moon). In alchemical symbolic language, the Sun always represents Gold and the Moon represents Silver.</note>. This is better than every natural and moral examination and malleability. I, however, the least of the prophets, intend to write the knowledge and the true art for my friends, both easy and infallible. Yet I write in such a way that those seeing may not see, and those understanding may not understand. Therefore, I ask and <term>adjure|To charge or command someone earnestly or solemnly, often under oath.</term> you by the Creator of the world that you hide this book from all the foolish. To you, therefore, I will reveal the secrets of this art. From others, I conceal the secrets of the science, for because of envy toward this noble science, many despise it. ## On the generation of silver

When, however, **white and pure sulfur** meets **quicksilver** in clean earth: from this **silver** is generated. And silver does not differ from gold except in this: that the sulfur in gold was red: and in silver it was white.

## On the generation of Copper

When, however, **red sulfur**, corrupted and burning, meets quicksilver in the earth, **copper** is generated. And it does not differ from gold except in this: that in gold there was no corruption, while here it was corrupted.

## On the generation of tin

When, however, **white sulfur**, corrupted and burning, meets quicksilver in the earth: then from this **tin** is generated, which "shrieks" <note>original: "stridet." ## On the generation of iron

When, however, corrupted, burning, and **white sulfur** meets quicksilver and pure [substance] in **fetid earth**: from this **iron** is generated.

## On the generation of lead

I have already laid the foundation for the Art. Let us see, therefore, what we should build upon it. For if we build with hay, or wood, or straw, the fire will consume everything. ## Concerning the eight precepts which must be observed

One must observe how one should act in this work: at what time, and in what place. And the first command is to keep eight precepts.

<column-break/>

<margin>That the artisan should be secretive</margin>
The first is that the artisan of this Art and work must be secretive and silent, so that he reveals his secret to no one, except to him whom he knows to be so faithful that for no reason will it be revealed further. For you should know that if many know, the secret will in no way survive without being spread abroad; and if it has been spread abroad, from then on the worker will be considered a counterfeiter <note>original: "falsario." The second precept: that the artisan of this Art should have a special place and house, out of the sight of men, in which house there are two or three chambers where the operations may take place: for sublimating, calcining, distilling, and dissolving, as I shall say hereafter. <margin>Concerning the time to be observed</margin>

The third, that he observe the time in which the work is to be done, and the hours for sublimating. Solutions and distillations are of no value in winter. Sublimations <note>The process of heating a substance so it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used for purification.</note>, however, can be done at any time; but we shall say more concerning the hours in their specific operations. <margin>Note</margin>

The fourth precept is: that he be diligent and frequent in his operations, and not be weary, but persevere until the end. Because if he begins and does not persevere, he will lose both his materials and his time. If, however, he works for seven days and rests for another seven, and thus delays from year to year, he will never complete it. <margin>Concerning diligence and frequency</margin>

<margin>Note the order of working in the essence</margin>
The fifth precept is: that he work according to this instruction: first in calcinations <note>Heating a solid to high temperatures to remove volatile components.</note>; second in sublimations; third in fixations <note>The process of making a volatile substance stable under heat so it does not evaporate.</note>; fourth in calcinations <note>The text repeats "calcination" here, likely referring to a second stage of heating.</note>; fifth in solutions <note>Dissolving a solid into a liquid.</note>; sixth in distillations; seventh in coagulations <note>Turning a liquid back into a solid.</note>; and so on in order. For he who wishes to "dye" <note>original: "tingere." In alchemy, this refers to the transmutation of the metal's color and nature.</note> after sublimation, and to dissolve and coagulate without distillation, will lose his powders.

Now it must be seen: how the furnaces are made, and where, and which ones are necessary. Regarding which it should be known: that the furnaces ought to be made according to the scale of the work. For if your materials are sufficient and you wish to begin a great work, then larger ones must be built. If, however, yours is a small amount, then you maintain furnaces according to the quantity of the powders and the medicine. Nevertheless, I wish to set down the doctrine and the size of the furnaces according to what is suitable for both the rich and the poor.

<margin>Concerning the physical furnace</margin>
First, therefore, we must speak of the physical furnace <note>original: "furnello phisico." In this context, it refers to a furnace designed for "natural" or constant, moderate heat, often used for the digestion of substances.</note>. Thus, the physical furnace is to be made in this way. Let the furnace be placed near a wall so that the air passage <note>original: "meatus ventus," referring to the draft or flue.</note> might have a better ascent. But let the furnace stand away from the wall by the length of an arm. Indeed, let a pit <note>original: "fovea"</note> be made in the ground to the measure of one ell <note>original: "ulne," an old unit of length, roughly 45 inches.</note> in depth. In width, however, to two spans <note>original: "spannas," the distance from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger, about 9 inches.</note> or a little more. This must be straightly <unclear>fortified</unclear> with the "clay of the mastery" <note>original: "argilla magisterij," a specialized clay mixture designed to withstand intense heat for long periods.</note>. Above this pit, let a wall be built of such clay. Take simple clay and add it in four parts to potter's clay, which can most strongly withstand fire. It should be perforated everywhere; it should have at least 40 holes, according to the size of the wheel, about the width of the little finger. And they should be narrow at the top, but wide at the bottom, so that the coals remaining in the holes can freely fall into the pit. In the pit, however, let an air passage be made through the ground and the wall before...

### What the Elixir is: how it should be understood.

For "Elixir" is an Arabic name: in Latin, indeed, it is called **ferment** <note>original: "fermenm(m)".</note>: because just as bread ferments and is raised by a good leaven, so the masses and matter of metals are transformed into white and red [silver and gold], but most especially through **quicksilver** <note>Mercury.</note>. For it is the fountain and origin of all metals.

### Concerning Mercury and its nature

**Mercury** is a viscous water in the bowels of the earth: just as follows under the substances of white earth, united by a gentle heat: such a union into the "first mixture." This continues until the humidity and the dryness of the earth, by cooking, flows over the surface of the earth; it is easily moved because of its wateriness which tempers it and does not permit it to adhere to things. For it is the matter of metals along with sulfur. But the "red stone" <note>Cinnabar (mercury sulfide).</note> is that from which Mercury is extracted. It is found in mountains, sometimes in mineral veins in great quantity. Its nature is cold and humid. It is the fountain and origin of all metals, and from it all proceed as was said above. It is mixed with all metals, except with **iron**; it does not mix easily with it, except through the art [of alchemy], for without mercury no metal can be gilded.

### Concerning Sulfur and its nature

**Sulfur**, truly, is the "fatness of the earth," thickened in the mineral of the earth by a temperate cooking: until it is hardened and becomes thick. And when it has been hardened, it is called sulfur, having a very strong composition. It is a uniform substance, homogeneous in its parts. Therefore its "oil" is not taken from it by distillation as it is from other things that contain oil, but by waters...

## On Orpiment and its nature

Orpiment <term>Orpiment: a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral (arsenic trisulfide) used as a pigment and in alchemy.</term> is a yellowish mineral stone. It is formed as a terrestrial deposit in the caverns of the earth through passing time: thus, by long boiling <note>The alchemists believed minerals "ripened" or "boiled" inside the earth over long periods.</note>, it is changed into this golden pigment. There is a twofold viscosity in it: one thin, the other thick. One is removed by washing; the other by boiling—even in urine—because if that [viscosity] remained, it could not be sublimated <term>Sublimation: the process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used for purification.</term>; it would immediately be set on fire and become a flame. It is whitened in two ways: namely, by boiling and by sublimation, as I will declare most clearly in what follows.

## On Arsenic and its nature

Arsenic <note>Likely referring to Realgar (arsenic disulfide) or other arsenic ores.</note> is of a subtle nature, possessing sulfurous heat, and it is a red stone. For its "flower" <note>The pure crystalline powder produced through sublimation.</note>, which is white and red, is like orpiment; it is sublimated easily and very quickly. It is whitened in two ways: namely, by boiling and sublimation.

## On Sal Ammoniac

Sal Ammoniac <term>Sal Ammoniac: ammonium chloride. A white crystalline salt used to clean metals and act as a flux.</term> is manifold: namely, natural and artificial.

And then it leaves its spirit there, mixed in the bodies and joined, united and persevering, and it is converted.

## On common Salt and its preparation

<margin>folio 9.</margin>
**C**OMMON salt also belongs to this art. For it, in this manner, closes and opens all things, and without it, no work of alchemy can be completed. It is prepared as follows: Take as much of it as you wish and dissolve it in hot water by grinding it in a mortar. That which is dissolved, strain through a cloth into some wooden vessel. And for that salt which remains in the mortar, pour other hot water over it again, doing as before, until you have it all dissolved. Then take that water and boil it in a lead vessel if you have one; if not, in copper, until the water evaporates and the salt returns to its previous state. Then take that salt and place it in a new pot, and put it in a calcination furnace <term>Calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to change its physical or chemical properties, often to make it more friable or to oxidize it.</term> and dry it very well. Keep it until I teach you how you ought to dissolve and distill it, as in the following chapter.

## On Alkali Salt and how it is made

**A**lkali salt <note>Likely potassium carbonate or a mixture of alkaline salts derived from wood ash.</note> belongs to this art: when it is well-prepared, it then dissolves all calxes <term>Calx: a powdery metal oxide produced by heating a metal or mineral.</term> of bodies and spirits into water, and afterward converts them into a solid mass. Its nature is hot and moist. It is made thus: Take ashes of rotten oak, well-burnt in great quantity, or specifically potash <note>original: "cinerem clavellam"; literally "nail-ash," a traditional name for potassium carbonate used in glassmaking and dyeing.</note> which is found for

<column-break/>

dyeing cloths: and grind it very finely. And take an equal amount of quicklime <term>Quicklime: calcium oxide, a caustic substance produced by heating limestone.</term> and mix them together. Take a strong and thick cloth and place it in a very deep, large earthen vat, and put the mixed ash with the lime on top, as much as the cloth can hold. Pour hot water over it well and allow it to strain like lye <term>Lye: a strongly alkaline solution (liquid) produced by leaching wood ashes.</term>. Likewise, pour hot water over it again, and keep pouring until you have all the bitterness of the lime and the ash. Now let it stand, and make another batch, and do with this as before. When you have all the water, let it reside in the same vessel until morning. Then boil it in a cauldron until all the water evaporates and it gives off neither vapor nor smoke. Then allow it to cool, and it will become quite hard; it is called Alkali Salt, that is, the "dregs of bitterness" <note>original: "fex amaritudinis."</note>. Then take this salt and place it in a pot until it is half full, and place the open pot in the furnace. Give it a very gentle fire at first until it glows red; afterward a stronger fire, until by boiling it catches fire, and moves, and boils like wax. Then pour it into a smith's mold <note>original: "folle fabreo." Literally "smith's bellows," but here referring to a casting tray or vessel used in a forge.</note>, holding the pot over another pot; do this immediately, because if you delay in pouring, it will be of no use, because it hardens very quickly. And thus you will have white alkali salt, which you should place in a glass vessel in a warm, dry place. For if you place it in a moist place, it would then dissolve into water.

### On Cinnabar and its composition
Among noble things, there is a valuable thing that pertains to this art. and it is called cinnabar <note>Cinnabar is the naturally occurring bright red ore of mercury (mercuric sulfide).</note>: and it is made of sulfur and quicksilver <term>Argentum vivum: literally "living silver," the common Latin term for mercury.</term>. [Take] it is made thus. [Take] nine parts of quicksilver: three parts of sulfur. and mix them together in the way you know: and put it in a narrow glass vessel having a neck. Let the vessel first be well coated with clay to the thickness of one finger and dried. Then put in the medicine as I said. and put it over a tripod: and block the mouth of the vessel: and give fire first slow for almost half a day: or until you see red smoke come out from the top. Then it is enough. Allow it to cool: and after the sublimation <note>original: *fumuatione*. This likely refers to the fuming process or sublimation where the sulfur and mercury combine and rise as a solid red crust.</note> is done: break the vessel: and you will find good cinnabar. If you are not practiced, you will not see wonders. Exercise therefore so that you see them.

# How red lead is made from white lead

<margin>m</margin> Red lead is made from white lead in this way. Take the white lead and grind it closely (upon a stone): and when it has been well ground, make a paste from it. Put it in an earthenware vessel in the shape of a basin, as is shown here below: having length, not roundness. But first you should place a large pot upon a stone or two walls made of clay, a span <note>A "span" is an ancient measurement based on the width of a human hand.</note> in width. And upon those walls place the pot: so that it lies upon one wall: and you place one small vessel with the white lead in the middle of the pot: and cover it with another vessel joined to it. Afterward, close the pot with a lid or cover suited to it. Give it first a gentle fire, and afterward a strong one, for half a day. Then allow it to cool, and you will find the white lead has become somewhat red. Grind it again, and first perform the roasting for half a day: then draw it out, and you will find the best red lead. From this is made the water which is one of the "remaking" <note>original: *remanchiō*, likely referring to a restorative or transmutative liquid.</note>.

# How red lead is made from lead ash

Red lead is made from the ash of lead in this way: Place a pot upon the hearth-stone <note>original: *pavietro*</note> as I told you: and put in the lead. Give it a strong fire. And when the lead has been liquefied, have a long iron spoon with which you must stir the lead here and there so that it turns to ash, little by little.

<column-break/>

### [Right Column]

Afterward give it a strong fire, always stirring, until it all turns to ash: and strain it through a sieve. That which was strained, grind again upon a stone with water: and do in all things as I said regarding the white lead: turning and roasting it until you have a very deep red.

# What sublimation is: and how and why sublimations are made

Now, proceeding to the definitions of alchemy, it must first be known what repeated sublimation <note>original: *sublimatio reitera*</note> is. Sublimation is the lifting up of a dry substance by fire, such that it adheres to its vessel. <gloss>Sublimation is diversified according to the diversity of the spirits to be sublimated.</gloss> Sublimation is diversified according to the diversity of the spirits to be sublimated <note>This sentence is repeated in the original manuscript.</note>, because some occur in high heat <unclear>ignition</unclear>, such as Marcasite <note>original: *Marchesita*, iron pyrite.</note>, Magnesia <note>original: *Magnesia*, historically used for various minerals, often manganese ore.</note>, and Tutty <note>original: *Tutia*, zinc oxide found in the chimneys of furnaces.</note>. Some occur with moderate fire, such as Quicksilver <note>original: *Argentum vivum*, mercury.</note> and Arsenic. Some with a weak fire, such as sulfur.

The purpose of sublimation is this: so that the purification of that substance might be achieved and its wateriness removed. It is, therefore, a clever way to remove the excess earthiness <unclear>by fire</unclear>: it consists of [mixing the substance] with things for which they have no affinity, and repeating the sublimation <unclear>of it</unclear>.

And this [mixing material] is sometimes eggshell lime <note>original: *calx ovorū*</note>, or white marble lime, or very finely ground glass; and every kind of salt prepared through these methods is not dissipated by them; and nothing is purified unless they are in the perfection of the "body" <term>Body: In alchemy, this refers to the solid metallic state of a substance.</term>, but rather the body has a superfluity of fluid. Before all things, those which ascend with it in sublimation <unclear>upward</unclear> are corrupted. And for that reason, in sublimation from tin or lead, you may see that after sublimation it remains stained.

...it will enter. Therefore, it should not be sublimated with those things it matches <note>original: *quibus convenit*, referring to substances with similar chemical properties or "sympathies."</note>. It is better with those it matches if it does not have "superfluities" <note>original: *superfluities*, referring to unwanted impurities or excess watery parts.</note>. However, the method of removing the wateriness or excess is this: when it is mixed with calxes <note>original: *calcibus*, powders produced by roasting or oxidizing metals.</note>, from which it ought to be sublimated, let it recede and be mixed with them until nothing of it appears. Then, the wateriness should be removed over a very gentle fire. As it recedes, the wateriness of the *azezac* <note>original: *azezacis*, a medieval term derived from Arabic *al-zāj*, usually referring to vitriol or various mineral salts.</note> will recede, as I will teach more fully in the following sections when I set down the method of sublimation.

### What calcination is, and why bodies are calcined

Calcination is the purification of a thing by fire through the removal of the moisture that holds the parts together. "Bodies" <note>In alchemy, "bodies" usually refers to the seven traditional metals.</note> are calcined so that the sulfurousness that settles and corrupts may be destroyed. For all wateriness of sulfurousness—from whatever thing it is derived—corrupts everything, and it cannot be destroyed without calcination.

### Why and how spirits are calcined

The special calcination of soft bodies is white lead <note>original: *Cerusa*, a pigment made from lead.</note>; we find them to be hardened by a clear technique. For it hardens things and is easily seen. The reason for the calcination of "spirits" <note>original: *spirituum*, volatile substances like mercury, sulfur, or arsenic that "fly" from the fire.</note> is so that they may be better "fixed" <note>made resistant to heat.</note> and quickly dissolved into water; for every kind of calcined material is more fixed and dissolves more easily than a body that is not calcined. For soft bodies can easily be refined by fire alone, as I taught above regarding red lead <note>original: *minio*.</note>. Hard bodies, however, require a violent fire, as I shall teach below.

### Why and how bodies are coagulated

Coagulation is the reduction of a liquid thing to a solid substance through the removal of moisture. The reason for its invention is for hardening, and—through the means of solution—for the liberation from the wateriness mixed into them. Mercury <note>original: *Mercurius*.</note> is coagulated from its frequent precipitation and by the violence and harshness of the fire. The harshness and fire remove its wateriness; and this is done in a vessel that is long and tall.

<column-break/>

### Why and how bodies are fixed

Fixation is the preparation of a thing to stand suitably against the fire <note>i.e., making a substance non-volatile so it does not evaporate when heated.</note>. The reason for its invention is so that every "tincture" <note>An alchemical "tincture" is the color or transformative essence of a substance.</note> and every alteration may persist in the thing that has been altered. "Bodies" that have fallen short of their perfection are fixed through their calcination, which frees them from the sulfurousness that violently corrupts them. Sulfur and arsenic <note>original: *arsenicum*.</note> are fixed in two ways: through long-lasting sublimations over these materials in a tall vessel until they "stay" <note>stop evaporating.</note>. Spirits are also fixed in another way: if they are in "metallic waters" or in "oil of tartar" <note>original: *oleo tartari*, a solution of potassium carbonate used as a reagent.</note>, as I shall teach later.

### Why and how calcined bodies are dissolved

Solution is the dissolving of any calcined thing into water. The reason for its invention is so that its "increment" <note>likely referring to the final refinement or enhancement of the substance's power.</note> may reach its limit, and it will arise in a form suitable for distilling. In this way, all of its corruption is purified. Solution is performed either by heat with moisture—as in dung <note>original: *fimo*, a common source of steady, gentle heat in alchemical labs.</note>—or in cold and moisture—as in a "storage pit" <note>original: *fovea repositionis*, a hole in the ground used for cooling or slow digestion.</note>—as I will teach below on leaf 12, in the following chapter.

### Concerning the distillations of vapors

Distillation is the collection of aqueous vapors from the things to be distilled, using their distilling vessel. It is diversified...

The general reason for any distillation is the purification of the liquid from filth, dregs, or foulness, and its preservation against putrefaction. For we truly see that by any method of distillation, the liquid is made purer. The specific reason, however, was for the spirit to be soaked in pure water and for the medicines to be cleansed. And if at times in the soaking we have pure waters—which almost after their seclusion do not leave everything behind—the roots and forms of the medicine can be cleansed, fixed, and ground. The reason for the invention of distillation by descent is so that there may be pure oil in its own nature by withdrawal; because by ascent, a combustible oil could not be obtained in its nature, as is evident in petroleum <note>original: *percoleo*, a variant of *petroleo* or rock oil.</note>. 

Distillation that is done through a filter has as the reason for its invention the clarity of the water alone, as I will teach hereafter.

### Why and how Waxing (Ceration) is done.

Ceration <term>Ceration: a process of softening a hard substance until it reaches a wax-like consistency, making it easier to melt or combine with other materials.</term> is the softening of a hard and non-fusible thing for the purpose of liquefaction. And it is clear that the reason for its invention is so that whatever cannot enter <note>original: *ingressum*, referring to the ability of one substance to penetrate and transform another.</note> due to a lack of liquefaction might be softened for alteration, so that it may flow and have the power of entry. Some have thought that the grinding should be done with liquid oils and waters, which is erroneous. For in no substance is the moisture for this ceration found to be better, more possible, or more suitable than in sulfur and arsenic. The method of ceration

<column-break/>

is this: that similar things can be ground and multiplied after their sublimations, until it provides a good fusion while its moisture remains within it. This does not happen before its perfect cleansing from all corruption. But it seems better to me that their oils first be fixed by oil of tartar <note>Oil of Tartar: a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate, used as a powerful alkaline reagent.</note>. And through all oils, a suitable ceration may be made.

## On how the sublimation of sulfur is performed
<term>He spoke</term> <note>original: *Dixit*; a common opening in medieval texts referring to an authority or the previous section.</note> of the sublimation of <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: *Mercurij*; quicksilver.</note>. Now follows the sublimation of <term>sulfur</term>. First, therefore, let it be boiled in strong vinegar for an entire day: and thus well ground, always taking away the "cloud" <note>original: *nebulam*; likely referring to the scum or impurities that rise to the surface during boiling.</note>: afterwards allow it to be dried. Then grind it: and add to it an equal amount of prepared <term>alum</term> <note>original: *alumine*; a mineral salt used as a drying agent and mordant.</note>: and place it in a vessel for sublimating: just like <term>azec</term> <note>original: *azec*; a term often used for vitriol or a specific processed mineral in medieval alchemy.</note>. Knowing that so much fire is not to be made as was done in our <term>azec</term> above. But it ought to be sublimated in a gentle fire for an entire day. Then take that which you find sublimated: and sublimate it again by itself in the same dregs <note>original: *fecibus*; the solid residue left at the bottom of the vessel.</note>: and you will find it white. And sublimate it a third time and it will be very white, surpassing snow in its whiteness. Furthermore [?], sublimate it a fourth time: and if there is need, a fifth: and reserve it.

## On the sublimation of Orpiment
There follows the sublimation of <term>orpiment</term> <note>original: *auripigmenti*; arsenic trisulfide, a yellow mineral.</note>. First, therefore, you must grind it and cook it for two days in urine and vinegar: afterwards add to it an equal amount of <term>iron soot</term> <note>original: *fuligine ferri*; likely iron scale or rust gathered from a forge.</note> and mix them together as with the <term>sulfur</term>: and thus sublimate it in all ways as I have taught regarding <term>sulfur</term>: and it comes out as a white powder like snow, which you will save well.

### How sublimated things are ground <insert>and fixed</insert>

Above, I taught how to sublimate and collect flowers and powders and to preserve them. Now, however, I will teach how to "plant" them: so that they may bear righteous fruit: and their fruit may remain for eternity. I will teach how to grind and <term>fix</term> <note>original: *figere*; to "fix" a substance means to make it "non-volatile," meaning it will no longer evaporate when heated but instead stay at the bottom of the vessel and melt.</note> sublimated powders: so that they can remain in the fire: to be united with bodies: to be joined and mixed. And this is done in two ways. Take 1 pound of whatever you wish, without any other thing: and place it in the vessels of fixation: and close the mouth well: then with good glassmaker's clay

<column-break/>

and place it in the furnace: and give it fire for one entire day: if there is a great quantity of fire, just as we explained in the sublimation: after half a day, or when the examination is done: see that what is above is placed below: and do this for at least 9 days. Then open it: and see if it is fixed by this method: place a portion of it upon a burning coal: because if it gives off smoke, it is not done: if, however, it does not give off smoke, it is good. And this is the sign in every fixation. If, however, it is not fixed, then again place the vessel in the furnace as before for 9 days. Or for so long until you hear a sound, like a stone scraping in the vessel: which often happens when it is not too burnt.

### Another method of fixation

The second method of fixation is by <term>imbibition</term> <note>The process of saturating a dry substance with a liquid until it is fully absorbed.</note> in oil of tartar. And give it a gentle fire first, lest the vessel be broken: and afterwards when it has been done as such, make the fire a little stronger and distill the medicine with the mouth open at the top. But I advise that you place an <term>alembic</term> <note>original: *alembicum*; a distillation cap with a beak to collect vapors.</note> over it, so that you may receive the water which distills from it, because it is useful for many things. ### On the reduction of the ash of bodies into a solid mass

The reduction of the ash <term>ash; original: *calcis*, the powdered residue left after a metal is heated or "calcined"</term> of bodies into a solid mass is done thus. Take the ash of any metal, and grind it, and place it upon marble and wash it with hot water twice or three times; and cast out the turbid water until the water comes out clear. Then dry it: and grind it upon a stone; and add alum water mixed with common salt water: and grind strongly: and repeatedly soak it with that water, grinding, roasting, grinding, and soaking until it becomes like white lime. And thus the sulfurous nature which it had taken from the earth is removed from it. Afterward, grind it together with white alkali salt <term>alkali salt; original: *sale alkali*, a basic salt used as a flux to help metals melt</term>: and place it in a crucible. And seal it well with clay: and make a small hole on one side at the top from which the matter may exit when it is fused; and let the hole be small. And place it in the forge: and blow upon it: and give it a vehement fire so that it may be melted. When, however, it is fused: you will see a white matter and you will rejoice. And this mass can receive another tincture, white or red, because it is clean from all heat <note>The author likely means the material is now "dead" or stable, having had its volatile "heat" or reactive impurities removed</note>. If we wish to work toward the red: then soak the same ash of metals with red water made from the flower of copper <note>verdigris or copper acetate</note>: without vitriol <note>original: *atramenti*; literally "blackening," used for iron sulfates</note> and without minium <note>red lead</note>. And do in all things just as was said above regarding alkali salt: and melt it as I have taught you. And it will be a red matter: and you will rejoice greatly.

### Medicine for whitening

And soak it in the water of sal ammoniac upon a stone three or four times, grinding and soaking and roasting, just as was said above. And place it upon a stone to dissolve: and that which is dissolved into <insert>water</insert>, save it. Another part which is not dissolved, grind it and add a little <insert>water</insert> of sal ammoniac: and thus the whole will be dissolved. I advise, however, that you do not dye any metal that is not purged with it, because as it evaporates after the second examination <note>a test of purity, such as cupellation or fire-testing</note>, it separates from it.

### On the three transubstantiating stones

Likewise, there are three precious stones principal in this art: namely, the Athene-stones <note>original: *athenes*; likely a reference to the "Athenian stones" mentioned in pseudo-Aristotelian alchemical texts as primary materials</note> which we have transcribed from the position set by Aristotle in the *Book of Stones*. And these three claim for themselves the leadership and the entirety of the work. And from this is made the tincture which is called the **elixir**: which transubstantiates <note>changes the very substance of</note> all metals—even those not purged—into the Sun <term>Sun; original: *solem*, gold</term> and the Moon <term>Moon; original: *lunam*, silver</term>: which is better than any natural metal.

## On Medicine and the Science of Things

**I**, however, wish to set down the teaching concerning one thing only, namely, the "scorpion" <note>original: *scorpione*; likely a code name for a specific reactive substance or a stage of the chemical process</note>. Take, therefore, the stone found everywhere which is called <term>Rebis; an alchemical term meaning "the double thing," representing the union of opposites like spirit and body or male and female</term>: and it is born in two mountains. <margin>7 1/28 twice</margin> From this, the "flying ones" <note>original: *volantes*; likely referring to volatile spirits or gasses</note> take their life-sustenance: and you should not take it unless it is fresh, with its own blood. And if this stone were not "airy" in nature, it would not be conquered by mercury, nor would it be "bitten" <note>corroded or dissolved</note>. But because they are of such a nature, they are mixed and cooked together, and fire does not separate them.

Take that substance, however, and clean it in the <term>tongs; original: *forpice*, referring to metallurgical pincers or forceps</term> to the size of your fingernail. Then take 12 ounces of it and put it into 4 pounds of alkali water and 4 pounds of boys' urine <note>A common source of ammonia and phosphates in historical chemistry</note>. Place all these things into a new glazed jar, and place the jar for some time under dung <note>A standard alchemical method for providing gentle, steady heat through natural decomposition</note> so that it may putrefy. After this <insert>apply fire</insert> and cook it over a slow fire for as long as it takes for half of the water to be consumed. You shall check this with a stick inserted through the hole at the top. Be careful that you do not smell the odor, because it would kill you <note>A warning against toxic fumes, possibly ammonia or sulfurous gases</note>. And when the water has been consumed to the halfway point, you will find the entire substance of those things already changed into water. Honor it, then, for it is said to be worthy of honor. Then allow it to cool, and strain it through a cloth, and it will become as it should. And this is the "stone and not a stone" <note>A classic alchemical riddle for a substance that is common and disregarded, yet contains the secret of the Work</note>. You will find this everywhere—in the plains, in the mountains, and in all waters.

Both the rich and the poor possess this same thing. It is most vile in name and yet most rare; by it you will be honored or dishonored. The "flying ones" praise it; blessed be God, who created it as something both most precious and most vile. Therefore, distill this water that follows, and keep the dregs which remain in its distilling vessel.

<column-break/>

Take your <term>quicksilver; original: *vivum argentum*, also known as mercury</term> and boil it in a pan with vinegar and salt, so that it may be purified of its blackness <note>original: *ingredine*, likely a scribe's error for *nigredine*, meaning the dark dross or impurities</note>. The end of its boiling is reached after four hours. Then have a small, round, glazed jar with a narrow neck, and into every half-pound of mercury, put 3 ounces of the water which you made <gloss>see above</gloss>, and close the mouth of the jar. Then have a round furnace made of good clay, having a hole at the top where the fire and the vessel are placed. Heat it until it glows white. Then remove all the fire and place the jar in the middle of the furnace, and close the mouth of the furnace very well, and leave it until morning. Then open it and remove the jar, and you will find the quicksilver somewhat hardened. Again, add 3 ounces of the aforesaid water, close the mouth of the vessel, and place it in the furnace. And do this a third time as before, and the quicksilver will be hard and fixed without <term>sublimation; the process of turning a solid directly into a gas and back to a solid to purify it</term>.

Place, therefore, one part of this substance upon a thousand parts of iron, and it will be good and white. Then take one part of this transmuted elixir and place it upon 40 parts of <term>Jupiter; alchemical code for Tin</term>, and it will become <term>Silver; original: *luna*, literally "The Moon"</term> much better than the natural kind.

**And** if you wish to convert this ferment into the best <term>Gold; original: *solem*, literally "The Sun"</term>: then take some of the prepared mercury itself and grind it upon a stone, adding to it one ounce of the dregs <note>original: *fenibus*, likely a variation of *fecibus*</note> which you have refined by grinding for half a day. Afterward, put it in the jar as before, adding to it one ounce of water, and place it in the heated furnace. In the morning, remove it and again add half an ounce of the dregs, and grind it just as before in all ways, as described above.

### On the purification of iron plates

### On the preparation of Jupiter

### When distillations ought to be performed

The works of distillation <insert>received</insert> ought to be performed from the month of March until the end of the month of April. At other times, indeed, the tinting does not happen well. The process must be paused until the smokiness of the odor evaporates; otherwise, the operation should be left in its current state of preparation. Allow the jar to rest in a temperate place in cold water or in a large sand bath, because in this way the strength of the water is preserved. Change the sand and the water every four days. Let this be done for ten days. In this way, the virtue of the water is gathered, and it gains greater substance and sharpness; thus you can fashion the **white and red elixir**.

# Another water to be used in place of the water of the moon; how it is made

Another water that is used in place of the "water of the moon" <note>original: *aq lune*; alchemical water used for silver-working</note> for the elixir is made as follows. Take <term>lime of Jove; lead or tin oxide, here referring to Jupiter/tin</term>, with <term>Yemen alum; a high-quality mineral salt used as a mordant</term>, and common salt. Dissolve this in white wine vinegar; let it stand for [...] days under <term>dung; horse manure was used as a consistent, low-heat source for fermentation or slow digestion</term>. Then distill the clear water once; this will be for the dissolving and coagulating of the "wine" <note>likely a reference to a chemical spirit</note> just like the water of silver lime, and it serves in place of the "water of silver" for the **elixir**.

# How the sharpest vinegar is made

The sharpest vinegar <note>original: *acetū acerrū*</note> is made as follows. Take unripe grapes from a warm place—not from the south—and squeeze them with your hands, rotating them in white or red wine vinegar over your hands. And do not press [too hard]; strain it through a round cloth seven times, and let it settle for 3 days and nights. Let it be sealed with washed oil and <term>bitumen; a naturally occurring petroleum substance used for airtight sealing</term> for 3 months. Afterward, open it and distill it once.

# On Saturn; how it is prepared and calcined

"Saturn" <note>lead</note> is prepared and <term>calcined; reduced to a powder through heat</term> in this way: Take Saturn and dissolve it, then quench it 14 times in salt water and very sharp vinegar, so that the salt is prepared; for the salt will corrode as it enters, and the vinegar binds its softness. Then grind it and put it in a sealed pot, closing it with clay. Place it in the furnace for one day and night; in the morning, take it out, and you will have the whitest "lime of Saturn."

# Water for soaking to be used for the Moon

A water for soaking <note>original: *imbibendū*; the process of a solid absorbing a liquid</note> "the moon" <note>silver</note> is made as follows. Take <term>dung; original: *merdem*</term> of the finest sort and make from it a very strong <term>lye; an alkaline solution made from ashes or dung</term>. Afterward, take 10 chicken eggs and boil them in this lye so that they become very hard. Then break the hard eggs, clean them of their shells, and grind them very well. Place them in the said lye so that it reaches the consistency of a paste; then set it to be distilled in an <term>alembic; a classic alchemical still</term> with a gentle fire. Collect the water distilled from it and save it, because it is useful for soaking whatever is to be "soaked for the moon."

# On the oil of Tartar; how it may be made, folio 77.

Oil of <term>tartar; a salt crust found in wine barrels</term> is made thus. Take as much tartar as you wish and roast it until it becomes perfectly white. Then place it in a linen bag, hung in a damp place, and collect the oil that drips from it into a glass vessel. This oil is effective for work with "the moon" <note>silver</note> and is an excellent restorative. And if you distill this oil, it will be even better.

# On the preparation of copper.

"Copper" <note>original: *eris*</note> is prepared thus: Take prepared common salt, very finely ground tartar, Yemen alum, and the sharpest vinegar. Mix them all together with the vinegar until they are dissolved. Then melt the copper and quench it seven times in this water; it will be prepared and as soft as "the moon" <note>silver</note>.

# How to fix mercury with Saturn or Jupiter.

Fix <note>original: *abar'*; likely *abaurare* or *abarrer*, meaning to harden or stabilize</note> "mercury" <note>quicksilver</note> with "Saturn" <note>lead</note> or "Jupiter" <note>tin</note> as follows. Take as much mercury as you wish, melt the lead, and pour it over it. [Add] 3 parts of silver and grind it well by itself. Afterward, use the best prepared salt and let them be dissolved in water; let it sit for seven days.

## Concerning the preparation of Mercury

The preparation of Mercury in a <term>reed; a hollow stalk or pipe used as a container</term> is done thus. Take <note>original: *Rx.*; Recipe, the standard medical and alchemical command to 'take'</note> as much Mercury as you want: and wash it in this way. Then set it to boil over a slow fire, or over hot ashes, until all the vinegar is consumed. Afterward, place the said Mercury in fresh water until all the saltiness leaves it: and by drying it well between your fingers, and after the washing, you will see it clear and bright. Take a section of said reed between two nodes: namely, let there be a node at each end. Make a small hole in the middle of one node, through which you fill the said reed with the Mercury prepared in this way. And afterward, close the hole well, so that the Mercury cannot escape in any way. Afterward, cover the said reed well with clay—specifically, with <term>alchemy mud; a special sealing clay or 'lute of the philosophers'</term>—and allow it to dry in the shade. ## On the preparation of Saturn: and its conversion

The preparation of Saturn <note>original: "Saturnum"; the alchemical name for lead</note> is done thus. Take Saturn and melt it: and when it is melted, sprinkle over it the aforementioned powdered salt, and stir well with a stick until the turbulence is over it. When this is done, pour it into flowing water, and the salt will be separated from the powder. Then wash the powder in clean water and dry it, and repeat. And if anything remains unpowdered, do as before. Then take one part of the said powder, and half a part of calcined eggshells <note>original: "calcis ozoai ouorū"; "ovorum" refers to eggs, and "calcis" to the powdery residue left after burning</note>, and as much salt water as is needed so that it becomes well mixed. Afterwards, place it in a glass flask and put it in warm dung for 12 days, and you will find the lead converted into quicksilver <note>original: "argentū viūū"; mercury</note>. Then pour off the salt water and cook it in a pan until it is reduced to its original state; wash it with the calcined eggshells twice or thrice until it becomes clean, and dry it in the sun, and keep it for use as described above.

## On the explanation of the metals

Concerning the explanation of the metals: Know that the Sun <note>Sol</note> is gold; the Moon <note>Luna</note> is silver; Mars is iron; Mercury is quicksilver; Jupiter is tin; Venus is copper or <unclear>rannum</unclear> <note>perhaps a variation of brass or tin-alloy</note>; and Saturn is lead.

## On the medicine for the white and the red

Medicine for the white: let this elixir for the white and the red be made in one

<column-break/>

operation, and it is a Roman work of 21 days.
Take the purest gold, purified by cementing <note>original: "p̄cemezuz"; a process of heating gold with salts to remove impurities</note>. <margin>... <unclear>galy le roud</unclear> ...</margin> Take pure silver, purified by mercury, an equal weight of 1 ounce. Melt them together in a crucible. Then throw upon this silver drawn through a <unclear>camisium</unclear>, 2 ounces. Stir it a little with a stick so that they may be mixed more quickly and better. Then throw it into strong vinegar, and it will become like liquid lime. Then grind it on a marble slab with 2 ounces of alum <note>original: "alisar?"</note> and 2 ounces of live sulfur, and mix them well together by grinding strongly until it becomes a blackish powder. Put this into a glass flask well-luted with the "lute of wisdom" <note>a protective clay sealant used to prevent glass from shattering in the fire</note>; place this in a furnace and apply heat as if for sublimation. And when it has been sublimated like snow, you will bring forth those things which remain in the bottom, colored like gold. Take each one by itself and grind it on marble; place them in two glass flasks and stop the mouths well so they do not "breathe" <note>evaporate</note>. Place them to dissolve under horse dung for 3 weeks, renewing the dung at the end of every week. When these weeks are fulfilled, take the flasks out of the dung and you will find the substances sublimated so that they can be kneaded. From these you shall form small pills, like a vetch seed <note>original: "grannū orobi"</note>; and this will be the elixir for quicksilver, or upon the "body of Venus" <note>copper</note> as you know.

# To remove the cry from tin

If anyone wishes for Jupiter <note>original: "iupiter"; the alchemical name for tin</note> to lose its "cry" <note>Tin makes a crackling sound, called the "tin cry," when bent; alchemists sought to remove this to make it more like silver</note>: melt it and cast it into the juice of leeks three or four times; or in the juice of pomegranates, or strong unripe vinegar, and juice of henbane; and it will lose its cry.

# On the method of subliming arsenic

You shall sublime the best arsenic thus. Take as much shining red arsenic <note>original: "Arsenicū rurim sohantiū"; likely "rubrum" (red)</note> as you wish, and sublime the whole of it. Place it all in a glazed jar with 4 parts of its own strongest vinegar, in which common prepared salt has been dissolved for three days prior. Place it over a gentle fire so that it boils until all the vinegar

<column-break/>

is consumed and the arsenic remains at the bottom of the jar as if dried out. Then extract it from the jar and place it in a glazed dish <note>original: "parapsidem"</note> and wash it very well in clear water so that the saltiness departs. Then dry it in the sun, grind it, and place it in a glazed jar with 4 parts of its own alum water, and make it boil so that the arsenic is well dried. Then extract it from the jar and mix it with double its weight of prepared salt, and set it to sublime from morning until midday. Then allow it to cool and open the vessel; you will find it sublimated and clear like crystal. Take it, therefore, and grind it finely, and put it in a glass vial. Pour over it as much alum water as there is arsenic, and stop up the mouth of the vial well so it cannot breathe, and let it stand thus for 8 days. At last, you will find on the surface of the vial a clear water which, like curdled milk, is floating above the arsenic. Then collect that water and place it in a vial having a narrow and long neck, and fit it for coagulation. Then coagulate it over a very gentle fire upon warm ashes, and it will become a crystalline stone, which you should keep: for it is a useful material for silver <note>original: "lunam"</note>, as you know.

# How saffron of iron is made

You should make saffron of iron <note>original: "crocū ferri"; iron oxide, used as a pigment or alchemical reagent</note> thus. Take 2 lbs of steel filings; wash them from the dross
<margin>3 [ounces] of... saffron</margin>
<gloss>saffron</gloss>
with rainwater or clear, warm, sweet water, rubbing them strongly in your hands. Afterwards, dry them in the sun. Then place them in a glazed dish having a very wide bottom, and pour over them 4 lbs of the strongest red wine vinegar. Place the said dish in the strong sun for 8 [days].

# Another way to make saffron of iron

Another way to make <term>saffron of iron</term> is: Take 2 parts iron filings and one part <term>native sulfur</term> <note>original: "sulfuris vivi"; naturally occurring sulfur</note>. Let them be melted together with <term>oil of tartar</term> <note>original: "oleo tartari"; a solution of potassium carbonate</note>, and let a small cake be made, which you should cook over glowing coals, ensuring they do not touch it. Leave it there until the sulfur is separated from the filings, and this is called saffron of iron. From which, if you wish to extract the <term>oil</term>, take 1 part saffron and 2 parts sublimated <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>original: "salis armoniaci"; ammonium chloride</note>. Mix and sublimate well from the said saffron. Put this in a glass flask and place it under <term>manure</term> <note>original: "fimo"; alchemists used the steady, gentle heat of rotting horse manure as a low-temperature incubator</note> for six days. It will dissolve, and you will have the oil of iron.

# Method for reddening Roman vitriol

<term>Roman vitriol</term> <note>original: "vitriolum romanum"; usually copper sulfate or iron sulfate</note> is reddened thus: Take 2 lbs of Roman vitriol and dissolve it in <term>boy's urine</term> <note>urine was a common source of ammonia and phosphates in early chemistry</note> or red vinegar made from good wine. Let it boil until it dries out. Then close the vessel with <term>glass-maker's clay</term> <note>original: "luto vitreo"; a sealant for high heat</note> and place it in a potter’s furnace for half a day or more, and it will be well reddened.

### On the calcination of copper

<margin>Chapter 6, folio 2</margin>
<margin>copper is purified</margin>
The **c**alcination of copper <note>original: "eris"</note> is done in this way: make one layer of salt in a new pot; afterward, place plates of copper <term>cemented</term> <note>original: "cementataʐ"; covered or layered in a corrosive mixture</note> with all the said salt, as before. And afterward, a layer of salt; then the plates as was said; and so on until the top of the pot. Then <term>lute</term> <note>original: "luta"; to seal a vessel with a paste of clay and dung to make it airtight</note> the pot well and place it in the furnace for one day. Afterward, take it out and pulverize it; and wash it with <term>lye</term> <note>original: "capitello"; a caustic alkaline solution used for cleaning metals</note> many times, and calcine again, and grind, and wash. Afterward, reduce it into a body with <term>saltpeter</term> <note>original: "sale nitro"</note>. Afterward, [shape into] plates and calcine as before; and do this three times—calcinating, grinding, and washing—as was said above. And then you will see in your work how the copper is purified.

# The regimen and the substances from which the philosophers’ stone ought to be composed for the white and the red.

<margin>
Note that this work conforms to the opinion described by Raymond Lully <note>original: "V. lully," likely referring to the influential 13th-century polymath and alchemist</note> in [his work] on the wood <note>original: "super lagneū," possibly referring to a specific alchemical treatise like the *Lignum Vitae*</note>, but it does not seem to be exactly theirs, just as this opens or is something else.
</margin>

## On the dissolution of the Moon and the separation of earth from water.

Take 7 ounces <note>original: "℥," the symbol for ounce</note> of the most noble imperfect body, namely the Moon <note>symbolizing Silver</note>, and place it to dissolve in 15 ounces of the Water of Mercury <note>likely an alchemical solvent or purified quicksilver</note>. Afterward, place it to putrefy in horse dung <note>a natural source of gentle, constant heat</note> or a Maria bath <note>a water bath or bain-marie</note> for 30 days. When you see a blackness floating on top, remove it as carefully as you can. Continue this process, removing the blackness until no more appears and the Water of Mercury is clear and pure. Thus, by the grace of God, you will have two elements: namely, water and earth.

<margin>
On the dissolution of the Sun and the separation of earth from water.
</margin>

Do the same with 31 [parts] of the Sun <note>symbolizing Gold</note>. Mix the black earth separated from the Sun (as described above) with the earth of the Moon. Set the Water of the Sun aside until I tell you [otherwise].

## On the calcination of the earth of the Sun and Moon.

Place the earth of the Sun and Moon to be calcined <note>burned to a fine powder</note> in a very well-sealed vessel for 3 natural days; you will then have a white and bright earth.

<margin>
On the congealing of the earth with the water of the Sun and Moon.
</margin>

## On congealing the earth finely

Grind this earth finely <note>original: "subaliter"</note> and imbue it with the Water of Mercury that you extracted from the Moon—specifically, a fourth part of it. Place it to be cooked over a temperate fire, and the water will gradually combine with the earth. Continue this process of imbuing and drying until it has "drunk" all its water, such that it absorbs 4 weights of its water, and becomes white, bright, and fully impregnated. This is what Marienus says in the *Assembly of the Philosophers*.

<margin>
Marienus in the Turba <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>
</margin>

<column-break/>

"...unless you have cleansed the unclean body and rendered it whitened, and are also instructed by my method, you have directed nothing in this mastery."

## On the extraction of Air.

Take, therefore, with God’s blessing, the said white, bright, and impregnated earth. Place it in a glass gourd <note>a cucurbit</note> to be sublimated <note>heated until it turns to vapor and reforms</note> over a temperate fire until the moisture existing there ascends into the alembic <note>the lid of the distilling apparatus</note> in the manner of a white oil. This is called "Air." Increase the fire until everything is distilled and the earth remains in the bottom of the vessel, white and calcined; this is then called "Fire." Thus, by the grace of God, you will have Fire and Air, just as you previously had Earth and Water. In this way, you possess the four elements.

<margin>
On making Fire through separation.
</margin>

## Elixir for the white

Imbue the earth with its own Air, imbuing and drying until it has absorbed all of it; it will then be as fluid as wax and will be perfected for the white <note>The *albedo* stage, capable of transmuting metals into silver</note>.

## On composing the elixir for the red

Likewise, if you wish to work toward the red <note>The *rubedo* stage, the final perfection for making gold</note>, proceed in this manner: Take half of the white stone perfected as described above and imbue it with the Water of the Sun that you saved earlier. Place it to be cooked, and continue imbuing, grinding, and cooking until it has absorbed all its water.

## On the separation of the Air of the Sun from its earth

Once this is done, place it to be sublimated as you did with the Moon; then the Air of the Sun will ascend, very saffron-colored, and the matter will remain in the bottom of the vessel, very red. Imbue this in that Air and cook it, continuing until it has absorbed everything.

# On the Middle Cementation

Take salt of Sardinia <note>original: "sal Sardinie"; likely a high-quality sea salt used as a flux or purifying agent.</note>: make a layer four fingers thick. Afterward, take 4 parts of salt and 1 part of saltpeter <note>original: "salis nitri"; potassium nitrate.</note>. Pulverize and mix them. Take one part of **Gold** <note>original symbol: ☉ (Sol).</note> and **Mercury** <note>original symbol: ☿.</note>; melt and mix them. From this, make thin plates the thickness of a penny. Cement them with the aforementioned salts, layer upon layer, and finally place the salt on the bottom. Seal with clay <note>original: "luto"; "luting" is the process of sealing an alchemical vessel with an airtight clay paste.</note> and so on, and perform the cementation. Let it last for seven days <note>original: "7.o"; likely septem (seven) or the seventh stage.</note> or for as long as it takes, remaining for 12 hours, always renewing the salts. Afterward, trust [your work] and test it in the <term>testing cupel</term> <note>original: "brega"; a specialized vessel for assaying or refining metals.</note>. Use broad plates, which you should place for 6 hours in this **strong water** <note>original: "aqua forti"; nitric acid.</note>.

# On the Cement

Take 1 part Roman vitriol <note>original: "Vitrioli romani"; iron or copper sulfate.</note>, 1 part saltpeter, and 3 parts each of **Cinnabar** <note>original: "Cinabrij"; mercury sulfide.</note> and "Saracen" roof tiles <note>original: "tegular. farzacenoz"; likely red terracotta or clay pieces used to provide bulk and regulate heat.</note>. Distill these through an alembic. The tiles, however, must be fired. Heat them until they glow, and throw sulfur over them as you please.

<margin>Note: the best cinnabar 20</margin>
# The Roasting of Cinnabar and the Method of Making It

First, make **strong water** in the proper way as you have seen from me—namely, by distilling it in a two-part distillation so that the flame is entirely separated from the "good water" <note>pure acid</note>, and the good water will be excellently rectified.
<margin>On silver to be cupelled and amalgamated</margin> In this water, dissolve **Silver** <note>original symbol: ☽ (Luna).</note> from the cupel <note>a shallow porous bowl used in refining.</note> as you please. When it is dissolved, put enough **Mercury** (quicksilver) into that water until the silver is amalgamated with the quicksilver. Once the <term>amalgam</term> <note>A soft mixture of mercury and another metal.</note> is made, extract the water by pouring it off <note>decanting</note>. Take the amalgam remaining at the bottom and wash it repeatedly until the water comes out perfectly clear. Save all the waters in which you washed the amalgam, because the aforementioned silver is still located there in the strong water which you extracted by pouring it off.
<margin>To recover the silver</margin> To recover that silver from the strong water, add fresh water and distill it through an alembic; the silver remaining at the bottom can then be reduced to its [metallic] form, which is worth nearly as much as before. Take the amalgam washed in this way and dry it in the sun.

<image-desc>A small schematic line drawing of a conical alchemical vessel or furnace with a small chimney. Beneath it is written: 'earthly vessel where', 'cemented', and 'cinnabars'.</image-desc>

<column-break/>

Then place it in a wine-vessel over hot ashes and stir it with a small stick until it is perfectly dry. From this amalgam, make a very fine powder and reserve it <margin>To make cinnabar for that work</margin> for making the cinnabar for that work. After this, make cinnabar from one part sulfur and three parts **azure** <note>original: "azurij"; this may refer to lapis lazuli or a purified blue mineral used as a reagent.</note>. <margin>What and how it should be done with this cinnabar</margin> Then reduce the cinnabar into small fragments the size of a bean. Moisten these fragments in distilled vinegar and dry them in the sun. <margin>On the method of making the caustic lye</margin> Afterward, make a <term>capitellum</term> <note>A caustic alkaline solution or lye.</note> from soda and quicklime in equal parts. <margin>On things to be placed in the caustic lye</margin> From this lye, take 3 ounces and add to it 1 ounce of **oil of tartar** <note>potassium carbonate solution</note>, 1 ounce of **oil of sal ammoniac** <note>ammonium chloride solution</note>, and 1 ounce of distilled vinegar. <margin>On the weight of the lye</margin> And note: if the lye were one pound mixed with rust—that is, oil of tartar—then it would be considered good, but it is not necessary. <margin>On the moistening of the cinnabar</margin> In this mixture, moisten your fragments of cinnabar many times and dry them in the sun. Finally, regarding the boiling of the cinnabar: boil the said cinnabar in the aforementioned lye for the space of one hour over a slow fire. Then extract it and dry it in the sun. <margin>On making the layer and covering the cinnabar with the amalgam powders</margin> Afterward, moisten the aforesaid fragments in egg white—each one individually—and place the aforementioned powder from the amalgam over this cinnabar like salt, so that it is perfectly and uniformly covered. Create a "solar layer" <note>a base layer</note> of that same amalgam at the bottom of a potter's vessel. In the said vessel, arrange the cinnabar so that no fragment touches another, and then create another solar layer over the said cinnabar so that it is well covered by the said amalgam. <margin>On sealing and placing the vessel in the reverberatory furnace; on giving and increasing the fire and the brittleness of the matter</margin> Then let the vessel be perfectly sealed with clay <note>luted</note> and dried. Afterward, place the vessel in a <term>reverberatory furnace</term> <note>A furnace that reflects heat onto the substance being heated.</note> and provide a slow fire for 12 hours. Afterward, strengthen the fire for 6 hours until the vessel is red-hot. When this is done, allow it to cool and inspect your material. If it is brittle and has the **color of Mars** <note>original: "colore martis"; a deep reddish-orange or iron-red color.</note>, it is well. If not, return it to the fire as before until it happens, and the work will be done.

# Purification of Copper <note>original: "purgatio Veneris"; Venus is the alchemical name for copper.</note>

First, purge the <term>copper</term> <note>original: "Venerem"</note> according to the same custom. Afterward, <term>cement</term> <note>A process of heating a metal in contact with powdered reagents to change its properties.</note> those purged plates with powders of <term>orpiment</term> <note>original: "auripigmenti"; a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral used in alchemical whitening.</note> for 24 hours. Afterward, take this cemented copper and melt it in an unglazed pot; and pour over it the <term>regulus</term> powder <note>original: "puluerem regulax"; the metallic part of an ore that settles at the bottom during smelting.</note>, and let it sit for a while among the coals without melting; and afterward melt it again, and put over it a portion of the powder, and do as before. And do the same with <term>crushed glass</term> <note>original: "vitro pistato"</note> and with <term>tartar</term> <note>original: "tartaro"; a potassium salt used as a flux in melting metals.</note>. Afterward, transfer this matter in portions, according to that method which I taught in the <term>fixation</term> of <term>cinnabar</term> <note>original: "cinabrij"; mercury sulfide.</note>; and thus it will be excellently purged. From this, take eight parts and project over it one part of the aforesaid medicine, and you will have a perfect mass.

# Sophistic Copper for Silver <note>original: "Coprimū sophisticū ad lunā"; "Sophistic" copper refers to copper treated to look like a precious metal. "Luna" refers to silver.</note>

First, take eggshells in a large quantity; and remove the little skins; once these are removed, grind the shells in a mortar, and place them in a crucible to be melted with a very strong fire, so much so that they turn white. Take that which is best whitened and keep it.

Next, take one part of <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>original: "salis ar."; ammonium chloride.</note>, one part of the salt of eggshells, and one part of <term>sublimate</term> <note>original: "sublimati"; likely mercury sublimate.</note>; and let all be ground into a fine powder and incorporated. This sublimation ought to be repeated three times, always joining the sublimate with its dregs. On the last time, the matter will remain liquid at the bottom, like honey.

From this oil, take 2 parts and place it in some glass vessel over hot ashes, so that it boils. After it begins to boil, take 1 part of <term>crystalline arsenic</term> <note>original: "arcenici cristallini"; white arsenic used to whiten copper to make it look like silver.</note> in a very fine powder and cast it in little by little, so that the aforesaid arsenic is dissolved in the oil. Once it is red-hot, apply the melting heat, and afterward put a little powdered <term>tartar</term> <note>original: "tartaro"; potassium bitartrate, often used as a flux to help metals melt and purify.</note> into the crucible and melt everything together; and then pour it into the ingot mold. You can bind this copper [to silver]... and you will have <term>silver</term> <note>original: "luna[m]"; literally "the Moon," the alchemical name for silver.</note> which comes out white from the fire.

# Purification of Copper <note>original: "purgatio Veneris"; Venus is the alchemical name for copper.</note>

Copper is purified in this way: let copper be <term>cemented</term> with salt and tartar in equal weights, and let it be washed with vinegar distilled three times and once with water of alum.

# For the Solidification of Mercury

Take the herb called <term>monkshood</term> <note>original: "Napellus"; Aconitum napellus, a highly toxic plant often used in alchemical experiments for its supposed "constricting" properties.</note> and extract the juice from it; place <term>mercury</term> <note>original: "argentu[m] vivu[m]"; literally "living silver."</note> in this juice and heat it over a slow fire, and the mercury will be solidified.

# A Most Wondrous Dissolving Water

<margin>folio 76. Note the above among other gold-making works.</margin>
[Which dissolves] all metallic bodies and precious stones without damaging them, and extracts mercury from bodies, and works many wonders.

First make <term>aqua vitae</term> <note>original: "aquam vite"; literally "water of life," usually refers to concentrated ethanol or brandy.</note> from a very strong dark wine, distilled at least seven times by distillation alone; and keep it very well in a strong glass vessel, well-sealed. But when you have extracted the proper <margin>so that you make the <unclear>purification</unclear> of the vessel</margin> water from the wine, put the residue to dry in a leaden or glazed glass vessel so that the moisture recedes and the earthiness remains. Let it boil gradually until the water vanishes and the earthiness remains at the bottom, which you must <term>calcine</term> <note>To heat a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or oxide.</note> in a reverberatory furnace until it is as white as snow. Then dissolve it in warm fresh water and solidify it over a slow fire, and you will have the true <term>salt of wine</term>.

And take half a pound of it and put it, hot as it comes from the fire, into the aforesaid water (taking one pound of the said *aqua vitae*); and let it stand for a day, and afterward distill it, and you will have a rectified water. You can do the same with salt of tartar. And note that this is a great secret among <term>philosophers</term> <note>original: "phos"; shorthand for "philosophos," the term alchemists used for themselves.</note>, because it is the true water that dissolves all bodies and even pearls and other precious stones without damage, and it extracts mercury from bodies and works many wonders.
