## A Very Good and True Medicine for Whitening upon Purified Copper <note>original: "ad Albu(m) sup(er) venere purgatu(m)"; 'The White' refers to the alchemical process of silvering, while 'Venus' is the alchemical name for copper.</note>

<margin>Royal entry</margin>
**Recipe** tartar <note>Potassium bitartrate, a salty crust found in wine barrels, used here as a flux and purifying agent.</note> calcined very well, as white as snow: and dissolve it in fresh water. Once dissolved, congeal it over a slow fire. Take 2 pounds of this congealed substance. Of white crystalline arsenic, take 1 pound. Grind everything together very finely. Afterward, dissolve it again in lukewarm fresh water as you did before with the tartar, until it is dissolved. Then congeal it again over a very gentle fire as before. Likewise, grind it very well: and put all of it into a glass vial to dissolve under dung <note>original: "sub fimo"; alchemists buried vessels in piles of fermenting horse manure to provide a constant, gentle, "natural" heat for weeks or months.</note>. Once dissolved, remove it from the dung, and you will have a perfect oil, which is called the oil of arsenic.

Afterward **Recipe** 2 pounds of sublimated arsenic and 2 pounds of <term>azure</term> <note>original: "azurru(m)"; likely blue vitriol (copper sulfate) or a specific blue mineral pigment used in the process.</note>. Grind them very finely and well together upon a <term>porphyry</term> <note>A hard igneous rock slab used for grinding substances into fine powders.</note>. Moisten or soak it many times with the oil described above, soaking and drying it very often until they have absorbed their weight of the aforesaid arsenic and azure, in the sun or over a slow fire.

Likewise, afterward **Recipe** 2 pounds of Roman vitriol and 1 pound of saltpeter, which you should take without separation; and make <term>sharp water</term> <note>original: "aquam acutam"; an early name for a mineral acid, likely nitric acid, capable of dissolving metals.</note>. Afterward **Recipe** 1 pound of <term>silver leaf</term> <note>original: "lune foliate"</note> and dissolve it in 2 pounds of the aforesaid water in hot ashes, as you know how to do. Afterward take the reserved arsenic and azure and dissolve them in 4 pounds of the aforesaid sharp water, just as you did with the silver. Place everything together with the aforesaid silver, mixing it well and gently so that it combines, in a glass vessel; and place it over ashes and distill all the water. Collect the water and distill it again; and proceed in this way until no more can be distilled, but it remains at the bottom like an oil. And if it happens to be not like an oil, but like a stone, take it and grind it

<column-break/>

upon the porphyry; and repeat the process again in sharp water until it is like a paste. And in this way it does not happen unless it has an <term>entry</term> <note>original: "ingressum"; a technical alchemical term for a substance's ability to penetrate and merge with another substance.</note> for dissolving under dung or in a <term>Bain-Marie</term> <note>A water bath used to provide gentle, even heat.</note>. Once dissolved, congeal it in the sun or over a gentle fire in ashes.

And note that the more often you dissolve and congeal it until it can no longer be congealed, its perfection will increase. From this congealed substance, cast it upon purified copper <note>original: "venere purgatu(m)"</note> as stated above. Experience will teach you how many weights are needed, because sometimes it works upon a larger quantity and sometimes upon a smaller, according to how well one is experienced in the operation.

## Medicine discovered in a most beautiful book for converting silver into true Gold <note>The symbol ☉ represents 'Sol,' the alchemical name for Gold.</note>

There was once a <term>metalworker</term> <note>original: "erarius"; a smith working with copper or brass.</note> living in his workshop in the land of the Moors. A certain Moor gave him twenty silver coins, asking him to melt them in the fire. Once melted, the metalworker threw in green powders, which made a <unclear>dense</unclear> smoke in the fire; and the melted <term>silver</term> <note>original: "luna"</note> was turned into <term>gold</term> <note>original: "solem"</note>. The metalworker sold that gold to the goldsmiths at a very high price; and the goldsmiths found it to be of the highest quality. Then the metalworker gave the gold to the poor Moor. This happened to the metalworker many times with the same Moor. Finally, the Moor, moved by mercy toward the metalworker, told him the recipe for this powder.

1 part of <term>saffron of iron</term> <note>original: "croci ferri"; iron oxide or rust.</note> and 1 part of <term>burnt copper</term> <note>original: "cris vsti" (aes ustum); copper that has been oxidized by heating.</note>.

# Also How Gold <note>The ☉ symbol represents Sol (Gold).</note> Should Be Calcined and Powdered

**In this** manner we must powderize gold: Let lead be melted in a vessel that has a small vent or hole at the top, about the size of a gold coin. Place the gold over it so that it receives the fumes of the melted lead. Afterward, turn it so that it receives the lead fumes from the other side. When this has been done several times, the gold can be ground and reduced to a powder.

# How Saffron of Iron Should Be Made

<margin>see above on leaf <unclear>n</unclear> [...] above on leaf <unclear>b</unclear> another [...]</margin> **Saffron of iron** <note>original: "Crocus ferri"; a term for iron oxide (rust) used as a pigment or alchemical reagent.</note> is made thus: Take iron filings and let them be soaked in strong, clear red vinegar. Place them in the hot sun for two or three days. Afterward, pour off the vinegar and let it sit(?). Add other fresh vinegar and let the filings sit in the sun until all the filings are dissolved and reduced to a very fine powder. Again, let all the vinegar with the filings be dried in the sun. Before it is mixed with anything else, it must be washed with pure water, or with water and salt, until the water comes away clear. I saw that preparation <note>original: "erazium"; likely referring to a specific metallic preparation or "bronze-work."</note> of Taletus, and he related these same things to me—he told them to a certain relative of his, and he [worked] with that same preparation

<column-break/>

at Taletus's place. But regarding the aforementioned method of iron slag <note>original: "scoro ferri"</note>: and behold, they used "burnt copper" <note>original: "vstrum" (aes ustum); chemically copper(II) oxide, used to color glass or metals.</note> without adding gold, and finally they placed it upon silver melted in the fire, and that silver took on the color of gold on the outside, though not on the inside. It is well known that whoever works with these materials needs a greater degree of dissolution and sublimation so that the substance can penetrate the metal. This is the method of sublimating:

**Take** 1 ounce of sulfur of tartar <note>A preparation of cream of tartar, often used as a flux.</note> and 2 ounces of salt. Grind them and place them in a good glass vessel. Do not fill the <term>cucurbit</term> <note>The lower, gourd-shaped part of a still used for boiling liquids.</note> even halfway, but less than half. The first water burns; the second, however, does not, but is a medicine against "cold" ailments of the arteries <note>original: "arteniam frigide cause"; likely referring to joint pain or circulatory issues thought to be caused by an excess of the "cold" humor.</note>.

# To Make Sal Ammoniac

# For converting into the best gold from base material.

Take hens and put them in captivity: so that they are able to eat nothing but this legume: namely, lentils. Then take a small bowl that has been very well-crafted: and place fifteen of their eggs inside it. Leave them until they have become potent <note>original: "vertuose"; implying the eggs have absorbed the "virtue" or essence of the lentils and the hen's restricted diet.</note>. Afterward, take them and place them in a secret place: and allow them to stand there until they are all reduced into one mass. Then take this and place it in a furnace: and allow it to burn with sufficient heat. From that very powder, you will make the best gold <note>original: "solem"; literally "the sun," the standard alchemical symbol for gold.</note> if you have worked wisely.

# For making gold.

Take one ounce of pulverized matter; one ounce of the powder of grey tutty <term>tutia: zinc oxide collected from the flues of smelting furnaces</term>; one ounce of Egyptian vitriol <term>vitriolum: a sulfate mineral, likely copper or iron sulfate</term>; and one and a half ounces of the roots of *brustomi* <note>original: "brustomi"; possibly butcher's broom or a specific plant used for its carbon content</note> that have been washed, burned, and reduced to powder. But first, let a layer of *brustomi* charcoal be placed in the bottom of the vessel, and afterward the aforementioned powders; and then layer them with the powder in order; and let this be done for the sake of gold.

# For reducing gold or lead into powder

The method for reducing gold or lead <note>original: "saturnum"; Saturn is the alchemical name for lead.</note> into powder, namely: when it has been melted, let vinegar and [reagent] <note>original: "azet aūg"; likely vinegar and alum or mercury (argentum vivum). These were used to quench or amalgamate metals into a brittle state.</note> be mixed together with it until it cools down.

Tortoise blood is excellent for gold:
Similarly, golden marcasite <term>marchestia: iron pyrites, known as "fool's gold" due to its metallic luster</term> is excellent.

<column-break/>

# For creating the color of good Lupine gold

Human blood is useful for gold: If it came from a red-haired man, it converts from red to black, and from white to red. <note>In medieval alchemy, the blood of red-haired men was believed to possess unique transformative "sulfurous" properties.</note>

Fresh tortoise blood gives or increases weight: and it makes the metal "savory" <note>original: "sapozare"; referring to the alchemical "taste" or essential quality of a substance.</note> and clear; it acts just as if the metal had been dissolved with harsh substances, or those that produce harshness.

# For making 22-carat gold

Take one Venetian or Florentine ducat <note>High-purity gold coins used as a starting material.</note>: and an equal weight of purified silver; and melt them together in a crucible. Once melted, take as much powdered verdigris <term>viridis eris: "green of copper," a green pigment formed by the action of vinegar on copper</term> as you can pick up with three fingers and throw it into the crucible and mix well. Then, pour the melted metal into an iron mold, and afterward wash your metal rod in urine. Then melt it again, throwing in more verdigris, mixing it, pouring it into the mold, and washing it with urine. Perform this process six or seven times. Finally, smear that golden rod with cinnabar <term>cinabrio: mercury sulfide, a bright red mineral</term> diluted with urine, and then melt it one last time. Form your rod from it, and it will be twenty-two carat gold.

# **For making silver from iron**

### The Preparation of the Amalgam
**T**ake 1 ounce of mercury and put it in a glazed bowl that is warm; and pour this strained liquid over it: testing it and drawing it out with a rod until it moves; and so that you can catch it in your hand. And to this vessel <term>azerario: likely a specialized alchemical vessel or a crucible for 'azarium'</term> you shall add 5 silver coins <note>original: "denarios argenteos"</note> of *falto* <note>possibly referring to a specific alloy or mint</note>. And sitting over the fire, you will see a pale color. Immediately then, remove it from the fire and cool it; then strike it hard with a hammer; and the outer crust will be removed; and you will find a good work.

### The Preparation of Sulfur
**T**ake sulfur and put it in a pot with strong vinegar; and also put into it a little tartar; and let it boil strongly over the fire. And when you see that a third part has cooked away, remove the pot; and wash the sulfur well with fresh water. And grind it well upon a stone <note>original: "zalmā"; likely a grinding slab</note>. Then take a flat-bottomed vessel <term>albotum: a flat-bottomed alchemical dish or crucible</term> that is very level on the bottom and not deep; and spread parchment on the bottom; and upon it make one layer of these powders and add silver. And so, up to the top, you should cover the vessel.

Beware of this, however: that the silver be well thinned <note>beaten into thin leaves</note> and washed in water of alum and salt; and let it be washed three times. And on the fourth time, let it be put in the vessel <term>azerario</term>. Finally, let it be put in the flat vessel <term>albotō</term>, as is written above. And apply a great fire night and day continuously for up to 5 days. After this, look: if you find it white [it is ready]; but if it is red, apply fire until you find it white. Thus let this be the fixation <term>attachz: likely 'attachia,' the fixing or stabilizing of a volatile substance</term> of the Moon <note>The Moon (Luna) is the alchemical symbol for silver.</note>. And let it be the same for the Sun <note>The Sun (Sol) is the alchemical symbol for gold.</note>; but that one you must afterward wash in vinegar.

### The Refinement of the Fixation
**T**ake the fixation of the Moon and grind it much upon marble with roasted salt. After this, wash it with much water until all the salt leaves, and the water is hard and clear. After this, put it in a glazed earthen pot over a gentle fire. When it has become hot, pour blessed water <note>original: "aquam bndicam"; while literally 'holy water,' in alchemy this often refers to a purified solvent or distilled mercury water</note> over it, stirring it constantly over the top with the same; and when it has been absorbed, let an amalgam be made. Cook it in oil in an "egg" <note>an alchemical egg, or 'ovum philosophicum,' a sealed glass vessel used for long heating</note> until it becomes dense. After this, grind it on marble with vinegar that has been roasted by fire and tempered in cold water; after this, wash it in iron-water <note>water in which hot iron has been quenched</note> until the oil leaves. Then put this in well-prepared salt, arsenic, and sal ammoniac; and grind it much. After this, wash with clear fresh water until the salty taste recedes, and let it dry; and return it to the fire. But when it has been heated, add to it <insert>some</insert> good water as before; and when it has become an amalgam, again...

### There follow the petitions and responses made by Agadmus the philosopher to the Holy Spirit regarding the philosopher's stone

<margin>Note the fruit of this [work]</margin>

> **Tell** me, you Spirit: can a stone be made which, from its own stone-like nature, transforms all metals into gold or silver: looking toward the judgment of all kinds?
> **Spirit.** In gold, all metals are in essence in their earth of various colors: and from this essence the stone is made from its own nature; removing the superfluous and supplying the diminished at one and the same time; when projected upon metals, it makes this proportion perpetual.
> **Philosopher.** What is this essence of gold?
> **Spirit.** It is the soul mediating through nature, that is, <unclear>assigning</unclear> <note>original: "segnante"; possibly "signante" (marking/assigning) or "segregante" (separating)</note>, which does not permit one species to be changed into another.
> **Philosopher.** By what means does the soul work through nature?
> **Spirit.** Neither angels, men, nor the abyss, because of its intrinsic subtlety, can see nor perceive it: God has retained this for Himself: and all other things He has granted according to its species.
> **Philosopher.** Can a man compose this stone?
> **Spirit.** All things that God created by abundance, that work abounds in man: But it is very difficult for a man to compose this stone.

**The Philosopher.** Does the soul, through a medium, possess any body?
**The Spirit.** The color of gold is a body through a medium, for—
**The Philosopher.** It is one thing for the color to be separated from the gold.
**The Spirit.** A middle nature <note>original: "media natura"; a central concept in alchemy referring to a substance or force that bridges the spiritual and material worlds</note> in its heat and moisture separates and joins in various ways.
**The Philosopher.** The color of gold is white or black, or of whatever color it may be. <gloss>Yellow</gloss>
**The Spirit.** It is white to human sight, the golden spirit.
**The Philosopher.** Of what kind is that color, or from what is it generated?
**The Spirit.** Nature generates it from pure earth and pure water. And work as if the water might be of benefit: while it remains longer in the fire, it is made more complete and more beautiful.
**The Philosopher.** Is this color in every metal?
**The Spirit.** No, not only in metals, but in every fire, earth, water, and air that color is hidden.
**The Philosopher.** What power does this so-potent stone possess?
**The Spirit.** It heals all metallic and human bodies from all leprosy <note>original: "leprositate"; in alchemy, "leprosy" refers to the impurities, corrosion, or "sickness" of base metals that prevents them from being gold</note>. It heals metals even until the fire of eternal judgment. <margin>÷</margin> It heals humans even until natural death; by whatever quantity of medicine [is taken] from it, they shall suffer no infirmity except for natural death itself. And their generation is most strong; it shall be terrible among others who work more.
**The Philosopher.** The quest is, <gloss>as you have heard</gloss>, other things of the human body.
**The Spirit.** It is the pure fire of heavenly life.
**The Philosopher.** Does this pure fire of heavenly life have within itself a middle nature?
**The Spirit.** Because of this middle nature, he is called God, the creator of all, since those things are in himself; if he were to possess the middle nature, he would have the power to create a new heaven, earth, sea, and all things that are in them. And all things would obey him. He would speak, and they would be made; he would command, and they would be given. For the middle things are the emperor and the way of nature.
**The Philosopher.** Did Virgil <note>The Roman poet Virgil was often reimagined in the Middle Ages as a powerful magician or alchemist</note> possess this stone?
**The Spirit.** Not he alone: but many philosophers have held this stone; and they wrote about it by many names, hiding its [true] name.
**The Philosopher.** By what name is this stone called?

<column-break/>

**The Spirit.** In this, I [show] two stones to you: no more gold is to be given to me from above.
**The Philosopher.** Within what time can this stone be made?
**The Spirit.** Twelve months are necessary from the first day of the beginning: for thirty days the nature of the earth is generated by Saturn <note>Saturn corresponds to lead and the "blackening" stage of the work</note> within. After a hundred days, the water is to be generated. When sixty days are completed, the air is generated by Jupiter <note>Jupiter corresponds to tin and a transitional stage</note>. In the remaining days, the fire is dominated by the Sun <note>The Sun corresponds to gold and the final "reddening" stage</note>. At the end of the present year, the middle nature descends from heaven into this earth: and between the "let it be done" of the superior and inferior virtues, the fire will conquer man and confirm his region in the heart of his belly: even until the generation of the fire of eternal judgment, and no more. <margin>÷</margin>

# On the composition of the philosophers' stone

**Y**ou should know that the first body is lead, which by another name is interpreted as *azozop* <note>original: "azozop"; likely a variant of Azoth, a term for the "universal solvent" or the essential mercury of the philosophers</note>.
**T**he clean body, however, is tin, which is called by another name *aleuet*.
**T**he "Short Lion" is *biten* <note>original: "Leo brevis est biten"; alchemical manuscripts often used animal names to hide the identity of reactive chemicals</note>.
**A**lmaga is *Laton* <note>original: "Laton"; a copper-based alloy often representing a metal in an intermediate state of purification</note>: whence it was said above to be "red earth."
**B**lood is that of orpiment <note>orpiment: a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral used as a pigment and in chemical experiments</note>.
**T**he "cleaved earth" is split sulfur.
**T**o be sown among all these is the secret which, namely, is called by another name *mescha fuma*; which in Latin is called the dross of glass, or rather, its impurity.
**T**hey call the "good red smoke" red orpiment.
There are also there <gloss>two</gloss> kinds, namely, arsenic and the red.
**A**lso, the white smoke is *az. vi.* <note>original: "az. vi."; shorthand for "argentum vivum" or mercury/quicksilver</note>.
**T**he "nitric smoke" is native sulfur <note>original: "sulfur vivum"; literally "living sulfur," meaning sulfur found naturally in its pure, elemental state</note>.
**I** have also set forth for you new species, of which it is proper for you that they suffice for the whole Work. Likewise <margin>~~white~~</margin> <gloss>white</gloss> white smoke, the "Short Lion," and stinking water <note>original: "aqua fetida"; likely a reference to a corrosive acid or a sulfurous solution</note>.
**T**herefore, these three species and their infection <note>original: "infethionem"; likely meaning the "dyeing" or "tincturing" process where the metal changes color</note> you should tell or teach to no one. But keep this mastery regarding all other things: that you extract them until the Sun and Moon <note>Sun and Moon: symbolic code for gold and silver</note> are reduced into one body, which cannot happen before God's command.
**H**owever, some estimate that the secret of this mastery is earth, or egg, or blood, or urine, or vinegar; and all these things are deceptive by themselves (that is, they fail). And they extract from their boiling <note>original: "decoctione"; the process of heating a substance in a liquid to extract its essence</note> and bury the extract, which they foolishly believe according to their own opinion, so that their error might be strengthened, and

<column-break/>

nor should they despair of that which they believe they will find. But I know that earth and stones and all such things are useless to the masters of these things and lead to a bad end. It is fitting that you know this: that the greatest workshops of this Work proceed in their own fire. For they are adjusted in the least ways, and are poorly held by the air in their bodies. The fire and the whole truth and perfect proof of this matter shall be whatever you have completed for this mastery. If the truth does not appear at the beginning of the undertaking, it is useless. For how can the good be separated unless the thing itself is dissolved, nor should it mix itself with the unclean. Namely, so that they are reduced into one body. But if, according to what we have said <gloss>thus in the treatises</gloss>, they are reduced to a good <gloss>treatise</gloss>, by the help of your divinity your intention shall be fulfilled.
**T**herefore, what we have already said, you must understand well; and once understood, commit it well to memory. Prepare those things according to their order, and study frequently in their preparation. For frequent study of it will show you its truer way.
**S**imilarly, know that the great root of this Work is in the investigation of the things or species that are better, and of these masters. For every mineral is of many kinds. Also, regarding the smoke about which you inquired, we want you to know that the white smoke is in *dtuza* <note>reading unclear; likely a technical term for a specific vessel or refined substance</note>, and all

### On the philosopher’s stone

<image-desc>A simple line drawing of a human profile (head and neck) is sketched in the left margin, facing the opening paragraph.</image-desc>

Our blessed stone <note>The "stone" is the goal of alchemy, a substance capable of perfecting matter</note> is a revealed matter, just as Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> said: "True, without falsehood, not merely certain, but most certain." <note>original: "verum sine menda non certum certissimum"; this is a famous quote from the Emerald Tablet of Hermes</note>

Sublime the subtle from the dense gently and with great skill; let it ascend from the earth into heaven, and again descend into the earth, until it has been well rectified. From the hidden white stones, take up what you wish while they are fresh; join them subtly and move them into a glazed vessel without any other thing. There, let it be left to ferment for a day and a night, and then place it in horse manure <note>original: "fimo equi"; decomposing manure was used as a consistent, low-heat source for incubation</note> in a glass vessel, well-sealed so that it does not breathe. Let it be left for burial <note>term: inhumandum (inhumation); the process of placing a vessel in a warm medium like manure or sand</note> for three weeks. The manure should be renewed every single week.

<margin>3 weeks, changing the manure</margin>

And when the number is complete: let half a pound of the stone be placed in an aludel <note>term: aludel; a pear-shaped pottery vessel used in sublimation</note> with two receivers, sealing them well with the master’s lute <note>term: luto magisterij; a specialized clay or paste used to seal laboratory apparatus airtight</note>. Let it be luted over a prepared brick with its vessels, and let water and ash be used in moderate measure. This should be done at the beginning with a slow fire for two hours at your pleasure; afterward, increase the fire gradually until its white water distills. This water is called by the philosophers "sal ammoniac," "quicksilver," "virgin’s milk," "water of life," "penetrating water," "the seeder," and "the illuminator of houses"—for if you light candles there, all darkness is put to flight from the house in which it was rectified until the end. For its entire substance is in the water, the oil of fire, and the calcined earth. It shall be made manifest. Likewise, you shall bury it in the following way for a week, and distill it as was said before; and this shall be done three times after the first burial: burying and

<column-break/>

distilling. This being done, let it be distilled only in a vessel in ashes three times. Afterward, keep it for your work in a glass vessel well-sealed. For the earth remains. After the water has been distilled, let it be tested somewhat on copper in the fire, after the manner of mixtures, in water three times; and if it is seen to be whitened inside and out, it is well. If not, return it to the first work until it becomes so. In a similar way, it is necessary that it be rectified, for its oil is from its humidity, so that it becomes white; and in the testing of it, it is taken so that it may be whitened in it. Afterward, reserve it for your work in a glass vessel well-covered, as was said above regarding the water of life. The fire will truly remain in the bottom of the vessel, <unclear>slarg</unclear> and black: which you shall set aside separately in a closed vessel. When these things are finished, you shall purge the exterior of the stone from its film, and in a glazed or unglazed earthen base, protected on all sides with clay and with a diligent, well-rubbed earthen cover in which three holes have been made, leave it in a potter’s kiln for four days so that it may take on an exceeding whiteness. One part of this, with 6 parts of the rectified water of life, should fill a glass vessel up to two-thirds; place an alembic <note>term: alembic; a distilling apparatus consisting of a gourd-like container and a cap with a beak</note> on top with its receiver, the joints closed with the master’s lute so that it does not breathe. Place it in an earthen vessel stained with manure. Then let it be placed in another vessel in water, and apply a slow fire for a whole week, or until no water is distilled from it. Permit it to cool day and night, and you will find in the bottom of the vessel a crystalline plate; return to it its water which

# On the white elixir
## This is the composition of the truest elixir for the white work <note>The "white work" or albedo is the second major stage in the alchemical process, aimed at the creation of silver.</note>

¶ Take, therefore, with the help of God, half a pound <note>original: "lib. .s."; libra semis</note> of prepared white quicksilver <note>term: quicksilver (argentum vivum); often abbreviated as 'az.' or 'ar.' in this manuscript</note> and dissolve it with double its weight of prepared white salt ammoniac water. Dissolve and distill it through an alembic <note>term: alembic; a distillation apparatus consisting of a gourd-shaped vessel and a cooling cap</note> and saturate <note>original: "imbibe"</note> with it one pound of white sublimated calcined quicksilver. Again, dissolve and distill, and saturate with it one pound of white sublimated and calcined quicksilver, taking 3 ounces <note>The symbol "3" represents an ounce (uncia)</note> of each. Repeat this dissolution and distillation three or seven times, for that is the final stage. Then coagulate it into a stone and grind it. While sprinkling it, saturate it with 3 ounces of the aforementioned philosophical oil <note>original: "oleo phico"</note> and cause it to descend onto a metal plate.

And when it has descended, make a light fire under it for two days and nights; then a moderate fire for another two days and nights; and make the strongest fire for one day and night. Then let it cool and break the crystalline plate which you will find at the bottom. Take one drachm <note>original: "dragma"</note> of it and place it in a thin gourd <note>original: "cucurbita"; a glass flask</note> over a charcoal fire. Drop the white philosophical oil onto it, drop by drop, until it melts like wax without smoke. This is certain. If it does not, return it to the gourd over the coals, dropping it drop by drop until it happens. Then test it: and project 1 ounce of it onto 3 pounds of separated silver; it will become the best silver <note>original: "luna optima"</note> by God’s help and His power. And this makes the medicine from its own species: project 1 ounce of it onto 40 ounces of prepared silver, and it will become the best gold <note>original: "sol optimus"</note> by the power of God.

<column-break/>

# On composing the elixir
## This is the method for composing the elixir

Take half a pound of separated silver filings and half a pound of quicksilver separated once and rectified with quicklime. Sift <note>original: "criba"</note> it with the aforementioned filings in a stone mortar and grind them together strongly until the quicksilver drinks up the filings and becomes like butter, so that you find no trace of the filings left. Wash it strongly with vinegar and salt (unless already separated) until the vinegar comes out pure and clear. Then wash away the salt with clear fresh water and allow it to dry.

When it is dry, add to it arsenic and white sublimated and calcined sulfur, 3 ounces of each, and grind them as if into one body. Then wax <note>term: incera (ceration); a process of softening a substance to a wax-like consistency by adding liquids</note> it with 6 ounces of dissolved and rectified sublimated salt ammoniac. Put this into an aludel <note>term: aludel; a pottery vessel used for sublimation</note> with an alembic placed above and its receiver, sealing it with the lute of wisdom <note>term: luto sapientie; a specialized sealing clay used to make laboratory equipment airtight</note>. Place it over the heat and make a light fire under it until all moisture is dried out. Then strengthen the fire under it until it sublimates <note>term: sublimation; the process where a solid turns into a gas and reforms as a solid at the top of the vessel</note> and let it cool.

Then extract it, and take that which was raised to the top and return it onto its dregs <note>original: "feces"</note>. Grind it and return its water to it by grinding and saturation. Then return it to the aludel to be sublimated in the same manner, and do this until nothing less sublimates <note>meaning everything in the vessel has been transformed and rises as vapor</note>, always returning its water over it until nothing more distills from it. Afterward, place it in the vessel <note>original: "ozina"; likely a specific type of furnace or container</note> as has been described. Then project 1 ounce of it onto 34 ounces of prepared copper <note>original: "enis"; likely aeris/copper</note> and it will become good Silver. And if it has been properly prepared...

## Concerning the elixir for white.

# The Distillation
<note>original: "Declixitio," a medieval variant of "elixatio" or "distillatio"</note>

Here begins the method for composing the elixirs <note>original: "phoꝝ," likely an abbreviation for "philosophorum" or "pharmacon"</note> from the aforementioned species. Therefore, with God’s help, take one pound of hematite <note>iron ore</note>, one drachma of prepared water, and one ounce of oil. Also take prepared and calcined <note>reduced to powder by heat</note> [material], one pound; mix it in salt water that has been prepared and rectified. Take one pound of this, filter it, and roast it with a light roasting; then grind it finely. Put it into an aludel <note>a pear-shaped subliming pot</note> with a distilling head <note>alembic</note> and a receiver. Seal the joints with clay <note>luting</note> and place it over a heat for sublimation. Watch for a light fire, until all the moisture settles in the receiver and is returned by the alembic. Then increase the fire gradually for two days and two nights, until one part of the middle adheres to the sides of the vessel and the other is fixed at the bottom. Let it cool and break the vessel. Turn that which ascended above onto that which remained at the bottom, strongly returning to it its own water which had returned from the alembic into the receiver. Roast it with a moderate roasting. Then grind it again and return it to be sublimated in the aforementioned manner. Repeat the sublimation, grinding, and roasting upon it, always increasing the roasting until nothing more sublimates from it. Then grind it and soak it with a third-part soaking of one drachma of philosophical oil <note>a specialized alchemical solvent</note>. Let it descend into the vessel <note>original: "butazū," a flask or vessel</note>. Watch over it with a light fire until it is well heated. Then make a strong fire day and night.

# Concerning the elixir: 1 ounce tints 40 bizants <note>term: bisantios. Gold coins of the Byzantine Empire, used here as a measure of weight or value.</note>

Elixir of Mercury <note>symbol: ☿</note>. Take 1 ounce of Mercury congealed with yellow *azarcafita* <note>term: azarcafita. Likely a variant of "asarcot" or a vitriol/sulfur compound.</note>: and an equal amount of *atramentum* <note>term: atramentum. A term for black liquids, vitriol, or ink-making minerals.</note>: and as much as there is of *atramentum*, take the same of [the secret substance], and as much as there is of that, take the same of [the other]. Grind all of this with water made from oak ashes that has sat in water for 4 hours: so that it may be dissolved. Afterwards, roast the whole with a slow roasting: and thus grind: and roast it 24 times. Do not soak it in water except for the first time. Then sublime it in an aludel 3 times: and it will come out red. And if it comes out white, soak it with the water in which the *atramentum* and lime <note>calcinam</note> were dissolved. And let there be of each as much as 4 parts of the water. Roast it until it becomes red like a liver: soak it and roast it. Test it upon a plate to see if it dissolves. Immediately afterwards, dissolve and soak with it the "certain Mercury" mentioned in chapter 102. Place it in dung <note>A common alchemical method for providing gentle, steady heat for fermentation.</note>: and it will be dissolved into red water. Afterwards congeal it, and it will be congealed into a mass. 1 ounce of this tints 40 gold bizants.

# Concerning the elixir for the Red

Elixir for the Red. Take 3 parts of Mercury <note>symbol: ☿</note> and ten drachms of Gold <note>symbol: ☉</note>. Make an amalgam <insert>upon the stone</insert> and wash it with rock salt and with water. Sublime it as many times as necessary until the Gold is fixed with the Mercury. Afterwards, soak it with Red Salt <note>symbol: 🜔</note> to rubrify <note>turn red</note> and fix it. And of this mixture, put one weight upon 10 weights of Gold.

Place the stone in a secret place and tilt it slightly to one side. Place a glass vial beneath it so that whatever is dissolved may fall into it. And always, from day to day, grind it at least once, until no more of that liquid substance <note>original: "aqua" (water), here referring to the dissolved matter</note> comes out of it. Take that liquid and put it with the powders that are on the stone, grinding and soaking them in the sun until all that liquid is absorbed and is no longer with you. After it has been soaked in this way, place it in another vial as was described for six days, making a fire above it with coals day and night. When those days have passed, break the vial, and you will find a stone as hard as iron. Pulverize this in a mortar, then grind it upon a stone until it becomes like soap or marrow; and this will be its sign <note>a physical indicator that the process is working</note>. And when this sign appears, then take a vial like a urinal which has a neck like the first one and a narrow opening, in which you shall place your medicine. Close it well at the top with wax or with clay. Place this vial in a small basket of sticks, and let it be in the middle so that it does not touch the bottom. Then place it in horse manure <note>used as a source of steady, gentle heat</note> for forty days, always changing the manure every ten days and putting in new. And this is the perfect dissolution and the perfect medicine, which is made in forty days, if you have completely performed what is written above.

<column-break/>

When those forty days have passed, draw out the vial and distill the medicine through a filter or a cloth <note>original: "palembium," likely a straining cloth</note>. Place it, thus dissolved, in a thick glass vessel like a bowl. Place this glass in a basin full of sifted ash in your furnace, and give it fire day and night until it evaporates into a powder. Of this powder, place one part by weight upon one hundred parts of Gold <note>symbol: $\odot$</note>. And without any falsehood, it is excellent in the highest degree and in all trials. But if, when you join these spirits, you add a third part of Silver <note>symbol: $\mathbb{C}$</note>... <note>The text here "talonare" is obscure, likely meaning to "heel" or "fix" the metal</note>. And if you have done as was said before, and the whole is mixed, dissolved, and congealed, one part falls upon forty parts of unpurified Gold. But if it is purified as was said above, one part falls upon ninety parts of Gold, and it will certainly be better than mineral Gold. Thus ends the Work of the Four Spirits, which was experienced by Master Cozaldo and presented by him in four months. Dearest friend, do not speak of this, because it is truly a great secret.

# For the Red
Take verdigris, the best being Roman, and heat it in a furnace in a raw earthen vessel; place it in the middle of the furnace. Afterward, dissolve it in "water of urination" <note>distilled urine, used for its ammonia content</note>. Distill it through a filter and put it over a gentle fire. Afterward, grind it with a portion of sal ammoniac and place one dram upon four of **silver** <note>luna</note>. You will have **gold** <note>symbol for Sol/Gold</note> of 20 carats and more.

### For the Red
<margin><image-desc>a manicule pointing to the start of the recipe</image-desc></margin>
Take <term>one pound of silver</term><note>original: "lune libram vnã"; "Luna" (the Moon) is the alchemical symbol for silver.</note>, 3 or 4 ounces of <term>orpiment</term><note>A yellow arsenic sulfide mineral used as a pigment and in alchemy.</note>, and mix everything together. Soak it, and afterwards grind it into a powder. Then take this powder and make it into a paste with egg white. Place this at the bottom of a vessel, and let the vessel be made of glass in the shape of a pyramid. Over this paste placed in the bottom of the vessel, place a layer of <term>vermilion</term><note>original: "vermiculi"; a bright red pigment made from mercury sulfide.</note> so that one layer does not touch the other, nor the sides of the vessel. Afterwards, place more of the aforementioned paste on top, tamping it down well as before. Do this until the vessel is full. Afterwards, cover it and seal it well with <term>lute</term><note>original: "luta"; a clay or cement used to seal alchemical vessels airtight.</note> so that it cannot breathe. Place this glass vessel, thus prepared, into a good earthenware pot over a jar in which there is <term>sublimated mercury</term><note>original: "mercuribellate"; likely a corruption of "mercurio sublimato".</note> at the top. Above this, let there be a layer of ashes two fingers thick, well-jointed and covered everywhere with ash. Then make a charcoal fire for 10 or 20 days. **This being done:** extract it and grind it thoroughly. Mix it with an equal amount of crude mercury and put it in a <term>urinal</term><note>A rounded glass flask used in distillation.</note> with an <term>alembic</term><note>The hood or cap of a still used for distilling liquids.</note> and sublimate it. Do this three times, always putting back that which is found at the bottom of the flask with the vermilion, 4 or more times. **Afterwards**, take that melted substance and cast one part of it over 10 parts of molten silver, and it will be the finest gold.

### The Calcination of Gold is as follows.
Take Gold, Mercury <note>original: "☿" (Mercury/Quicksilver)</note>, and Gold: 3 parts to 1, and amalgamate it all together. The sharpness should be quicklime <note>original: "calx viva"</note>; potash <note>original: "cineres clauellati"</note>; the ashes of wine dregs, that is, ashes of tartar; and very strong vinegar. Place these in a gourd-shaped vessel <note>a cucurbit</note> for distilling, and thus through dissolution, you will receive the fullness of the upper body in the most beautiful water that was ever seen. And that is the powder of saffron <note>likely iron oxide or "crocus martis"</note>, which we have never seen before in the art. We pray that you may have it in your hands; I made it with my own hands, by our soul, and by this way we achieved the dissolution of silver <note>original: "lune argenti"</note> and mercury <note>original: "azerari"</note> in an instant. This is the very day from which we received the water of crystalline salt, which, when added to oil of tartar in the water of egg whites, dissolves all bodies.

<margin>¶</margin>However, the salt for the "red" work <note>the stage producing gold</note> does not need fixation because the openings are already fixed; but mix it with the distilled red oil of egg yolks, which is prepared as follows:

<margin>¶</margin>Once the oil of egg yolks is made by distillation through an alembic, the dregs that remain should be very strongly calcined <note>burned to ash</note> in a sealed vessel. After the calcination is done, let it be ground on a stone with its own oil. Let them boil for a little while, and let the united tincture release its bile, and distill it through a filter. And that is the Red Oil. And this medicine of gold is held to be a file <note>perhaps a refining tool</note>, and our work was most beautiful. ### How Saffron of Iron is Made
<note>original: "Crocus ferri" - a red iron oxide (ferric oxide) used as a pigment or alchemical catalyst.</note>

Take steel filings and dissolve them in **strong water** <note>original: "aqua forti" - nitric acid</note>; then congeal a small portion of the dregs <note>original: "fexei"</note>, and it will remain red as blood. Take this powder and place it in a crucible to be calcined <note>burned to a powder</note> in a glass furnace or a lime kiln for 6 days or more; the longer it stays, the better it is. And this is the best **saffron of iron**.

## For the Red
Take silver <note>original: "azentū" / argentum</note> and purge it just as you will find its purification described in books. # A Work for the Red, as the masters said
## Our Almus Terart of Mostah
<margin>Note concerning the experiment...</margin>
Take <note>original: "Rx" / Recipe</note> sulfur, magnesia, and red arsenic in equal parts. And grind each one very finely by itself. Then place them in vinegar to boil until the vinegar is dried up. And once dried, place it in a pot well-sealed with lute and cover it well. And leave it for one natural day in a hot fire. And open the pot and you will find the whole to be magnesia. Then make it boil in linseed oil, and then place it in warm horse dung for 40 days. And extract it: and melt 20 drams of lead <note>original: "saturnī" (Saturn)</note> and pour 3 ounces of the nourishment over it, and you will have gold <note>original: "solem" (the Sun)</note>. When you wish to melt the lead with one medicine: put 20 parts together for one part of the medicine. For all these things, you should have a <term>cucurbit</term> <note>a gourd-shaped chemical vessel used for distillation</note>
<margin>Note: prepare the crucible for the work</margin>
prepared in the <unclear>merino</unclear> so that it resists the heat. Place the lead in the medicine and place the cucurbit over the coals and melt it with <term>bellows</term> <note>original: "follibz"</note> in such a way that the wind does not blow away the medicine, until the lead boils. Do not stop blowing with the bellows: and you will see that the vessel does not boil over. Extract it and let it cool in the form of a base.

### On the composition of the medicine for the white
### and for the red

**The work** for the white or the red: grind the copper and quench it in clear seed oil until it becomes soft—do this 40 times. And after it has been made soft, file it while hot; if it cools, reheat it, and

<column-break/>

file it many times. Afterward, mix the filings with double their weight of arsenic again; grind it for a very long time until it becomes a most subtle powder. Then, place the powder thus prepared into a bronze vessel made in the likeness of a urinal <note>a common shape for alchemical flasks</note>. Next, build a furnace in which there is a small pot. Place that bronze vessel containing the powder inside the pot, so that it does not touch the pot itself but is as if hanging within it. Have a cover made of earth <note>clay</note> in the manner of a furnace for the bronze vessel, the opening of which should be small. Then, let a moderate fire be made beneath it, and you will see smoke of diverse colors coming out. After the smoke has ceased, remove the vessel from the fire; the powder you find inside is very black. Place this in a mortar and mix salt with it. Add water to it, half of which is <term>alkali water</term><note>original: "aqua alkah"</note> and the other half the urine of a boy. Then place it in a glass bowl and leave it until it settles. Afterward, pour off the water and place the powder in the mortar with salt, then water, and do as you did before. Do this for a long time until the powder is a clear red or a clear white. Finally, add salt to it in the mortar, repeating as before, until it no longer tastes of salt. Then let it dry. If it is placed on a shovel <note>original: "renabulo"</note> so that it can tolerate the fire and neither smokes nor breaks, then mix with the aforesaid powder—if it is red—a third part of filed <term>Sol</term><note>original: "sol"; alchemical code for gold</note>. If it is white, a third part of filed Luna <note>silver</note>. Then let it be placed on the shovel with a bed of salt and some of the powder, until all the powder is on the shovel. Finally, let it be melted, and it will be gold or silver. Do this in the second hour of Leo, or when the Moon itself is in Cancer.

# On the Perfection of the Work

The arrival of perfection and completion is found in the result: if the preparation is diminished, the result is diminished. And as much as the preparation is more perfect, so much less failure of the work should be expected in proportion. Always, when something precious is expected from all things, a successful outcome must undoubtedly follow, provided the preparations are made perfectly and in the right manner.

This process is called "administration" by some, <gloss>cleansing</gloss> by others, "certification" by others, <gloss>washing</gloss> by others, and "separation" by others. It is the separation itself which segregates the purer parts from the impure, so that, once the <unclear>corruptible</unclear> parts are cast away, the work may be completed with all the smoother parts. And **Hermes** <note>Refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> gave this to be understood in his compendium which he composed concerning this work; for he says:

"You shall separate the earth from the fire, the subtle from the dense." <note>A famous line from the Emerald Tablet of Hermes</note>

And know this: that it is a great secret. Know also that the method of perfect preparation is concerned not only with the removal of superfluous things, but also with the addition of those things that are lacking. This is according to what I recorded in a certain work of mine entitled ***The Light of Lights*** <margin>Light of Lights</margin> regarding <insert>Hermes</insert> <gloss>Hermes</gloss>: which, among the secret papers that I clearly unlocked concerning the subtlety of this mastery, I said that to prepare perfectly is to supply what is absent and to take away what is superfluous.

For light things cannot be held back unless by heavy things <gloss>at the bottom</gloss>, nor can smooth things <gloss>at the top</gloss> be held unless the confusion of heavy things restrains them. Neither can the hot be tempered except by the cold, nor the cold by the hot; nor the moist except by the dry, nor the dry by the moist; nor the hard except by the soft, nor the soft by the hard, by means of a subtle joining in whatever way. Thus, everything is arranged fittingly in turn, and from them a tempered substance is generated,

<column-break/>

which the violence of fire cannot overcome, nor the insolence of earth spoil, nor the muddiness of water condense, nor the contact of air disturb <margin>cloud over</margin>.

And **Hermes**, the prince of this doctrine, wishing to make known in that statement at the end of his aforementioned secret work the manner and the materials from which the Stone he had predicted—which overcomes every subtle thing and penetrates every solid thing—was composed, insinuated this very thing when he said:

"Just as this world was created, so the Stone I have predicted was created."

That is to say <gloss>namely</gloss>, just as <gloss>this</gloss> world was made from the essences of the four elements, so also is the Stone. And just as this sensible world <margin>"sensible," he says</margin> in which we are is mixed from heavy and light, soft and hard, hot and cold, moist and dry—<gloss>namely</gloss> bound to one another by nature in a concordant peace—so it is made by perpetual acts. So too is the Stone I have predicted, which can overcome every subtle thing and penetrate every solid thing: it is created from the aforesaid things. And know this, for it is a great secret.

The perfect preparation of bodies and spirits, after the suppression of the superfluous and the addition of the absent, is fulfilled by the extraction of four regimes <margin><gloss>for the separation of the Philosophers' Stone</gloss> regarding the method of preparation <gloss>noted most clearly and made for practice</gloss></margin>:

1. The first is the reduction to the nature of **Fire**.
2. The second is their resolution into **Water**.
3. The third is their compression into **Air**.
4. The fourth is their compression into **Earth**.

The first <gloss>Fourth</gloss> is done by **calcining** <note>Heating to a high temperature to reduce to powder</note>; the second by **dissolving**; the third by **distilling** through an alembic; and the fourth by **congealing** in the fire. This is their great preparation. And **Hermes** remembered this in his aforementioned secret when he said:

"It ascends gently with great ingenuity from the earth to the heaven." <margin><gloss>Note the fire of Hermes... in the work of the philosopher</gloss></margin>

First, however, the subtle must be separated from the dense. Then it descends again into the earth. By this, he <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note> intended to be understood the **calcination** <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to powder</note> of bodies and the **sublimation** <note>Turning a solid into vapor and back to solid to purify it</note> and **fixation** <note>Making a volatile substance stable under heat</note> of spirits. For this is their calcination. And wishing to show the **solution** <note>Dissolving a solid into liquid</note> <gloss>and human virtue</gloss>, he says: *Its nurse is the earth.*
<margin>Now he speaks in the Emerald Tablet of the earth, i.e., toward fixation, as he would show.</margin>
In its human aspect, the earth is the life-giver; through it, the very thing which had previously been **mortified** <note>Alchemical term for "killed" or broken down</note> by the calcination of all things is nourished and brought to life when the cleansing liquor is brought back upon it. Water is first lightened into the air, although it afterwards returns to the earth. ¶ Likewise, in order to show **distillation** by means of the **Alembic** <note>term: Alembic; a classic alchemical still consisting of two vessels connected by a tube</note>, he says: *The wind carried it in its belly.* For when water is distilled through an alembic, it passes through the wind as an airy vapor and is lightened, and from the lower part of the vessel it is deposited into the "belly" of the alembic, although it returns again into water there because of the enclosure. ¶ However, some people consider this distillation in liquid things to take the place of sublimation, and they called it by the name of sublimation. In order to show **congelation** <note>thickening or freezing</note> or coagulation, he says: *Its force is entire if it be turned afterwards into earth* and through its artifice toward fixation. ¶ And so that he might show generally whatever he had previously expressed in parts, he said: *And it receives the superior and inferior power*, i.e., the nature of the superior and inferior elements. For although it takes its beginning from the lighter things, it must nevertheless <gloss>be terminated and</gloss> congealed into the heavier things, so that it may have perpetual efficacy or perseverance over the fire. Here he is speaking of

<column-break/>

the preparation of only one of those things which is required for composing the **Philosophers' Stone**. ¶ Having explained <gloss>exemplified</gloss> concerning one, he might briefly demonstrate the entire preparation in each of the individual parts. For then the "paste" is a perfect preparation: when they are turned into earth for fixation over the fire, and easy fusion without smoking. And then it will overcome every subtle thing and penetrate every solid thing, according to what he himself said. And know this, that it is a great secret.

### Chapter 7: Concerning the various erroneous practices of those laboring in this art

Whence these multiple compositions have emanated from the aforesaid, according to the various processes of different philosophers: some only with fire, some only with solution, some only with each one of those. For those who work with fire alone, the process was twofold.

Some, however, fixed the aforementioned spirits with a solution: and afterwards they sounded them <note>likely meaning they tested or combined them</note> with white bodies: and from them they made one body by fusion: and they said that it was an elixir fixed upon the fire. And these are the ways of those who worked with fire alone.

However, for those who worked with solution, the path was twofold. Some, by the way of the aforesaid separations, dissolved each thing by itself, and [created] two anew—that is, according to weights—they allowed them to join and congealed them into a stone: which was a perfect elixir. Others, however, following these seeds of philosophy, took the aforesaid offerings and composed them all together, and dissolved and congealed them. Nevertheless, some, once the solution was made, distilled the dissolved waters through an alembic <note>term: alembic; a glass or metal apparatus used for distilling liquids</note>: saying that this was the completion of their clarity and the brilliance in the discovery: which nature produced in the clearest water, which it afterwards coagulated into a pure stone. And they said that this was the truest elixir.

For those, however, who proceeded with both [fire and solution], the path was double: for some dissolved the bodies and the dissolved spirits together: and afterwards they fixed them with sublimation <note>term: sublimation; the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again</note>. Some, however, dissolved the calcined bodies: and from there they imbibed <note>term: imbibition; the process of adding liquid to a dry substance until it is saturated</note> the sublimated spirits: and afterwards in the aforesaid

<column-break/>

manner they congealed them. Some, however, dissolved the sublimated spirits: and from there they imbibed the calcined bodies. But in so many days, it became an elixir. Some, however, with separated sulfur and arsenic, imbibed or otherwise coagulated the bodies, under a certain weight of flux: and afterwards they dissolved them. And they drank in <note>original: "potabant"; likely meaning the substance absorbed</note> double its weight of separated quicksilver <note>term: argentum vivum; literally "living silver," the common name for mercury</note>. And again they dissolved and coagulated: and they said that it was the right elixir.

And some of them, with dissolved bodies, with sulfur and arsenic as has been said, whitened the quicksilver: they dissolved and coagulated it, and said it was an elixir. Because an elixir ought to consist of four things of the same "Venus" <note>note: likely referring to the same nature or metallic family</note> and not diverse ones, and not from more or fewer, because then it would corrupt the work. Therefore, they composed the elixir from four principal spirits: namely, quicksilver, arsenic, sulfur, and sal ammoniac <note>term: sal armoniacum; ammonium chloride, used as a flux and in the preparation of spirits</note>. In such a way, however, that they first fixed the quicksilver by sublimating it, and afterwards they dissolved it with prepared, dissolved, and distilled sal ammoniac. And afterwards they first distilled the sal ammoniac with an alembic; finally, they distilled the quicksilver and coagulated it. And they said that this was the truest elixir of this art, and the "magnesia" <note>note: in alchemy, magnesia refers to a mystical primitive matter, not modern magnesium</note>: and the stone and not a stone: and the spiritual body: and the bodily spirit: and that which retains every volatile thing from flight: and the ferment: and the tincture of two elixirs. And the accidental quicksilver: that which is pressed—

**I**, however, say lastly, that whichever of the previously described bodies and spirits has been prepared by a perfect preparation—so that the highest part of the volatile <note>the "flying" or vaporous substance</note> overcomes the limits of the fixed, and it were by itself alone—it will be the white and red elixir. # Second section on the natures and material complexions of bodies or spirits.

### Chapter 10

**A**ll bodies which were created by the highest Creator from the lunar globe <gloss>celestial</gloss> of mixing, must participate in the four elements: the four natural humors; and the four complexions of natures; and the four principal colors; and the four flavors; and the four odors; and two sexes. Furthermore, their dimensions, namely: height, width, and depth. The four elements are: Fire, Air, Water, and Earth. The four natural humors are: Blood, Choler <note>yellow bile</note>, Phlegm, and Melancholy <note>black bile</note>. The four natural complexions are: Heat, Cold, Humidity, and Dryness. The four principal colors are: White, Black, Yellow, and Red. The four flavors are: Tasteless, Sour, Sweet, and Bitter. The four odors are: Good and fragrant, Stinking, Bitter, and Faint (that is, scented). There are two sexes: masculine and feminine. The height of a body is its manifest <note>visible</note> part; the depth is the occult <note>hidden</note> part; the width participates in the middle of these. Therefore, all the aforesaid bodies are according to these three aforesaid dimensions.

<margin>Concerning complete and diminished, or healthy and sick metals, and first concerning lead. Chapter 11.</margin>

Let us begin, therefore, to show you as much as I can more perfectly meditate upon in my mind and recite more openly in speech. Taking our origin from lead, it is congealed as both complete and diminished <gloss>by a proven multitude</gloss> and is considered coagulated; in which their dimensions are complete, and in which they are diminished and set free, and without fractures you will find a way to work. However, there are two "completes" here: those which in the present reasoning I have called healthy; and the diminished, which I have called neutral and sick. Its health is the aforementioned matter. Sickness and neutrality are the diminished state <margin>on account of their own power</margin>. The perfect mastery <term>Magisterium: the successful completion of an alchemical process</term>, therefore, is to reduce all bodies both to health and to neutrality. And when one has done this, both should be easy and possible; although certain sophists <note>original: "sophiste" - here meaning false philosophers or pretenders</note> who are ignorant of natural things and <column-break/> <gloss>ignorant</gloss> of the secrets of philosophy, and who are improvident regarding its regimens, may disparage the writings because they do not understand the matters. When afterwards they find a true <gloss>metal</gloss> in their hands, they blame the error on their philosophy; asserting this work to be not only difficult, but even preaching it as impossible—which philosophy does not care about. For my philosophy does not call everyone to this exercise, but only those who are worthy to recline at this table and partake of such feasts, having been found fit for refreshment. Strive therefore <gloss>that is, you sophist</gloss>—do not be a sophist! So that you may know the virtues of things not only in meditation, but also know meditation through experience. For meditation without experience profits nothing; rather, experience is better even without meditation. Whence experience is to be sought more than meditation. For in the experience of this thing, you shall attain the fruit; in this, you will be a disciple of philosophy, and consequently to be numbered among the guests of the aforementioned table, and to be satisfied forever by its abundance, which surpasses all ceremonies of gifts, by the sweetness of prayers and perpetual affection. Since no one can be perfect or discerning by themselves at first sight <gloss>that is, through experience</gloss> of this thing, I have seen fit to persuade you that you should not cease from this method; <gloss>and reasoning</gloss> if you have not worked it perfectly the first time, do not cease by repeating it twice, three times, four times, or more if necessary, until you perceive most perfectly that which you desire. Nor let the labor of your hands draw you back from this matter on account of the expenses.

## On the altitude of Gold, Chapter 14

Gold in its **altitude** <note>The "altitude" refers to the outward, visible properties of a substance.</note> is airy, hot, moist, sanguine, saffron-colored, sweet, fragrant, and masculine. Magnesia and Marcasite <note>Marcasite here likely refers to various metallic sulfides with a brassy luster.</note> are fusible stones of many kinds which represent the appearance of the Moon <note>Silver</note> and the Sun <note>Gold</note> and of all metals. They are naturally composed of mercury and sulfur compacted in the veins of the earth. And because they flee from the fire, they are therefore <term>sublimated</term> <note>The process of turning a solid into vapor via heat and then back to solid.</note>. For they represent the voice of that which they are and the nature of the metal. And therefore, concerning their altitude, depth, and sides, one must speak just as with the similar metals. Know therefore that this is a great secret. Tutty <note>original: "Tutia," a byproduct of smelting, used in medicinal salves and alchemy.</note> truly is accounted for under the category of the vapors of lead and tin, as is clearly demonstrated in the *Greater Summary*.

Ink <note>Atramentum/Vitriol</note> is a certain kind of alum: red, lemon-yellow, or green in its manifest appearance. It is an oily, very fatty substance of the earth's mineral, composed of sulfurs, which to the taste of the tongue is pungent and styptic like twin white alum. And for this reason, our ancient wise men called it "red alum"; by them it is called vitriol and chalcanthum. By some of our people, it is called the spirit of tragacanth, which is very necessary in the sun <note>gold</note> tincture and for retaining the spirit. And this is because the ink itself <margin>of enigmas</margin> is the greenness of the work in this art. It greatly exalts the tincture of the sun by itself through dyeing, and adds tincture to red mixtures. It is the light of lights, and the green sulfur of the philosophers: fixed and established. But by itself, it is of very poor penetration unless it is mixed <margin>... sulfur of the philosophers ... sun ...</margin> with its white companion, which is called the fixed white sulfur of the philosophers. For from these two, mixed according to the weights of truth through <margin>Ingenuity</margin> a subtle fixed means, there flows a certain divine sulfur of the philosophers, abstracted from those two sulfurs, which the philosophers themselves called "poison": because it passes through the body of the philosophers just as poison passes through the bodies of men. They also called it the sharpest vinegar: because just as vinegar dissolves, it dissolves the philosophical body, extracts the soul from it, and converts it into spirit and much else. In almost infinite ways it was hidden by my fathers. And for this reason, God brought it forth above all stones.

## Concerning the six species of atraments, their names, and qualities

There are also six kinds of atraments. The first, named by the discoverers, is called **Calcadis** <note>likely Chalcitis</note>, moderately fatty, which in its manifest appearance is lemon-colored. The 2nd kind is called **calcatar** <note>Colcothar</note>; it is entirely similar to the aforementioned in color, but is not very lasting for this science. The 3rd kind is called **Sotiram**; it is more upright and glassy than all other atraments. For it is a certain blackish earth, sulfurous and heavy, having a square window <note>likely referring to the crystalline structure</note>.

<column-break/>

It is brought from Gaul. And therefore it is commonly called **Gallican earth**: which, when it is allowed through all things by a great fire, becomes light and is refined. And when they are placed in hot water, it does not dye it; and it is impressive to this science. The 4th kind is called **calcanum**, which in its manifest appearance is green; saffron-colored or crocus-like. Concerning which it was formulated above: that it is fatty,
<margin>see folio 145</margin>
and better and more noble than all atraments. A great abundance of this is found in Spain <note>original: "hyspania"</note>. This alone is commended among the others in the science. Yet it differs in nature from all others because all other atraments are manifestly warm and dry, irony and airy, and fiery. This alone is warm and moist, as was narrated above. And because it has the nature and quality of the purest gold, it is therefore often named "the golden" by some. The 5th kind is called **Cyprian** <note>original: "Ciprinum"</note>, because it is brought from the island of Cyprus. Red in its manifest appearance, and glassy in its hidden aspect; it is pertinent to this science. The 6th kind is called **Roman Vitriol**: which is very false, of two colors, somewhat sky-blue; which is named **copperas** <note>original: "cuperosa"</note> by some. This is rejected in every way from the science. From these aforementioned atraments, therefore, the second is most necessary: that one may be composed from it and its white companion.

Of which there are three species: One which is called **vulturine** <note>original: "vulturinum"; likely a reference to a corrosive or "soaring" quality</note>, which is prepared as **crystalline**. This is called by some <margin>gloss: y. of glass <note>original: "de glaz"</note></margin> **sword alum** <note>original: "alumen gladiei"</note>. From this alone, and from saltpeter, is made **strong water** <term>aqua fortissima: nitric acid</term> which dissolves all metallic bodies except the Sun <note>Gold</note>, and all sublimated spirits except quicksilver <note>Mercury</note>. The second is called **saccharine alum**, which is brought from Alexandria and Greece; when prepared, it is suitable for certain works of a minor order. The third <margin>others [call it] another [name]</margin> is **plumed alum** <note>original: "plomosum"; likely asbestos or feather alum</note>, which is called *gamem*. This is better, more beautiful, more noble, more fatty, and more useful than all those mentioned above. For it is bright in itself, shining like the moon; it is found or discovered in no provinces known to us except in Spain. All alum that is found to be foul or false is considered septic; when mixed with other salts, it doubles one, triples the second, and quadruples the third, and thus always adds one weight of perfection. It brings clarity to all white and red [works] and receives the tincture. Good alum can be placed in the stead of fixed, flowing, living sulfur in the [work of] the deserted fire, in the composition of the sharpest **vinegar of the philosophers** <term>acetum acerrimum: a potent alchemical solvent</term>, and especially for the white work. For in its manifest [outer] form it is silver; in its profound [inner] depth it is gold; on one side it is tin, and on the other side it is copper.

### Here follows the nature of all salts and the extraction of the same: Chapter 27

<column-break/>

Others are multiplied. Of these, some are **mineral**, some are **fixed vegetable**, and some are **fixed animal**. But among these species of salts, we find many—whether animal, mineral, or vegetable—that are not fixed, as will appear below. Fixed minerals include **common salt** <note>original: "sal panis"; literally "bread salt"</note> which is extracted from the sea or from well waters. Likewise **gem salt** <note>rock salt</note> which is bright, white, and transparent like crystal, and softer than the aforementioned. There are two species of it: one is crystalline white, the other is transparent red. It is born and found in the mineral mines of sulfurous places, having its substance divided through great stones; they are found and obtained especially in Spain.

### Concerning fixed and mixed mineral and vegetable salts: Chapter 28

Among the non-fixed minerals are **saltpeter** <note>original: "sal nitrus"</note> and *retineus*, which is also found in Spain in watery places, from the gathering of rainwaters that have no outlet. The fixed and mixed vegetables are almost infinite, because from all trees—namely from their marrow—and from herbs, strong **lyes** <margin>on the method of extracting salt from vegetables</margin> can be made; when the water is evaporated from them, salt remains at the bottom of the vessel. According to the quality and complexion of these, there remains a fixed or mixed salt. Trees and herbs <margin>on fixed salt, namely water for glass</margin> make fixed salt, from which, in every casting, **glass** is melted. It also mixes with the non-fixed. Experience will teach you which is fixed or mixed.

Fixed salts of animal origin are extracted from the horns of all kinds, from the eggs of hens, and from all birds. Unfixed salts, however, are extracted from all the calcined <term>calcined: burned to a powder</term> essences of egg yolks and whites, and from all the dregs and superfluities of animals, such as from blood, urine, dung, and the like. There are also two types of salts: one of which is fixed, and the other is unfixed. The fixed salt is called **Saltpeter** <note>original: "Sal nitrum"</note>. The unfixed is called **Sal ammoniac** <note>original: "sal armoniacũ"</note>. And these two are very necessary in this science. Saltpeter is a sulfurous mineral. In its highest state, it is a fixed white sulfur, a fusible white silver, and equal to the sulfur of the fixed melting green. In this art, it is praised with exceeding great honor. From it, through its composition, emanates the **divine sulfur of the philosophers**, as was declared above in the section on the "ink of the philosophers." In its depths, it is a red-golden sulfur; that is, on one side it is a pale sulfur-tin, and on the other side it is a copper-sulfur, that is—

Sal ammoniac is a flying <note>volatile</note> cleansing spirit that is possessed by and extracted from human and animal minerals <note>likely referring to organic waste</note>. It has the power to quickly cleanse all calcined things and convert them into water. From it and from saltpeter <note>original: "sale mizo," likely a corruption of nitre</note> emanates a **most strong water** <term>aqua fortissima: nitric acid or aqua regia</term>, which dissolves gold and removes the foundation of many compositions of this art. And some say that this is the **angel** who, by divine power and virtue, joins the soul with the body and the body with the soul, and makes it rise again glorified. And so it acts with all spirits and the bodies of the dead. Fixed salts of every kind, when prepared in a mixture, retain the unfixed elements.

### On Talc and its Nature, Chapter 28

**Talc** <note>original: "Talchus"</note> is an earthy stone of two kinds, very similar to the sun, most bright, naturally layered <note>foliated</note>, and composed of the ash and flower of the whitest and most sulfurous earth. Its tiny leaves are bright on both sides and very thin to the touch of the fingers, like very fine shining sand. Because this stone is earthy, it does not combine well with metals. The philosophers say: "earthy with earthy, metallic with metallic." This stone, when prepared, belongs to this science. In its outward appearance, it is hot and dry. In its inner depth, it is cold and moist; on one side white and moist, and on the other side cold and red.
