### Next follows the water of clarity of Egg Whites: and the rectification of the same. Chapter 30.

**T**ake egg whites <note>original: "albumina ovorum"</note> in a large quantity: and beat them vigorously in a glazed dish until they are entirely converted into foam: and leave it for a day and a night. And the foam will be converted into oil. Let it be buried for three weeks in horse dung <note>A common alchemical method for providing gentle, steady heat for fermentation or digestion.</note>: finally, distill it with an alembic <note>term: alembic (a chemical still consisting of two vessels connected by a tube, used for distilling volatile substances)</note> by means of water and ash <note>A "water bath" or "ash bath" to regulate heat</note>. And you will have the semi-distilled water of clarity: let it be distilled three times without the dregs <note>original: "feabus/fecibus"</note> by means of water and ash. And you will have the water of clarity distilled three times. Finally, distill it four times through the alembic with dry ash: and each time, for one pound of the liquid, add one pound of cooked lime made from calcined eggshells <note>original: "calcis coctam ovorum calcinatorum"</note>: and you will have the perpetual water of clarity, rectified seven times. Extinguish glowing copper <note>original: "es ignitum"</note> in it: and if it whitens the metal inside and out, it is perfectly rectified. If not, however, rectify it with the cooked lime until it serves. And let it be reserved in a securely sealed vessel for necessary work.

### Next follows the water of clarity of egg yolks and its oil, and the rectification of the same. Chapter 31.

**T**ake egg yolks in a good quantity: and add to them a fourth part of white fixed flowing sulfur <note>term: fixed flowing sulfur (sulfur that has been chemically treated so it no longer evaporates easily and melts like wax)</note>. Let them be mixed very well: and placed in warm horse dung for three weeks in a small, securely sealed vessel.

<column-break/>

Finally, let it be set to distill by means of water and ash: and you will have a water <margin>rectification</margin> of clarity more noble than the aforementioned. Let it be rectified three times by means of water and ashes: and four times by ash: and each time mixing into one pound of the water one pound of cooked lime of eggs. In the final four acts of distillation, let it be tested just as the first was with glowing copper: and then let it be reserved, securely closed: because the water of clarity is proclaimed most perfect in this art, praised above all things. Regarding the dregs <margin>concerning the dregs and their distillation</margin> which remained after the first distillation, let them be set to distill with a very strong fire: indeed, with a slow fire in the beginning: and thus increasing to a strong fire: until a thick, saffron-colored oil has emanated from those dregs. Let it be rectified <margin>rectification of the oil of clarity</margin> seven times with caution, each time putting into one pound of the oil one pound of green fixed flowing sulfur, separated and calcined red. And you will have a fragrant, lemon-colored, and precious oil of clarity. Let it be reserved in a securely sealed vessel for necessary works.

### Next follows the divine water of clarity, suitable for elixirs, brought near to its salt, and optimally rectified. Chapter 32.

**T**ake one part of cooked lime of calcined eggshells. Take eight parts of the water of clarity rectified seven times: let them be mixed together in a small vessel well, so that the whole lime is dissolved. Closed <margin>divine clear water</margin>

## Following is the Lunar-making water, which is said to be simply separated by the sharpest vinegar. Chapter 33.

<margin>vitriol and saltpeter 8.</margin>
Take 18 ounces of green vitriol, which is called <term>calcantis</term> <note>original: "calcantis" - a traditional name for copperas or ferrous sulfate</note>. Take 8 ounces of saltpeter. It is necessary to have a great quantity of this, as well as of the Clarifying Water, since all the materials of this art are cooked and purified in them.

## Following is the Solar-making water, made in two ways. Chapter 34.

<margin>sal ammoniac, saltpeter</margin>
Take 4 ounces of sal ammoniac and one ounce of saltpeter; let a water be made as is fitting, which dissolves the Sun <note>gold</note> and talc in one hour, or

<column-break/>

otherwise and better: Take 1.5 pounds of the sharp Lunar-making water and dissolve in it one pound of sal ammoniac and a half-portion of saltpeter. For this is called the sharp Solar-making water <note>aqua solifica: a solvent for gold (Sol), likely a form of aqua regia</note>, more noble than the aforementioned. Let it be kept in a closed vessel.

## Here begin the Reddening Waters, of which this is the first. Chapter 34.

Take one pound of the sharp Lunar-making water; two ounces of copper; and one ounce of molten iron filings. First, let the copper be dissolved in the aforementioned water. Afterward, add a smaller amount of iron filings. Add powdered "sulfur of wine" <note>likely tartar or a sulfurous extract</note to the weight of a fourth part of the iron, and common red arsenic to the same quantity as the sulfur. Let all be mixed well with the water and set to distill, first with a slow fire, then with a strong one. Let all the distilled water be poured back over the dregs and distilled again. Afterward, renew the dregs using only calcined copper and iron, leaving out the white substances. Let it be distilled, <unclear>placing</unclear> it over those dregs and renewing them every two distillations, until it distills red—otherwise let it be like blood. Then it will tint everything upon which it falls with a firm dye, resistant to every test.

### Concerning the fourth rubifying water by which precious alfadida is made. Chapter 38.

The water shall be reserved in a closed vessel.

### On the sixth reddening water made with the second alum. Chapter 40.

## Concerning the twelfth reddening water which dyes all bodies upon which it falls with an excellent and firm color. Chapter 44.

<margin>water of life, water of death</margin>

<margin>permanent water, sharpest vinegar</margin>
It is called **permanent water**: because it remains steadfast against the fight of fire. ## Concerning the preparation of the water that rectifies all bodies and spirits quickly.
### Chapter 18.

<margin>Seth, son of Adam</margin>
**A**fterward, take the stone noted in the chapter: of which Hermes, the aged one, our father, speaks even on the stone tablets: which Seth, the son of Adam, left behind: just as Noah the father hid them away in the ark. Know that no medicine is made unless it is obtained from the red stone <note>original: "lapis rubeus," often associated with the final stage of the Great Work or the Philosopher's Stone itself</note>. Then you shall powder the stone most finely: and dissolve it in strong distilled vinegar of horns <note>likely an ammonia-rich solution derived from animal horns</note>: and let it settle: and distill it through a filter, holding it until it takes on a redness and clarity. Finally, set it in the sun during the days of June or July at a slow heat for some time; when it is set, let it be powdered most finely: and take of it a pound and a half; and of the sharpest vinegar of the philosophers, simply separated and reserved above, take three pounds: let them be mixed: and immediately the aforesaid stone will be dissolved. You shall reserve it in a vessel kept inviolably closed. The dregs, however, which will be red and thick, should be reserved in a small closed vessel for necessary works. Because although the mediocre substance of those two things was abstracted from them in the first regimen: it will not yet be fit for perfecting the body of the philosophers <note>the refined metallic state</note>, nor for the creation of gold or silver: until it has been thus rectified upon its own body from which it drew its nature and origin. For the small ones <note>perhaps "the humble" or "the lesser secrets"</note> have told me: that to perfect this vinegar, a purging of the moisture is necessary: which is airy and oily, burning and dividing metals. And the second, which is phlegmatic, evaporating or conferring perfection: but dividing and withdrawing. If, therefore, you wish the sharpest vinegar to be purged in such a way that each part lacks its infirmity: the first and second superfluities [are removed] and the third, which is the mediocre substance of it, remains: which is its radical and natural moisture, pure gold, for the perfection of gold and silver. Concerning the reddening of the white ones, a suitable distinction follows. This aforesaid most precious water rectifies all bodies and spirits quickly, as will appear in what follows. ## Next follows the separation and preparation of all salts, alums, and vitriols, the best that can be: Chapter 49.

Let every kind of salt be dissolved in hot water and allowed to settle; then filter it through a cloth <note>original: "distilla filtro" - referring to capillary filtration or straining through felt</note> as many times as necessary until it achieves the highest clarity. Let it be congealed <note>crystallized</note> in a leaden vessel over a slow fire, so that the water evaporates without boiling. For the best results, it should stand in the sun to congeal. In this way, it will be perfectly separated. Their preparation is done in this manner:

<margin>On the method of preparation and separation of all salts, alums, and vitriols</margin>

### Chapter 50.

Take one part of any of these separated substances; let it be powdered and dissolved in four parts of "sharp light-water" <note>likely a reference to a specific distilled acid or "aqua acuta"</note>. Then set it to distill with a very gentle fire, and reserve the distilled water. Let the salt be dissolved in eight parts of "water of clarity" <note>highly purified water or alcohol</note> rectified seven times. Let the aforementioned water of clarity be distilled through an alembic seven times over the salt itself, or until the salt melts upon a glowing metal plate without smoke and penetrates it. Every kind of alum is separated and prepared in the aforementioned way. Every kind of vitriol <note>term: atramentorum - metallic sulfates like copperas or ink-making minerals</note> is separated and prepared in the same way, but in place of the water of clarity, use "oil of clarity" <note>likely a purified oil or thick spirit</note> seven times rectified.

### Next follows the perfect Borax of this art, and its composition: Chapter 51.

Take four parts of separated alkali salt; one part each of common salt, rock salt <note>original: "salis geme"</note>, Jamen alum <note>original: "aluminis gameni" - a high-quality alum from Yemen</note>, and separated salt ammoniac <note>term: salis armoniaci - ammonium chloride</note>.

<column-break/>

Let them be powdered and mixed together. Dissolve one part of this mixture in four parts of "sharp light-water" and set them to distill over a very gentle fire. Reserve the distilled water. Let the Borax <note>term: atinchar - from the Arabic 'al-tinkar', referring to borax or a flux</note> be dissolved in eight parts of water of clarity rectified seven times. Let the water be distilled through an alembic seven times over the aforementioned Borax with a very gentle fire, and it will be optimally prepared. These are the best preparations and separations of salts, alums, and vitriols that can exist in the art of alchemy.

# On the preparation of Marcasite, Tutty, and Magnesia
### Chapter 43

**E**very kind of Marcasite <note>iron pyrites</note>, Tutty <note>zinc oxide</note>, and Magnesia <note>manganese or a general term for mineral ores</note> should be sublimated, as is held in the *Greater Summary*, Book Three. # Following is the calcination, separation, and preparation of Talc for composing the white elixir. Chapter 44

**T**ake white foliated talc <note>mica or magnesium silicate</note> as much as you wish: place it in an iron vessel over a great charcoal fire until it is most strongly ignited; and let it stand thus ignited for one hour, and it will be changed from the earthiness that is in it. Then let it be pulverized most finely and ground; and take of it one part, of sal ammoniac <note>ammonium chloride</note> one fourth part, of salt alkali <note>potassium or sodium carbonate</note> one and a half parts, and of saltpeter <note>potassium nitrate</note> a fourth part of one; let them be pulverized and mixed together, placed in a crucible, and immediately melted with a very strong fire with bellows. The salts indeed will settle, and the talc will remain melted. By this melting and excellent separation, it will be obtained. Finally, let it be prepared thus.

# A medicine of which one part converts a thousand parts of tin into Silver. Chapter 44

Dissolve in it little by little one pound of sal ammoniac, or as much as you wish, because the first water in the ammonia can be multiplied infinitely. Then set it to distill, and you will have a most clear water which, in place of the "sharp luminous water," can be used in all works where that is required, because it is better, stronger, and redder. In eight parts of this water, dilute or dissolve one part of the talc separated above: Give this water to the prepared quicksilver <note>mercury</note> to drink.

### Another way of separating and preparing quicksilver and vitriol, Chapter 47.

## Here follows the washing of Saturn and its perfection into gold and silver, and finally into the white and red elixir. Chapter 61.

## Here follows the washing and composition of tin for the composing of the white and red elixir. Chapter 62.

**T**ake eight parts of sharp light-giving water: dissolve in it one part of tin, submitted and hammered into leaves, leaf by leaf, little by little. Place it to be distilled through an alembic with a slow fire. When the water is distilled, let it be poured back over it and distilled again. And let this be done seven times. Let it be reduced into a body with our Armchar, and it will be true silver. It is converted into the light-giving elixir in this way: Before it is reduced into a body, let it be dissolved in eight parts of new sharp light-giving water: and let the water be distilled from it. ## On Arsenic, Chapter 69

Let one part of arsenic, sublimated <note>the process of heating a substance until it becomes vapor and then solidifies again to purify it</note> by sublimation, be dissolved in nine parts of sharp vinegar water; let the water be distilled from it through an alembic <note>a chemical apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube, used for distilling</note>. When it is distilled, pour it back over the arsenic. Let this be done three times, and let it be dissolved in eight parts of clarified water rectified <note>purified by repeated distillation</note> seven times. Let the aforementioned water be repeated over it seven times, and it will be a perfected elixir. And one part converts 15 parts of copper into true silver.
It is converted into a gold-making elixir <term>solificum: a substance capable of producing gold</term> in this manner: Take eight parts of sharp vinegar water; let it be distilled seven times over one part of arsenic sublimated seven times; finally, let it be dissolved in eight parts of sharp gold-making vinegar water. Let the water be distilled from it through an alembic. When distilled, let it be dissolved in eight parts of clarified oil rectified seven times. Let it be distilled over it seven times, and it will be a perfected elixir. And one part converts 15 parts of silver into true gold according to every test. In the same way, with nothing added and nothing removed <margin>by making it melt</margin>, white sulfur rightly sublimated is converted into a silver-making <note>original: "lumificum," likely a scribal error for "lunificum"</note> and gold-making elixir.

## On how cinnabar is converted into a gold-making elixir, Chapter 70

Take powdered cinnabar <note>mercury sulfide, a bright red mineral</note> and place it in a crucible over a charcoal fire. On how elixirs for white <note>silver</note> <unclear>or</unclear> red <note>gold</note> can be made from bodies and spirits by themselves, Chapter 71.

All the aforementioned operations of prepared bodies <note>metals</note> and spirits <note>volatile substances like sulfur or arsenic</note> are of the second order. From these, our word of the first reasoning of this book is shown to be true in the fourth chapter: that whenever the prescribed bodies and spirits have been prepared in a perfected preparation, by themselves alone there will be a white and red elixir with perpetual adherence. With salts, alums, inks, marcasites, tutty <note>zinc oxide</note>, and similar things, many particular operations of the first order can be performed. As has been sufficiently narrated by us in the "Greater Summa" in the third book, expressed in many particulars, we omit them here because in this volume we have placed only firm operations.

Take one pound of quicksilver <note>original: "argenti viui"; mercury</note> with the scent of tin <note>original: "stagni"</note> or congealed lead <note>original: "saturni"</note>. Take seven ounces of rock salt <note>original: "Salis geme"</note> and let them be mixed together until the whole forms a mass or marrow. Afterward, place beneath it one pound of the sharpest common vinegar and mix it all well. Place it in a glazed vessel over a slow fire and let it boil with a gentle bubbling until all the wateriness of the vinegar is consumed and the salt remains dry. And when all the blackness of the quicksilver appears on the surface of the salt, let it be washed well with vinegar until the saltiness completely departs and the quicksilver has a silvery brightness. Let it be dried so that all the moisture of the vinegar leaves it.

Finally, place it in a vitrified vessel, and over it [pour] three ounces of the sharpest vinegar of the philosophers <note>original: "phoꝝ"; likely referring to *philosophorum*</note> which has been rectified seven times—that is, a fourth part of the quicksilver. Let them be mixed well, the vessel being closed inviolably and sealed with a lute <note>a paste used to seal chemical vessels</note> made of quicklime, ochre made from mallow, egg white, and a little wool or hair. Once the luting has been dried twice or thrice, let the vessel be placed in a furnace made in the manner of a small book <note>likely a specific shape of portable furnace</note>, with the mouth turned downward, but first having been well heated. Let the furnace be closed very tightly, with a very small hole left in the upper part of the furnace, and let it stay there for twelve hours. When the vessel has cooled, open it, and you will find the quicksilver congealed, having drunk all the water. Add another three ounces of the aforementioned sharpest vinegar of the philosophers, rectified seven times, and let it be done as above; and let this be done three times. But after the third time, you will find

### **How the white elixir is converted into the sun-making elixir <note>the elixir for gold</note>. Chapter 73.**

And God be praised, who honors whom He wills; and there is no other God besides Him, the wise and honored. The white elixir is converted into the sun-making <note>gold-making</note> elixir in this manner: You shall take it after you have brought it to this [previous] state, and cast upon it eight ounces of the sharpest vinegar of the philosophers and half an ounce of the dregs <note>original: "fenibus"; likely *faecibus*</note> which remained thick and coarse and red, over which the vinegar of the philosophers was rectified seven times (as was said above regarding the "twelfth water" which is called the sharpest vinegar of the philosophers). Let them be mixed well in the smallest details and replaced in its vessel in the manner previously mentioned for the white [elixir]. And let this be done three times, just as in the sum of the silver and water, and you will find the sun-making elixir. One part of this converts a thousand parts of silver <note>original: "lūe"; *lunae*</note> into brittle gold, and one part of this gold converts forty parts of tin <note>original: "Iouis"; Jupiter</note> into firm gold. This, therefore, is the congealing and the dissolving which results in a softness like soft wax and moisture. And it is that which the philosophers obscured and covered up; they placed the "greater solution and coagulation" in the Great Work. And among them were those who set eight days, and among them nine, in the moisture.

## Into the Greatest Elixir. Concerning the Greatest Elixir.

<margin>Composition of the elixir</margin>
Make an amalgam of one part gold and twelve parts quicksilver. Afterward, take one pound of the "Vinegar of the Philosophers" <note>a specialized solvent, not household vinegar</note> rectified seven times, and let four ounces be mixed together. Place them in a chamber in heat for one night. In the morning, extract it and add another four ounces, and let this be done three times; then the matter will be converted into the elixir. One part of this converts a thousand parts of mercury or another imperfect body into perfect, grindable "Sun" <note>gold</note>. One part of this converts fifteen parts of Jove <note>term: "iovis"; alchemical code for tin</note> into gold, passing every test.
Its power can be multiplied unto infinity through the addition of the "Vinegar of Vinegars" of the philosophers. This is the work of Kings and Emperors. Once the "sharpest vinegar" is obtained, it is completed in three days. This can be done with mercury and other spirits, both together and separately, and with the same weights: using white [ingredients] for the White [Elixir/Silver] and red [ingredients] for the Red [Elixir/Gold].

# In the testament of Geber, the extraction of salts from all things is treated, as much from corporeal living things as from other things and metals.

->Introduction<-

From all animal things and even minerals—likewise from fish, birds, and other living things—salt can be made once they have been burned and reduced to a fixed ash or earth. This is done in the same manner that salt is made from the ashes of wood or from the lime of stones, from which the white or red elixir <note>The "Elixir" refers to the philosopher's stone in its liquid or powdered form, capable of transmuting metals or healing the body.</note> is made. And if the substances were naturally white or red, their salt will become white or red. 

However, the combustion of all natural things ought to be done in a closed vessel. And if it should be blood, let it first be dried. It is not a bad thing if two parts of common salt are dissolved in eight parts of blood. It is also calcined <note>term: calcination; the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to cause thermal decomposition or oxidation.</note> in a furnace, then dried. Afterward, let them be burned in a glassmaker's or potter's furnace, or a reverberatory furnace, for a day and a night, or gradually over two days without the nights. 

And if there should be flesh or other animal parts that cannot be stolen <note>original: "furari"; likely a scribal error or archaic usage for "pulverized" or "separated".</note>, then you shall burn them in a well-closed vessel for two days and nights so they do not breathe <note>i.e., so the vapors do not escape</note>, without any salt. After the combustion, boil it in four times its weight of rainwater until two and a half parts are consumed. Let it rest

<column-break/>

and distill it through a filter until the water becomes very clear without any cloudiness. Then congeal it over a slow fire, or what is better, in the sun; and you will have the animal salt which surpasses others in its sensitive virtue. 

Then resolve it in twice its weight of rainwater; place this in dung <note>Dung was used as a source of steady, gentle heat for fermentation or digestion.</note> for a week, and it will be sharper. Finally, congeal it as was said. Or do it without the dung and place it upon metals; if it enters them, the animal salt is good. If not, repeat its solution and congelation, and its efficacy will be declared to you through experience. 

And know that the ash of a whole burned mole <note>original: "talpe"</note> congeals Mercury <note>Mercury/Quicksilver</note>, and converts Venus <note>Copper</note> into the Sun <note>Gold</note>, and Mars <note>Iron</note> into the Moon <note>Silver</note>. Some, however, work with its powder, yet by adding double the amount between the animal salt and the salt of urine or sea salt <note>original: "vūri vel miri"; likely abbreviations for "urinae" and "maris".</note>.

---

### Concerning the salts of all metals and their calcination

In like manner, salts are made from metals after their calcination; and these salts are living, penetrating, and fixing, by reason of their subtlety and sharpness. This is either because they are from fixed things, or because they have been calcined in the fire for a long time. Truly, because metals are calcined in the fire in different ways, we must see to the calcination of those which are for the "red" <note>The "Red Work" or Rubedo, the final stage of the alchemical process.</note>, such as the Sun <insert>Gold</insert>, Venus <insert>Copper</insert>, and Saturn <insert>Lead</insert>.

### Concerning the salt of Venus, and its calcination.

**V**enus <note>Copper</note> is calcined in an open vessel: in thirty-five days, or forty. Indeed, even for two months in a glassmaker's furnace: and there remains only its red tint in the appearance of blood: from which you should extract the salt: as was said concerning the Sun: and it will become an elixir.

### Concerning the property of the salt of metals.

**A**lso know this: that the salt of each and every metal, made in the proper manner, fixes and tints Mercury. And it changes it from color to color: and from state to state by reason of its sharpness <note>Acidity or corrosive power</note>.

### Concerning the salt of Saturn and its calcination and vivification into the Sun

**S**aturn <note>Lead</note> is calcined into a lemon-yellow color: in a reverberatory furnace: and it is better in a closed vessel: or in a glassmaker's furnace: which indeed is not purged of its blackness in fifteen days, nor in twenty-five. Therefore, by keeping it in the furnace for about forty days: or for two months. It finally perfects itself, whether purged or not purged. And it will have a blackness <note>original: "atrimitatem"</note> to ascend.

## On the reduction of Jupiter into the salt of alkali and silver

Tin <note>original: "Jupiter"</note> is calcined in seven days. # To make borax.

**T**ake one pound of rebelled mercury <note>mercury that has been processed or "subdued"</note>: and 4 ounces of sal ammoniac: and 4 ounces of salt of Nuri <note>possibly a reference to a specific alkali or "fire salt"</note>: from which they produce fire: and dissolve all these in clear cold water: distill all these through a filter: and congeal it: and it will be borax. <margin>X a.</margin> And if you wish the borax to be stony—which is better—or pasty. If you wish it to be stony: take care to congeal that distilled water in the sun: and it will be stony. If, however, you wish it to be pasty—which is worse—then congeal that water by the fire: and then it will be pasty. Note that a pound of the stony kind is sold for three pounds of pence, and the pasty kind for 24 shillings.

# Regarding the sublimation and extraction of the tin of Jupiter <note>tin</note>.

**N**ote concerning the acetate of Jupiter: and its sublimation, which is perhaps sublimated in salt of nitre <note>potassium nitrate</note>. Try to sublimate Jupiter <note>tin</note> thus: Take 3 ounces of it, which you should amalgamate with 3 ounces of mercury and 24 [parts] of sal ammoniac: and the calx of eggshells or gypsum, 3 ounces. Sublimate it; let it be somewhat thick so that it remains at the bottom; what resides after sublimation should be reduced into a "body" <note>returned to a metallic state</note>: an amalgam of silver if you wish. Also note that the salt of metals is distilled by itself through a filter, and when congealed in the sun, it allows that which came out in the urinal to congeal. Also note that the salt of metals allows mercury to be dissolved under dung, and that coagulated mixture will be a perfect medicine.

**Now** you, who seek this knowledge, know that we have explained it in many ways. # Here begins the twelfth book of words which Geber composed concerning the vinegar of the philosophers: the first word

<margin>The philosophers' vinegar <note>Latin: acetum philosophorum. A specialized acidic solvent used in alchemy, not common table vinegar.</note></margin>
Take water distilled from egg whites seven times, and one part of lime made from eggshells <note>Latin: calce costirum ovorum. Likely referring to calcined or burnt eggshells reduced to a powder.</note>. Place these in a vessel, seal the joint, and place it in dung <note>Latin: in fimo. Horse dung was used as a consistent, low-heat source for slow digestion or fermentation.</note> for seven days. Remove it and distill it with a warm, moist heat. Save what remains in the bottom of the distilling vessel <note>term: cucurbite (Cucurbit). The lower, gourd-shaped part of a still.</note>. Again, place one part of lime into the aforementioned water, ensuring there are seven parts of water to one of lime, and proceed as above three times. This is called the "Vinegar of the Philosophers."

## The Second Word

<margin>The composition, distillation, and the philosophers' broth</margin>
Next, take as many fresh eggs as you wish; place them in a glass vessel and fill it with the "Vinegar of the Philosophers" from the first word. Seal the joint carefully and place it in dung for fourteen days. Afterward, remove them and wipe the moisture from the eggs. Place them in a perforated vessel <note>Latin: vase cribellato. A vessel with small holes, acting like a strainer or sieve.</note> and seal the joint. Place this in dung for fifteen days, then remove it. The water that distills into the receiver from the eggs is called "Red Wine."

<margin>Concerning red wine and clear water</margin>
Likewise, distill the water called the "Vinegar of the Philosophers" from the first word as described above; this is called the "Clear Broth" <note>term: brodium (Broth). A liquid extract or decoction used as a base in alchemical recipes.</note>.

## The Third Word

<margin>The composition of the cold and the moist</margin>
Break the stone <note>The hardened or transformed egg material.</note> that you placed in the perforated vessel. From the whites, extract the yolks and rub them

<column-break/>

in the palm of the hand. Save that which is most red. Place it in a distilling vessel and distill it as is customary by means of a warm and moist heat. That which distills is called the "Cold, Moist Soul" <note>Latin: anima frigida humida.</note>; it is the "Western Matter." Keep it aside along with its dregs <note>Latin: fetibus. Literally "offspring" or "fetuses," but in this chemical context refers to the residues or sediments left after distillation.</note>.

## The Fourth Word

<margin>Concerning the composition of the hot and dry spirit</margin>
Afterward, take half of the dregs from the first word and place them into sponges made of hair, and suspend these in the distilling vessel. Fill the vessel with the vinegar you distilled and the dregs of the "Clear Broth" from the second word. Boil this over a warm, moist heat for a natural day <note>A 24-hour period.</note>. Afterward, open it; carefully collect the oil that you see on top of the water. Do this two more times, always distilling the clear broth. Save the oil, for it is the "Hot, Dry Spirit" and the "Eastern Matter."

## The Fifth Word

<margin>Concerning the red oil, the great tincture, the white body, and sulfur</margin>
Next, place the sponges with the dregs into the distilling vessel and fill it with the distilled clear broth. Seal it and place it in dung for seven days. Remove it and collect the oil that rises to the top. Do this two more times, always distilling the broth, placing it in dung, and collecting it again until no more rises in the water. This is the "Red Oil" and the "Great Tincture" <note>term: tinctura (Tincture). A potent substance capable of transforming or coloring other materials, often a goal of the Great Work.</note>. That which is left behind in the sponges is the "White Body" and the "Sulfur" which does not ascend and has not ascended. Save this.

# On the composition of the paste of purity

Now take <gloss>The 6th Word</gloss> another half part of the dregs <note>original: "fenis," likely referring to the faeces or dregs of a previous distillation</note> which remained in the 3rd word, and place it in a glazed vessel: and distill through it. ### Concerning the seven magisteries, namely:
**Sal ammoniac** is hot in the 3rd degree, dry in the 2nd, porous in the 4th, white in the 3rd. It has the power to diminish weight and brings [the metal] back to the state of Silver <note>original: "lunae"</note>. Thus it is held to give heat, dryness, porosity, whiteness, and the weight of silver to metals that are being rarefied. It is made from human blood, mineral salt, and sea water or brine.
**Salt gem** <term>Sal gema: rock salt or pure crystalline salt</term> is hot in the 1st degree, white in the 3rd, fixed in the 4th, and not porous in the 3rd. It has the power to give greater weight, heat, purity <note>or perhaps "oiliness"</note>, whiteness, and fixity. It is made from salt alkali, mineral salt, and sea water.
**Salt nitre** <term>Sal nitri: potassium nitrate/saltpeter</term> is hot in the 1st degree, dry in the 1st, white in the 2nd, porous in the 4th (otherwise 3rd), and has the power to lighten weight. It is made from salt gem and salt alkali.
**Salt of lime** is hot in the 2nd degree, moist in the 3rd, white in the 1st (otherwise 3rd), fixed in the 2nd (otherwise 3rd). It is not porous, lightens weight, and confirms moisture. It is made from salt nitre and white salt, or by ablation, or from salt alembroth.
**Salt of Jove** <note>Salt of Tin</note> is hot and dry in the 2nd degree.
**Salt alkali** is hot in the 1st degree, not porous, heavy in the 4th degree, dark in the 3rd. It is made from salt gem and nitre well-ground.
**Salt alembroth** <term>Sal alembroth: a "salt of art" or double salt of mercury and ammonium chloride</term> is the master of all magisteries. It is hot, moist, heavy, and red by itself; it congeals and holds quicksilver, and silver, and <unclear>...</unclear>

<column-break/>

<unclear>...</unclear> is turned into the purest gold <note>original: "solem"</note>, afterwards one eighth in any other, then one over ninety in any other.

### Concerning the requirements in the transformations of metals
The mastery in transformations is this: when you wish to transmute one metal into another, then retain those things which agree and remove those things which disagree with the "Lord of the Magistery." For example, if you wish to reduce Saturn <note>Lead</note> to Silver <note>Luna</note>, consider what that magistery is which is seen to be necessary to bring the heavy weight back to that of Silver: namely, salt gem and nitre; and that which has the power to give porosity and whiteness: sal ammoniac. You should therefore place it with the Lead in the fire with good light <note>or perhaps "good sealing clays"</note>. And know that you show no perfection unless, in whatever degree nature lacks that which you desire it to have, you add eight parts of that magistery which has the power to give that nature.

### Concerning the increasing of the weight of any body
Take salt alkali, salt of dew, and sea water. Let them boil, and there temper that which you wish to increase in weight.

# Here begins the twelfth book of waters
->Rhazes<- <note>original: "Rasis" - referring to the famous Persian alchemist and physician Abu Bakr al-Razi.</note>

I will arrange the sequence of this little book into 12 chapters: 1. on red water; 2. on the burning of copper <note>original: "naassu" - likely from the Arabic 'nahas' for copper</note>; 3. on rust; 4. on saffron of iron; 5. on red agate; 6. on sulfur water; 7. on the arteries of the soul <note>likely a poetic or technical term for vital chemical vapors</note>; 8. on juniper; 9. on penetrating water; 10. on the water of marcasite and the dissolution of silver; 11. on glassy water; 12. on ferment. First:

### On how red water is prepared.

Grind the yolks of eggs <note>original: "Elixyroz" - a corruption of the Greek 'lekithos' for egg yolk</note> equally until they return to the appearance of marrow. Place the whole mixture in a glazed vessel smeared within an alembic <note>a distilling apparatus</note>. It will give off a thick, reddish-saffron water. When it cools, it will be darker and liquid, but of a reddish color. The signs of this are such: if you dip a reed or pen into it and mark something white, its surface will show a saffron color, which it afterwards transforms into a blackish hue. Second:

### On the burning of the test

When the copper <note>naassa</note> is melted, add sulfur and saffron bit by bit, stone after stone. When it is burned so that nothing remains, take the glass. Then grind and save it; generally, it has no shadow. You shall scrape that or the red water we spoke of above two, three, or four times; and placed in an earthen vessel, press it down with a weight and cook it inside until it reaches redness. When these are the

<column-break/>

signs, namely the second part of the mixture, you shall pour it carefully both above and below the balance, and allow it to stand. What has been extracted will take on a little more weight and a devoted saffron color. This must be repeated two or three times until the surface appears clear even when rubbed, and remains golden. For it can be mixed with any kind of lead. But if you pour it again onto prepared iron <note>original: "marte" - Mars is the alchemical symbol for iron</note>, you will see the copper changed into a red color and transformed outwardly, and there will be a tincture in the mixture. It is strong in the work, yet it will render the metal more brittle. Fifth, concerning the prepared lead.

### 3. On rusty water

Take five pounds of oxide composed from vinegar. Since it consists of one part vinegar, grind it on a marble slab for two or three hours until it softens. It ferments after this heat; add two parts of water and grind again for two hours, and keep it dried. For it is approved by this sign: a small amount is to be placed upon silver plates; then close them and let them sit for one hour. When it is washed off, you will find its redness.

### 4. On iron water

Take one part of unripe "aleedidu" <note>likely a mineral or salt</note> and half a part of saffron-colored orpiment <note>arsenic trisulfide</note>. Grind them together and roast them in a sealed vessel for one night. When it has been extracted once, repeat until the liquefaction becomes clear.

### 6th: On the Sulfurous Water

Take 3 parts or 1 part of yellow sulfur, crushed: and in a pitch-coated flask, bake it in hot ashes for one day and one night. Then, having extracted it, crush it again. Whenever you rub a hand or a ring and things of that sort with the same, it will take on a golden color.

Or rather, if it is melted: and you wash a coin therein, it will appear like gold: however, it will not last.

### 7th: On the Lutarzu Water <note>possibly 'lute' or 'litharge' water</note>

Take 2 or 1 part of cinnabar; 3 parts of red orpiment; 3 parts of wine dregs: when these are placed in a luted vessel, add boiling water three times over. And this is the sign in boiling and pure water of this kind: if you wash a coin, it will take on a golden color, yet it will not last.

### 8th: On the Red Water

From the yolks of eggs: let their water or oil be sublimated. Subjected to almost the same process, it exalts the white of the eggs. And mix the distillate so that it covers it more: and cook it with a slow fire over hot ashes until it grows red. It is of small virtue. Then, from the oil of that gum, with the water almost melted, you shall place it in the gourd of an alembic <note>a chemical still</note> with fire added until it is sublimated white: and the tinted part remains, retaining the likeness of gum. If therefore you wish to test it: place it upon coins in the manner of grains: for it will obtain the appearance of gold on all sides: which, if you heat it much, will vanish, and it will be white. If you heat that same thing upon silver for a moment, it will return to a golden color.

### 9th: On the Penetrating Water

Holding alkali dissolved in water, we command it to be <unclear>isquerdo</unclear>: until you consume 14 pounds of alkali for 14 pounds of water, repeating it 19 times. Hence, this water penetrates all things that are in the world; vinegar dissolved with <unclear>reaf</unclear> produces a sediment.

# Alchemical Compendium

### 10. Concerning Saffron Water.
Take as much of the best saffron <note>original: "crocee"</note> as you wish: and cook it for a day with distilled vinegar. Afterward, you shall strain it. Place the same in a cucurbit <note>a gourd-shaped chemical vessel</note> with an alembic <note>a distilling lid</note> placed on top; it will distill a water. These are its signs: for if you paint a sword or a mirror with it, it will become black; after you have wiped it away, it will turn red and take on a golden color.

### 11. Concerning Softening Water and Slow Fires.
Take two or three parts [of the substance] and one or two parts of lime <note>original: "calas"</note>. Take one part of alkali salt <note>potash or soda</note>, having first added twelve or twenty parts of water. Leave it for a week and stir it well. Afterward, you will find a most clear water. The power of this water consists in its clarity.

### 12. Concerning the Water of Atramentum.
Take the purest vitriol <note>original: "atramentu vtreide," likely green vitriol or iron sulfate</note>. Place it carefully in a luted vessel <note>sealed with clay</note> and put it in a bath furnace or a similar place for one night until it cooks and turns red. Once it has become red, add three times the amount of distilled vinegar. Place the whole mixture in a large flask and leave it for seven days, stirring it three times daily. Afterward, distill the water, which will be red. Indeed, this water lights candles and illuminates the gods <note>likely a reference to brightening metallic statues or icons</note>, works which are highly necessary.

Here ends the Book of the Twelve Waters of Rhazes <note>original: "Rasis," the Latinized name of the 9th-century Persian physician and alchemist al-Razi</note>.

Take 3 lbs of Vitriol <note>iron or copper sulfate</note>, 3 lbs of Saltpeter <note>potassium nitrate</note>, and 4 lbs of Cinnabar <note>mercury sulfide</note>. A certain clear water will distill, the power of which is great. Keep this in a glass vessel very well sealed with wax. From this, a second water of many virtues will be distilled.

The sign for recognizing this second water is sought in this way: if you place a knife under a falling drop, it will corrode it, blacken it, and bubble upon the iron as if it were on a fire. Another sign is this: a certain red smoke will rise into the head of the alembic, as if there were a dark cloud there. Another is that if you place a drop of mercury <note>original: "mercurij"</note> under a falling drop of the water, it will devour it. Then, having seen these signs, or any that suffice, change the flask or receiver—namely, by lifting the flask and placing a sufficient receiver, sealing it well so it does not breathe. Then, strengthen the fire, for then the water begins to distill, of which I shall make mention below. Arrange it so that the receiver stands in a pot full of cold water, so that the vapors of the water may be cooled. Then you shall strengthen the fire until...

# For making potable gold <note>original: "Ad faciendum aurum potabile." Potable or "drinkable" gold was a legendary medicinal elixir in alchemy believed to grant longevity and cure various ailments.</note>

In the beginning, cement the gold <note>original: "aurum," represented by the symbol $\odot$</note> so that it is fine and without any alloy, and file it very finely. Afterward, take 4 parts of well-ground white sugar <note>original: "cuitari candi," likely a variant of "zucchari candi."</note> and one part of the said washed Sun <note>The "Sun" is the alchemical name for gold.</note>. Grind everything together on a porphyry stone for 4 hours, so much so that nothing of the aforementioned gold appears. And do this in a place without wind. Afterward, take a vessel of polished brass, like a barber's basin, and put in it two parts of rose water distilled through an alembic <note>A chemical still used for distillation.</note>. Put the sugar itself inside until it dissolves, and place the vessel itself upon an iron tripod. Make a fire beneath it as if for the boiling of water; and afterward, remove the said vessel from the fire and allow it to cool. Gently pour off the water, and in the bottom of the vessel you will find the gold, which you should dry by the fire. Once the gold is dried, return to the porphyry with 4 parts of white sugar, as you did before, grinding it well. Place it in the aforementioned vessel in the same order as before with new water, doing in all things as the first time. And do this four times. Afterward, take two vessels of fine silver; in one, place the aforementioned gold, and over it place a quantity of the essence of water of life <note>original: "aqua vite," usually referring to concentrated alcohol or brandy.</note> so much so that the light of the gold you saw is covered. And afterward, set it on fire with a wax candle. Then take a thick iron plate like a knife, and cover it with the other silver vessel so that there is space between one bowl <note>original: "tasteam," a small tasting cup or shallow bowl.</note> and the other, so that the water of life can burn inside; and let the bowl cool.

<column-break/>

And take the powder of the gold and grind it on the porphyry for a good hour, or until it is an impalpable powder <note>A powder so fine it cannot be felt between the fingers.</note>, which you must keep from the wind. Afterward, put it into the bowl, doing as before by putting into the gold the same amount of fire as the first time. Afterward, allow the bowls to cool, and likewise grind the said powder as before. And do this seven times, and it will be an impalpable powder. Then take 3 ounces <note>The symbol .3. denotes an ounce.</note> of the aforementioned powder of calcined gold <margin>folio 78</margin> as above, and 1 ounce of vegetable salt <note>Likely potash or a salt derived from plant matter.</note>, and 1 quarter-ounce of quintessence of water of life. Put these in a flask <note>original: "bozza."</note> and place it in the furnace to be distilled with the receiver stopped up; and distill 6 ounces of the quantity. And if it does not all distill, take the distillate and put it in a flask. Put over it a good quantity of the phlegm <note>The watery, non-active byproduct of distillation.</note> of four fingers' depth, and make it boil a little. Afterward, let it cool, and gently empty the aforementioned phlegm into a bowl so that nothing remains in the flask. After it has settled, pour the phlegm back into that same flask from which you took it, and save it. Place the bowl with the powders over a slow fire to dry. Put water of life over it and set it on fire with a wax candle, covering it with the other bowl in the manner aforesaid. And after the water of life has been consumed, grind it upon the porphyry. And do this 4 times, just as it was done seven times the first time. Afterward, weigh it, and put into it 4 parts of its vegetable salt and a quantity of quintessence of water of life, and set it to distill as in the first time.

# To separate sulfur from the fifth essence

Take "Baale" wine <note>likely a specific regional wine or a symbolic name</note> and place eggs in it as described above. And place in it 3 ounces and 20 grains of common distilled water, and 1 ounce of the <term>fifth essence</term> <note>quinta essentia: the purest, most concentrated medicinal or alchemical spirit of a substance</note>. Cast this into the water standing in a basin: and let it stand for 2 days in quiet. And you will find the sulfur in the depths: strain the water: and again allow it to stand for 2 days in quiet. If any sulfur remains in the bottom, look at the bottom and do as above. Afterwards, dry it by the heat of a fire; and once the sulfur is dried, place it upon a porphyry stone in a humid place to be resolved into water, and you will have <term>potable sulfur</term> <note>a liquid form of sulfur intended for medicinal ingestion</note>.

# Method of making vegetable salt.

Take the best and strongest "Ruben" wine <note>red wine</note> and extract the fifth essence: and save it for the aforementioned operation. Afterwards, thoroughly remove the phlegm <note>the watery, non-potent part of a distillate</note> from the wine remaining from the fifth essence of the water of life <note>aqua vite: concentrated alcohol</note>: and reserve it for making vegetable salt as follows.
Take the dregs remaining in the vessel and produce a good quantity in the manner described. Having obtained a sufficient quantity, place it in a cauldron over the fire: and make it boil and exhale until it remains like liquid honey: because it cannot be dried further.
This being done, take the said dregs thus prepared: and place them in a vessel and put them in dung <note>a common method for providing gentle, steady warmth for fermentation or digestion</note> for 20 days. Afterwards, place it for distillation in the furnace: and distill the water perfectly like the first phlegm, and allow the dregs to dry. When they are dry, break the vessel. And take the dregs and place them to be calcined <note>reduced to ash by heat</note>

<column-break/>

like tartar in a reverberatory furnace, calcining with the dregs. Take a glazed basin, or one of unglazed earth, and grind those dregs thus calcined. Afterwards, take some of the phlegm remaining in the vessel and mix it with the dregs. And then distill it through a "tongue" <note>a strip of cloth or wick used for capillary distillation</note>. Afterwards, place it in a vessel to evaporate, either with an alchemical still or without. And it will be made into salt: and this is <term>vegetable salt</term>. Note that the aforementioned dregs ought to be well calcined until they reach whiteness.

# To dye the color of gold: and for binding it and silver to the sun.

<margin>Recipe</margin>
Take: <term>Sal ammoniac</term> <note>ammonium chloride</note>, <term>saltpeter</term> <note>potassium nitrate</note>, <term>vitriol</term> <note>sulfate minerals</note>, <term>verdigris</term> <note>green copper acetate</note>, and <term>ferzetto</term> <note>likely a calcined iron or copper byproduct</note> in equal parts. ### For making fixed silver which can and ought to be tinted and converted into true gold. And first concerning the preparation of common salt. —:

# The Book of Raymond Lull on Composing the Philosophers' Stone

## Here begins the third distinction, which concerns the living spirit <note>original: "aura vivi," literally the "living breeze" or "breath," referring to the volatile vital essence in alchemy</note> and the mastery of those things in the works, both greater and lesser, in a specific form.

<margin>living</margin>
**T**his is the third distinction of this book, which concerns the living spirit <gloss>of the stone</gloss> in this work of the philosophers, both in the greater and the lesser work. And we reveal the reason or intention of these established parts of the art so that each person, through those things which can be understood from above, Lord, may understand the *Testaments* and the *Codicil* <note>Two of the most famous works attributed to Raymond Lull in the alchemical tradition</note>. If, through these condensed and contracted writings, a true knowledge is held concerning the stone <note>original: "calculo," a small stone or pebble</note> and its composition. For in that art, we can place many principles under that part already held, so that with all study, one may perfectly and for a long time understand, love, and recollect, and through it have the true method concerning the living transformation <note>transmutation</note>. And also so that the artist of this art may be able to study the artificial path according to the condition of the principles of this art, and so that he may avoid the deceits and fictions of other philosophers under which they have hidden that secret. They have hidden it in such a way that to one reading their writings, <margin>fruit</margin> they deny the ability to draw fruit without great effort, by providing arguments against their own authoritative responses, which are of no utility but were made as cautions for their own sake. For this reason, we reject the origins of Lanius, Archelaus, Alexander, and those of the race of Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the famous Arabic alchemist</note>, and even Avicenna and Albert <note>Albertus Magnus</note>, who involved themselves in many deceits, figures, or verses. For we ought to know that writings which cannot be understood for practical use are to be considered as if they were not written at all. What I speak of concerns the bodies and the writings; do not care in any way for the principal treatise of this distinction in theory and practice, and first concerning the

<column-break/>

division of the implicit parts of the theory itself up to its practice, of which there are parts.

**A**nd first, the distinction is divided into two principal parts, namely into the theoretical and the practical. And the theory, having been made by God as a declaration, <margin>triangular</margin> we declare these very things through natural operations. Although in these first parts, each of them is placed in the art, and we intend that whole method in the principal <margin>and square</margin> tree and in the principal circular figure. And in the practical declaration, we place that which governs these principles. And of these, the method of the greater work is given through the tree, and one table is extracted from it, and through the figure of individuals, and also through six figures, of which one is triangular and another indeed quadrangular, mixed with the principles of physics and all things in the greater work. We designate the method through the circular figure and all other tables in their proper place, and also the species which we shall designate at the end, in which it will be seen whether transubstantiation is possible, and also what the modes of composition are. Concerning this, an argument can be made through those things which have been said; let the artist of this art find the perpendicular which shall be, and let him reach these things in which the whole mastery of this art consists. And there are 28 [parts of] Chaos or force, as volatile matter, as is evident through the circulations, the radiation of the tree, and the circular figure. And it must not be said that the figures themselves are the principles, but they are regulated according to certain things which are repeated, as is evident. Wherefore the third [distinction] shows that all bodies are reducible to that which is led from those principles.

## Concerning the constitution of the root of the physical tree which is noted in this chapter

Furthermore, from the aforementioned principles, the physical root is constituted, which is a single wheel in which each small wheel of the principles has its place, situated according to divided colors. And each of these is conditioned by a particular entry, which comes forth from those principles; it signifies and constitutes a few things in a certain circular figure. In this, each wheel of the principles is arranged and <unclear>lightens</unclear> itself, which is designated under the same theme of colors and other principles designated in a circular manner. As is established, each signifies its own way of entering into another, from the virtue and operation of which the unity of **M** or **Q** is established and individualized. Indeed, although **M** or **Q** arises from all the principles, by their virtue and accomplishment, it holds within itself **M** or **Q** from a single substantial virtue which is tripled within the multitude of the divisions of the principles.

## Concerning the mixture of the principles of this art and their foundation and declaration

Furthermore, this mixture is the root and foundation in this art, so that through it, the artificial construction may be understood, and through it, one may acquire the art and the method of operating in manifold ways according to a certain mixture of the said things. Thus, that same particular thing which is sought may come from potentiality into act. And because the understanding of nature consists of the manner according to which a spiritual substance arises, grows, lives, and is nourished. However, it must be known that a physical substance is never able to be led from potentiality to act if any of the said principles are lacking, or if it is habituated toward a <term>base end</term> <note>original: "fine genero," likely referring to a corruption in the generation process</note>. For example, if **P** or **B** should take **T**, and through the wheel **V**, the digestion is habituated toward rawness; this can happen unless it is demonstrated through act and administration. And it should also be noted that some of these principles are intellectual, which are: **Chaos, Potentiality, Operation, Generation,** and **Digestion**. Others are sensory, which are: **Universal or Prime Matter, Body or Form, the Elemental** according to being, **Transforming Poison** <note>original: "venenum transformans," likely a potent reactive agent in alchemical change</note>, **Colors, Fission,** and **Separation**. The sensory and intellectual principles are under the rules and order of the principles of **Figure B**. Furthermore, each of these principles retains its own proper property under its own proper reasoning of difference, since some properties are innate and others are the beginnings of profit.

Therefore, because this instrument retains itself under its own genus by reason, the properties of another are made by the principles of the craft.
</margin>

For that which holds priority is nature, the first or any of the principles in the figure of individuals; and it holds itself as the form of the past and the <term>first matter</term> <note>materia prima: the formless primordial substance from which all things are made</note> by reason of priority before the day, etc. From these two, all other principles arise through the mediation of the <term>craftsman</term> <note>artista: the practitioner or alchemist</note>. Thus, having placed these also through the mediation of various things, we propose to declare this first matter, which the principles of the **Physical Tree** [derive] from it as if from a worthier and higher mastery in the physical work; and first, concerning the first principle.

# Concerning the second theoretical part, which is the declaration of any principle through natural operations; and first, concerning the principle of the Physical Tree, which is A.

**Chaos** is the first principle in the **Physical Tree** and is designated by **.a.** in the middle of the wheel with the rays of the said tree. It is positioned and designated by this art as the confusion and obscurity of the intellect; for it is greatly confused and obscure to the intellect of those ignorant of it, so much so that some regard it as a <term>chimera</term> <note>a mythical beast; here meaning a fabrication or impossibility</note>, and many are those who consider the intellect more as a shadow than as a light. Therefore, we propose that the principle be designated so that it may be a demonstrative sign of the confusion and obscurity of the intellect. It also designates that there is a generated confusion in which all these principles are united in their consistency, or they themselves are in potentiality. <margin>S</margin> Whence, just as nature in the first matter constitutes chaos, so the blue square in **.g.** constitutes the principles themselves and abstracts from it the possible relationship to be applied, so that each of them may be under the reason of its proper difference; and nature [orders] each of the elements under the reason of the difference of quantity and operations.

<column-break/>

Recalling also that just as nature makes an instrument from the four elements from which the metallic substance is composed, so the square in the said aforementioned principles makes an instrument in which a particular mastery may precede, which seeks and by equal investigation returns to the truth, an abstract innate argument. For nature stands as a medium between the created and the uncreated. Just so, the craftsman in these arts [stands] between **.a.** and the medium, which are the various principles and the matter, such as **.q.** in the various triangles, understanding it to be possible and refinable—the matter or the **.q.**—and to lead it into act by the mediation of **b. c. d.** and the rest. And the reason is for the motion which the craftsman makes by moving the aforementioned principles which refer to the matter, so that **.q.** comes into **.c.** through the ordering of the principles which exist above them. This principle is placed in this location so that from the confusion of the intellect, the various principles may be made abstractly; thus, the particular is abstracted by the philosopher by touching each of the principles with the said species, by which therefore each is mixed with the other and made to combine so that the same particular thing which is sought may arise.

# Concerning the second principle of the rays of the Philosophical Tree.

**Form** is the principle in the root of the **Philosophical Tree** designated by **.i.**, which is considered as a double quality; and in this volume, it is placed as directing the principles with these arts and by the regulation of the matter, so that **.q.** may be adorned and led into being, moving the sensory principles and making the instrument with which the intellectual principles are moved and regulated in the operation of the matter, such as **.q.**; and the craftsman of this art transforms the form successively to different operations, and in this step, the intellect consists through the principles or the transformations.

**U**ltramarine or azure is the first principle <note>original: "1$^m$ p$^m$" (primum principium)</note> in this art, and it is understood through what is figured as the First Principle D. The color azure and the lines of the same color, along with the pale color, signify that which is celestial and of a celestial nature, as we fully described in the first distinction. When the rest [is explained] in the second part, do not consider that the mind appeared twice; it was captured thus without matter in this part. And you should understand what is said here by reason of its incorruptibility and duration; remember this through the angel above all reasons which are said of the First Principle D. Understand that this is not a difficulty, but it stands before the intellect as a rational, intellectual, and sensual man. For it has in itself the aspect of an incorruptible spirit, which is like the soul, and it has in itself the power of producing reason, which generates and produces from itself the [preeminent?] form; in this, it differs from other principles. It is also sensual because it is perceived through the senses, such as sight, taste, and smell, as was [stated] in the first distinction, second part. Furthermore, the Moon <note>symbol: $\text{\leftmoon}$</note> is the cause and the first mover, as the Sun <note>symbol: $\odot$</note> leads toward the white and the red; that which is in the cause, as the Sun in potentiality, leads toward the act, ruling and governing in its womb, just as a wife who procreates an infant. So the Sun, in this step, stands before the intellect of the artist, because the author has the Sun ruling and governing in its womb and leading into act, just as the rest of that which is exhorted in elemental things is led to act by the first movement.

<column-break/>

Indeed, in the First Principle D, there is that generative, progressive, and nutritive [force], just like the menstrual blood in the male fetus; for this reason, many names are given to the First Principle D in this art and throughout the entire volume. For it is called "superior" by reason of its motion, because just as the superior sphere moves all forms and primary matter and chaos and passions toward appropriate, finished, and individuated ends, so D moves the rest, as the Sun toward the four [elements], and this is what this species intends. Therefore, regarding formality, how great a species is added! Equally, we note in the First Principle D the menstrual blood or "menstruum," because it is generative, nutritive, and conservative, and it makes the result endure. Just as the menstrual blood of the embryo is so small, yet it creates through distinct quantities and putrefactions, changing and altering one thing into another quality and property and into other forms; and every form of such principles and qualities, being composed in every alteration under the forms themselves, differs from other principles. These are a certain being constituted in quality, through present discrete qualities, which is a body made of spirit and soul, brought into act. And so it is with the infant; in this step, it stands before the intellect that the First Principle D has a vegetative property, and it transmits a likeness into the matter, just as the vegetative power of the mother transmits the likeness of that which she generates, by which property the son retains the likeness. And it also establishes the difference, which property is retained when it extends its likeness in the subjects to which it is transmuted.

# On the Two Substances and the Royal Species
### Concerning the Vegetable Principle

It should be noted that this is called "vegetable" <note>original: *vegerabilez*</note> because it is drawn from vegetable things. This principle is placed in this part so that the intellect may grasp and arrive at the knowledge of it, and so that it may understand the operation, virtue, and equality which it possesses according to its own nature. This principle is very useful in this art for preservation, as it preserves the intellect to which it is led. For reason, by the reason of its own sublimity, is feared by the philosophers. Note that the philosopher and the artist understand that from two substances, from which the <term>Magisterium</term> <note>The "Mastery" or the completed alchemical process/philosopher's stone.</note> is composed, one of them is the principal. This principle also stands as both mother and female, conceiving the masculine seed and bringing forth another form by the virtue which was in the beginning. In truth, you can note this also concerning the composition in the principles of the completion of the thing and the mastery of the philosophers, which <insert>in the vessel</insert> digests, coagulates, and **turns into stone** <note>original: *lapidificat*</note> until the total perfection.

### On the Mastery of the Art

Those who are born into this house <note>The "house" likely refers to the alchemical laboratory or the philosophical school of thought</note>. Furthermore, the **artist** <note>original: "artista" - the alchemist or practitioner</note> wished to create a certain figure according to the proportions of the work. In this passage, it is understood that there is one **digestion** <term>digestion: the process of maturing or refining a substance through gentle, continuous heat</term> which occurs between the **Sun** <note>original: "☉" - Gold or the masculine principle</note> and the **Moon** <note>original: "☽" - Silver or the feminine principle</note> toward the medium. Another occurs from the medium toward the end, through which there is a different mixing, alteration, digestion, and operation. Just as things differ according to their predicates, so bodies differ first in their substances, which participate in their perfection and highest goodness. Thus, human goodness is perfected in its own way, differing by the reason of its formation; for the human form is made good through one form, while the animal is made good through its own goodness from another form, as is evident to the senses. This occurs through intellectual principles, understood as the digestion which is between the **Sun** and the medium, and the medium toward the end. In this formative process they differ, because from the first digestion arises a certain formal quality, and from the second a certain difference which is the nature of the perfected quantity. This principle is placed in the Art so that the reasons and subjects of digestion may be understood by touching upon the causes with the agent, according to the angle at which it is graduated. And this principle is also very useful because through this digestion, other particular digestions are understood which are performed by the operator. The operation of this art takes place in **Figure B** and in the tables abstracted from it, and in the table abstracted from physical color and the figures of the divine, and the works of stones which are in the work of the ancients, in which our principles of this art are found. Therefore, it must be managed by those who love the bath <note>The "balneum" or water-bath (bain-marie) used for gentle heating</note>, such as vapor and fire, whether external or internal, in such a way that the principles are not habituated to an end without generation, which is rawness. In this passage, it is understood that the greatest caution must be applied in the administration of fires.

<column-break/>

And all of this is done through the **mastery** <note>original: "magysterium" - the specialized skill or "Great Work" of the alchemist</note> of the artist, and this is designated by the **red color** <note>original: "color rubeus"</note> existing in the middle between the **saffron-yellow** <note>original: "croceum"</note> and the **azure-blue** <note>original: "azureum"</note>. **Ade** <note>Likely a shorthand for a specific alchemical principle or stage, possibly 'Adeptus' or a coded term.</note> is the principle in the required earth, which is the alteration and the bringing of heat. It is a principle in this art, and through this principle, the artist has the method of "tasting" the mastery of these arts, according to how it is tastable in different ways. First, the intellect tastes that all these principles are of the "incorporation" <note>The process of giving a spiritual substance a physical body.</note> and are purified in the manner of their distillation. Second, as the powers exist in potentiality, the intellect also tastes the other modes of power which are in "act" <note>Aristotelian terms: 'potentiality' is what could be, 'act' is what currently is.</note> within the mastery. This principle is placed in this art so that the artist may understand the different powers in the mode of the mastery.

<column-break/>

This principle is very useful because the practicing artist can, through it, taste the powers as they are coordinated in this work. He will also understand other powers in the works of the stones, of the <term>flas</term><note>Possibly a corruption of 'flos' (flower/essence) or a specific mineral.</note>, of the rubies, and of the porphyries, touching upon the powers that are in the "passion" from which the stones are made. This cannot be done except through the power which is in "act." We shall not run through this at great length, for the mode of the mastery has been specified and declared in the "Book of Stones." For there are also parts where the stones are destroyed by their own natural virtue, which can minimally show themselves. Therefore, let it be known in what and from what the fulfillment of the stones consists, and in what their increase lies.

**Oside** <note>Another likely shorthand for an alchemical stage or operation.</note> is the principle for the operations. Operation is another principle of the "branch of the trees" <note>A common alchemical metaphor for the branching growth of crystals or the 'Arbor Philosophica'.</note>. This art consists of four different colors, written and designated for the different modes of operation. The **first color** designates that which has the operation in the matter. The **second color**, which is seen through the act, has the power over the natural nourishment and the things that move the matter toward the goal. The **third color** designates the act of the forms themselves. The **fourth color** designates the operations which the artist has over all these things: the administration of the fires, the operations, and the separations. These designate the operations by which the mixtures are made through their virtues.

# The Principles of the Art

**Origin** is another principle of this art <note>Latin: *Origo*</note>. By itself, it is a figure represented by the letter **C**, marked with five colors as is evident in the figures. It is that which originates from **B, T, V, X, Y, Z**, and **R**. It is through this that **A, O, X, Y** are formed and perfected. This principle is placed in this art so that the artist may recognize the substances from which things are generated, not only through the form of **P** in **A, O, X, Y**, but so that **Q** may be produced.

<margin>See the fourth principle of Figure B, which is D</margin>
**Unity** is the fourth principle of this figure <note>Latin: *Unaria*; likely referring to Unity or Singularity</note>. The artist should carefully note that in this principle, **E, F, G, H, I, K, L, M, N, O, P, R** must be mediated through this figure and the *Physical Tree* <note>The *Arbor Physicalis*, a famous diagram by Ramon Llull representing the hierarchy of being</note>. This principle is placed in this art so that the artist may demonstrate the significance of what a thing is, and understand it as known through all the aforementioned things, leading to **M**. And because through the mode of **Y**, **M, P, P, A, O, X, Y** are led to **Q**, and so with all others according to the second mode, as was said concerning **D**.

<margin>See the fifth principle of Figure B, which is E</margin>
**Alteration** is another principle of this figure <note>Latin: *Alteratio*</note>, and it is the first of the five colors. It designates that all bodies, through nature itself, <margin>it is such</margin> must be considered in a twofold way. First, according to the double operation in the preceding bodies which are generated; this occurs when they are made with a mature redness. Under this is the pattern of **X** and **Y**. The method of this is explained and declared in the first distance, in the second part of the distance, in the chapter that begins there. And in this work, they are turned from black to this state through the whole process. The other way they are considered is as they are made in a very strong "arched" state <note>possibly referring to a chemical or geometric "arc"</note>, and this is a known method of being made, and under this **V** suffers. Another way they are considered is as they are made in sulfur and orpiment <note><term>orpiment</term>: a deep-colored, orange-yellow arsenic sulfide mineral formerly used as a pigment</note>, and the method is for them to be joined, and under this **Z** suffers. Another way they are considered is as was said of **D**, and under this **B, T, V, X, Y, Z** suffer, and they must suffer under those modes aforesaid, as is evident.

<column-break/>

They are for the purpose of judging **F** and **Y**.

<margin>See the sixth principle of Figure B, which is F</margin>
**Opposition** is another principle in this art <note>Latin: *Oppositio*</note>. It is a figure generated by five colors and is established in this letter **F** to denote the difference that exists between **F** and **H** of the Reason and the **B** of the *Physical Tree*. For under **F** of this figure, **B, T, V, X, Y, Z** suffer; but under **H** of the *Physical Tree*, they do not suffer except through **O** and **U**, as in **M**. For the five colors placed here denote that the said **B, T, V, X, Y, Z** suffer under it through the mediation of **D**. And in this, they suffer in that work primarily, all of them, according to the first "trituration" <note><term>trituration</term>: the process of grinding to a fine powder, often used in alchemy/pharmacy</note> of this to destroy **B, T, V, X, Y, Z** from their prior state. When they are presented to the standing trituration, they are with **D**, which is the agent of the work on **B, T, V, X, Y, Z**, so that it can corrupt them and place them under its operation in the time it attains the end. In the first trituration, it is for the purpose of corrupting them, and because they do not immediately present themselves to the second trituration, so that it can fulfill its desire in the destruction of the contrary. This principle is placed in this art so that the artist understands what kind of primary principle he intends to operate with, and to demonstrate the difference of **B, T, V, X, Y, Z**, and to have them through it if they are designated for what is sought.

<margin>(Concerning the seventh principle, which is Enunciation, G)</margin>
**Enunciation** is another principle of this figure <note>Latin: *Enuatiatio/Enuntiatio*</note>. It is a figure represented by **G**, and it is written in various colors to demonstrate to the intellect how **B, T, V, X, Y, Z** must suffer under the action of this principle. In it, through the mediation of **M, M, D**, the spiritual body is abstracted from the hidden mixtures. Which is the spirit and the matter that the form must have in **A, O, X, Y**, as is evident, so the form may be transformed into **Q**. This principle is placed in this art so that the artist may understand the difference of **B, T, V, X, Y, Z**.

### Regarding the 16th Principle, which is the Placement of the Stone

<margin>12</margin>
