### On the sublimation of sulfur
It should be noted that concerning native sulfur <note>original: "sulfure vivo," meaning naturally occurring sulfur</note>, the same method and order must be maintained for washing and sublimating it as was described for quicksilver <note>original: "argento viuo," or mercury</note>, except that a somewhat stronger heat is added for the sublimation.

### On the resolution and coagulation of the aforementioned spirits
Now that the doctrine for sublimating the four spirits <note>The "four spirits" of alchemy are typically mercury, sulfur, arsenic, and sal ammoniac</note> has been mastered, it remains to speak of their resolution <note>dissolving into liquid</note> and coagulation <note>solidifying</note>, which is done in this manner.
Take arsenic that has been sublimated seven times—or six times at the least—and incorporate it upon a marble stone with water of sal ammoniac <note>original: "salis ar̃. sublimati," ammonium chloride</note> that has been sublimated seven times. Place this in a glass vial, well-sealed, under horse manure <note>fimus equinus; used as a source of steady, gentle heat</note> for seven days so that it may ferment and dissolve. After dissolution, soak the lime of silver <note>original: "calcem lune," silver reduced to a powder through calcination</note> with it.
Then set it to resolve. After resolution, it shall be coagulated in this way: place the solution itself between strong, sifted <term>metas</term> <note>likely conical vessels or molds</note> and beneath it make a light fire of coals so that it may harden.
And do this three times, dissolving and coagulating until it is fixed <note>rendered non-volatile</note> and does not fly from the fire. You can test this on a glowing iron plate: if you place a small amount upon it and it sweats like wax and does not fly away, then the elixir is complete. If not, repeat the resolution and coagulation until it becomes fixed.

<column-break/>

### On the water of sublimated sal ammoniac
Water from sublimated sal ammoniac is made thus:
Take a hard egg, cooked hot in water. Once the shell is removed and it is sliced through the middle, remove the yolk. Fill the cavity with the aforementioned salt and compress it between your hands; the water will then drip from the salt.

### On the resolution of sublimated sal ammoniac
In another way: place the salt in a stretched ox bladder, which you should place in cold water with the neck of the bladder remaining outside. Within a day or sooner, it will be resolved into liquid.

### On the purification and resolution of metals
Likewise, you shall purify metals in this way: first melt them (or it) in a crucible. Once melted, cast them into sharp water <note>original: "aqua acuta," a caustic or acidic solution</note>, and do this seven times.

### How sharp water is made
Sharp water is made in this way:
Take the urine of boys, well-skimmed of froth, and good vinegar. In these, boil sifted ashes and quicklime <note>calcium oxide</note> until a third part has been consumed by the boiling. Once this <term>caprello</term> <note>the liquid lye/solution</note> has clarified and cooled, distill it through a filter and save it until it is needed.

### How the sharpest water is made
To the same end, for the sharpest water:
Take white wine tartar <note>potassium bitartrate deposits</note> and place it in an oblong, fire-resistant vessel with a little rock salt <note>original: "salis gem̃e"</note>. Burn it in a very strong fire until it whitens like metal; then, let it be melted and pulverized.

**Again**, water for dissolving all bodies <note>referring to the "bodies" of metals like gold or lead</note>. ### Concerning the purging of metals

**Lime** is calcined in this way for one hour. Grind common salt with vinegar: from which make a layer in the crucible. Or otherwise, make a layer of lime, and continue doing so until the whole crucible is filled: afterwards burn it among the coals.

### Concerning the whitening of metals.

# For hardening iron.

To harden iron so that it may soften and penetrate all bodies: Note that when **fixed Sal Ammoniac** <note>original: "sal Armoniacu fixu"; a chemical salt used in alchemy, likely ammonium chloride</note> is dissolved with **quicklime** in distilled warm water and filtered, and then distilled again through a filter, it has the power to harden every kind of iron to such an extent that it penetrates and softens all other hardest bodies.

## For making silver from mercury

## Concerning the Borissa tree: and its virtues

The Chapter of **Hermes** <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy</note> concerning the tree which is called **Borissa**: which is similar to *aparozane*; its leaves are of a celestial color, similar to the leaf of **pellitory** <note>original: "vitreole"; Parietaria officinalis, often used in glass-cleaning or medicine</note>; and on every Monday it puts forth a leaf for up to fifteen days. ## For whitening copper.

To whiten copper: Take 5 drams <note>The symbol "3" represents the dram or drachma, a unit of weight</note> of **Alexandrian saltpeter**, 1 dram of **Sal Ammoniac**, 1 dram of **saltpeter from walls**, 1 dram of **alkali salt**, 1 dram of **feather alum**, 1 dram of **rock alum**, 1 dram of **realgar** <note>arsenic sulfide</note>, and 3 drams of **tartar**. From these let a powder be made; let one part of it be placed upon two parts of copper.

## For softening every metal

To soften every metal: Take the juice of **lettuce** <note>original: "lacture parmule"</note>, the juice of **asparagus** <note>original: "spargule"</note>, **camomile** <note>original: "cumazelle"</note>, and **houseleek** <note>original: "sempevivue"</note>, and add some of the herb which is commonly called **pepper**. ## For softening steel

# For tempering iron
To temper iron, take flint stones, radish, and the roots of celandine <note>original: "Radices celidome"; likely Chelidonium majus, often used in alchemy for its yellow sap</note>. Let all these be ground and take their juices. In these juices, quench the iron, sword, or other metal three times, renewing the juice each time.

# For converting Jupiter into the Moon
<note>In alchemical code, Jupiter refers to Tin and the Moon refers to Silver.</note>
To convert Jupiter into the Moon: Take sal ammoniac <note>ammonium chloride</note> and make a water from it. Afterward, take half the weight of the same in filings of good steel and mix them well together. Then let them be dissolved, and when dissolved, distill through a filter. Then let this water touch the intended thing. Next, take purified Jupiter <insert>tin</insert> and melt it; pour it into the aforementioned water seven times, and it will become good Moon <insert>silver</insert>.

# For melting Crystal
So that crystal can be melted such that vessels can be made from it: Take as much of the crystal itself as you wish and calcine <note>heat to a high temperature to reduce to powder</note> it in a calcining furnace for one day in a crucible with a violent fire, and quench it in violently cold water. Then dry it. Afterward, calcine it well for half a day and dry it again as before. Then continue the same order a third time. Then take it and grind it very well in a mortar. Afterward, take calcined tartar <note>potassium carbonate derived from wine deposits</note> and grind it strongly, and pass it through a silk sieve <note>original: "zandatum", a fine silken fabric</note>.

<column-break/>

Afterward, take one part of this and one part of the crystal and mix them well together. Then take this mixture and place it in a mortar—one of those in which glass is melted—then place it in a glassmaker's furnace and let it stand there for a day and a night. In the morning, you will find the crystal melted, from which you can work as if with glass.

# Here begins the little book called the Flower of the King concerning the Philosopher's Stone.

<margin>Note this excellent and true treatise</margin>
Know, O King, that the wise have placed many things and many modes of operating into the Work: namely, dissolving and congealing, and many vessels and weights, which they set down to try the ignorant and to clarify the work for the intelligent. And note that the wise have condensed the work into brief words, yet they have placed and added many other words so that it might not be understood except by the wise.
<margin>On the nature and matter of the stone</margin>
The wise indeed have said that there is one stone which is composed of four natures: which natures are water, fire, air, and earth. This stone is a stone in appearance and to the touch, but not in its true nature. And it is called the stone or the <term>Composite</term> <margin>It is called the Composite</margin> <note>A "composite" refers to a substance made of multiple elements unified into one</note>. This composite, when it is led by the right path, is that which is sought. In it, there is nothing superfluous nor anything lacking; rather, all things that are in the stone are necessary to it, and it comes from nothing else.

# Here begin the authorities of the ancient philosophers concerning the Great Stone
## of the philosophers. And first, Hermes says:
Know, lords, that this stone is made from one single thing: and it exists in three. Namely: Sun, Moon, and *Quernizig* <note>likely a corruption of a Persian or Arabic term for mercury or a specific mineral</note>; and the three are one: since the Sun and Moon are born from a natural wine-colored union in the belly of the earth. The stone rises, yet it is not made from man alone. And its matrix is the earth: and the earth is the bodies of the metals, namely Sun and Moon; and the earth is soaked with the airy moisture of its own likeness. Namely, from the water of mercury and from its vinegar-like <term>quintessence</term> <note>the "fifth essence" or purest part of a substance</note>, it is raised up together. Namely: Sun, Moon, and *Quernizig*: and one is made in them, namely by a natural conjunction. Just as is to be seen concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, which are three, and the three are one. So our stone is made of two, and three are one in the beginning and in the end when it is completed. Because of this, the philosopher says the stone is made one: one medicine: to which we add no external thing, nor do we diminish it, except that in the preparation we remove what is superfluous. —

->Arnaldus de Villanova<-

<margin>1 substance is cold and moist | 2 cold and dry | 3 hot and moist | 4 hot and dry</margin>
Know, lords, that the philosophers have named our stone by many names, so that those who are not of the number of the philosophers might not understand that it is one thing; rather, it consists of diverse things: namely, from the four elements and from the four spirits. The first substance is cold and moist. The second is cold and dry. The third is hot and moist. The fourth is hot and dry. And because our stone contains these qualities within itself, the philosophers have named our stone by various names. And according to the colors, they vary and change as many names as they have imposed; and according to their opinion, they have set down diverse operations for that which we believe. But for you to know...

<margin>
The intentions of the philosophers regarding the **Great Stone**. **Hermes** says it is made from one thing. It is made of 13 parts: **Sun** and **Moon** in a primary proportion. It shall be made above every single thing. It is made and strengthened by two, namely the **Sun** and the **Moon**, and it will have the humidity of the masters, namely from the water which is the essence joined together. It is the **Azoth** <note>original: "gezezaizis", likely a corruption of Azoth</note> and the one of our author, treated of the father and the son. It is made of primary matter. And the primary principle shall not be made of elements, but is completed in the beginning. Because of this, it becomes one. Not added to from outside, nor if it is prepared, does it come from the common people.
**Villanova** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova</note> gave the Stone many names, but those who are not of the art do not understand what the dew of the philosophers is, or what it does. It is like a white primary earth, and it is cold and clean and moist, which is why it is called a stone, not by its quality, but by its name. Many name the stone or vary the names. They imposed these names and similar preparations so that the operation would be hidden.
</margin>

They showed this way through one single thing—but they imposed many names so that the science would be more hidden and would be carried out most wisely.

### **Aristotle**
Know, masters, that all bodies are like a curdled mass, and the spirit is like milk. And when the bodies are softened and dissolved, then the spirit itself coagulates with them and a firm mixture is made. Therefore, the spirit and the body, being resolved into water, shall be made resonant. Let them be distributed vehemently, proceeding to coagulate those waters, and one stone shall be made. If you repeat your work by dissolving, imbibing, grinding, and coagulating, the work will be made much better. And know that when the body of the **Sun** is resolved in water and coagulated with the spirit, it tints 45 times into true gold. Know and understand the same of the body of the **Moon** <note>Silver</note> resolved and mixed with water; the spirit tints better unless it is made into a lasting light. Therefore, separate each from the dregs in which there is corruption, until the white becomes <margin>primary water</margin> white and the red becomes red. And let them be joined into one melt, and it shall become gold or silver. And know for certain that he who does not know this process is like a blind man on the road, or one who shoots without a bowstring. For he who knows how to separate the body into its pure substance should know that the operation follows: because the Sun and Moon, separated and calcined <note>reduced to powder by heat</note> as has been said, are the ferment of metals in permanent color, just as the leaven of bread is in good bread.

### **Astunus**
Know, masters, that the first substance is reduced into one spirit. And this is what the philosophers call "dissolution," which is the foundation of the art. Regarding this, the philosopher says: "Unless you dissolve the body into a vapor, you labor in vain." Therefore, the dissolution of the philosophers is not the soaking of water, but the dissolution of the body into the water from which it was first created, namely into the "living water of the world," just as ice is converted into liquid water, from which it was first water.

### **Morienus**
Know, masters, that our whole Great Work is in our water of **Azoth** and from 
<gloss>that is, distilled water of which the distillation is [complete].</gloss>

<column-break/>

it, and not without it. For it dissolves the body, not with a [common] dissolution as the ignorant believe—who think it is converted into belly-water—but with the true dissolution of the philosophers, so that it is converted into the water from which it came from the beginning. This same water calcines the bodies and transforms them into a black earth, and it whitens, cleanses, impregnates, and waxes <note>softens to a waxy consistency</note> them. And this is what the philosophers said: "The earth is putrefied and cleansed by its own water." When it has been cleansed, by the help of God the whole mastery shall be directed. And for this reason the philosophers say: "Unless you cleanse the body into a clean state, and return it whitened, and mix the soul into it, nothing in this Great Work shall be directed."

### **Plato**
Know, masters, that when the earth is whitened and impregnated, then let it be sublimated until the spirit which you found in it comes out of it, which is called **Azis** <note>likely "Aer", Air</note>, which is air. And there remains at the bottom the calcined earth, which is of a fiery nature. And this is what the philosophers said: "When you have water from air, and air from water, and fire from earth, then you shall have the full art." And they spoke a certain truth, because water cleanses and washes; earth dries and fixes; air and fire rule and make it flow. And therefore it is necessary that there be much water and much air, because the greatness of the tint is as great as the quantity of the air was.

### **Albertus Magnus**
Know, masters, that the aforesaid white earth, calcined as has been said, which is the ferment of fire, is placed there; for the ferment is called the "soul" of the philosophers because of the redness [it gives] to the red. This is because, just as the human body is of no value without the soul, so it is with the earth or the body in the world: without the ferment or soul, it is worth nothing. For the ferment transforms the separated body, as has been said, and converts it into its own nature in color.

And you should know that there is no ferment <note>original: "fermentum"; in alchemy, a substance that "leavens" or transforms base metal into gold</note> except for the sun and the moon: each in its own grain, namely in the white or the red. To these, it appears through God, because just as the sun and moon rule over other bodies, and the rest are ruled by spirits, so these two bodies—namely the Sun and Moon—rule over other bodies; therefore, it is called a ferment. Because of this, the philosophers say that it is necessary for the ferment to be introduced into the same white body, because every soul is close to redness.

## Eximemus <note>Likely a corruption of an Arabic name or a specific alchemical authority</note>
Know, lords, that the water of gold is not first produced in the bodies until it has been perfectly stripped of its impurities, whitened, and purified as has been said. This occurs through the hour of their conjunction—namely of the bodies and the spirit—and then the greatest wonders appear. For all colors appear, as many as can be imagined, through their conjunction. Moreover, the imperfect body is colored by the mediation of the ferment, which ferment is the soul. It is converted into the color of the ferment and becomes one in all things, namely in our mixture, just as bread and water are mixed together.

## Daucus
Know, lords, that the performance of our mastery <note>term: mastery (magisterium); the successful completion of the alchemical process</note> is likened in its order to this generation: for he who makes the male and the female, who carries out the true conjunction of soul and body, and knows how to guide them, knows the entire mastery through himself. The whole mastery consists in the sun and the moon and in exercise <note>or "operation"</note>: because the first is coitus, the second conception, the third pregnancy, and the fourth birth. Fifth, nourishment follows. Because of this, the philosophers say: our sperm is the living mercury <note>original: "azocuq uiuu" (azoc/azoth); a universal solvent or essential spirit</note> which is produced in the earth, which is called our earth. This earth is the mother of all; then it is called our "all." And when the earth receives a little of the exercise, it retains the seed; then it is called conception. And then the male acts upon the female in exercise upon the earth. And this is what the philosophers said: for the mastery is nothing else but the male and the female, and their conjunction...

<column-break/>

...exercise. And the earth grows and multiplies and increases. And this happens when the earth is pregnant, and then it is called birth; then our stone is born to them, which is the thing named by the philosophers.

## Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most famous historical figure in alchemy</note>
Dearest lords, honor our King coming from the fire, crowned with a diadem, and enlighten him until he reaches the aforementioned age. His father is the sun; his mother is the moon. The moon is placed for the imperfect body, and the sun for the perfect body. The sun then follows the nourishment. He is nourished, however, by his own milk—namely, by the airy azure—until he increases by a great augmentation, namely from the ferment from which he was from the beginning. He is soaked in the azure often and more often, until he drinks what is sufficient.
<margin>Incb <note>Possibly an abbreviation for "Incipit" (It begins)</note></margin>

## Hermogenes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note>
Dearest lords, the first thing that must be done in the work is that the living mercury <note>azoc</note> should sublime the bodies; afterwards, dissolve it, so that it returns to its first nature or matter—namely, into water, from which it first was. And in that solution, place the bodies naked and liquid; for unless the body is dissolved, it does not retain the spirit. They agree in this: that no gold or nature was ever brought forth unless they grow, and only through putrefaction. Therefore, it is necessary that our stone putrefy; because in no other way will it take up the spirit through the whole, so that our water becomes the living azure.

## Dedalus
Dearest lords, you should sublime our bodies with the sublimation that the ignorant intend <note>meaning they misunderstand it</note>; for they think to sublime is to ascend upwards. Our sublimation is not merely to ascend, but it is the sublimation of the philosophers from the low earth and the dew... <note>The text here becomes highly abbreviated and cryptic</note> ...namely, the high magic earth makes it so. Sublimation is in dignity afterwards, namely white and pregnant, and thus two bodies are made subtle... so that the whole becomes our azure water. Thus, let it not be forgotten that unless the seed is first dissolved, the grace of the azure spirit is forgotten and afterwards dissolved.

# The Prologue:

<gloss>Because there is one God, <unclear>father</unclear> and <unclear>light</unclear>, <unclear>from whom</unclear> is its <unclear>beginning</unclear></gloss>
God is my witness, to whom I do not lie: that in <gloss>this 7th proposition</gloss> these seven propositions <gloss>the whole <unclear>science</unclear> of <unclear>alchemy</unclear> as it stands</gloss> are all the techniques of the <gloss>science</gloss> of <term>alchemy</term> <note>The medieval precursor to chemistry, focused on the transmutation of matter.</note>: so that <gloss>namely</gloss> one may know the natural principles: and all the <gloss>finite</gloss> causes of minerals: and the <gloss>form</gloss> or manner of their generation: which <gloss>in the form of the thing as it is</gloss> exists in the intended generation of nature. And those who have moved past the surface of these things will not be caught in many entanglements or varied thoughts: and they shall pray to God for the final mastery and the secret: and the total intention of the <term>philosopher's stone</term> <note>The legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold.</note> without any diminution or superfluity, through the ingenuity found in the science of philosophy. Upon these things their thoughts shall be firmly founded: and they shall rest: they shall fully find [the truth]: and often, more often, and very often revolve and handle the aforementioned propositions: and study them well in their entirety: from their beginning to their end, so that they may begin or approach the practice. For he approaches the operation who follows it: who through many thoughts, many operations, and various imaginings, finds they are all resulted and manifested. And if they remain ignorant, and God has sealed the truth from them, let them not blame me, but themselves. If God knew in them that the light

<column-break/>

of their thought was faithful, He would manifest the truth to them. For our art stands in the power of God: and it is reserved for whom He pleases, and He gives it to whom He wills, and He takes it away. For He is glorious: and most high: and full of all justice and all goodness. ¶ I, however, have set them on the right path: and have taken them out of falsehood: and I have paid my debt: yet I follow the paths of the philosophers with disguised words, strong and firm. I have covered those propositions; do not wish to scold or blaspheme me for this: for I do not do this out of envy, nor for the sake of greed. For my eyes are full [of tears] for the fear of God, and for fear of the wicked destroyers who, if they knew this science, could do many illicit and abominable things and others which are not to be spoken of, and it would be to their great detriment and damage: and thus the world would be laid waste. And for their sins, I would have to give an account and reason to God. Thus, to those who are obedient to God, the thing is patent and manifest and clear. For nothing that is hidden from the philosophers is achieved except by the grace of the Holy Spirit. And so ends the prologue: and the seven propositions follow, word for word.

## The second preparation or proposition. On the reduction of water into earth or body.
Pass the water into the body: For the one cannot dissolve if the other does not congeal. Therefore, let the quicksilver be congealed and conceive, and join this: and the quicksilver conceives the thin plate <note>original: "lamina"</note>. And this dissolves: and joins with itself: and it is made earth. And this is the second word of this work: of which the <term>philosophers</term> say: from the thickness of the water, earth is created. For the water is made earth: when the qualities of the earth overcome it. And the earth is made water: when the qualities of the water overcome it. The <term>solution</term> of the body is made: and the joining of the spirit. So that they may have one operation, and be one rose. To which no strange rose should be added.

## The third proposition. On the watering of the earth with water and fire, or heat.
Let the earth be, and it is, watered both with the fire and with the water by the grace of God. In the work it is set right. And this is the third word of this work, of which the <term>philosophers</term> say: this earth with the water is putrefied and purified. Then by the help of God the mastery <note>The "magistery" refers to the successful completion of the alchemical process.</note> is continued along the right path. For the earth does not germinate nor bring forth fruit: if it is not often watered. Nor does it receive watering: if it is not first dry. Children know this, and the women who sow the seeds and the fruits in the gardens: and they come to perfection. And for the love of this the <term>philosophers</term> said: that the operation of this was nothing but the work of women and children <note>A common alchemical trope suggesting that once the initial secret is known, the process is as simple as domestic chores.</note>. And for the love of this, every time that the body shall be soaked, so many times let it be dried. For to everything must be given <margin>its weight</margin> its weight: and to every measure its name, and to every work must be given measure. And then the right putrefaction of the <term>philosophers</term> follows. For the putrefaction of that is nothing else but the mortification of the moist with the dry. Because the humidity is only contained by the dryness. And it would be that the moist and the cold naturally flee from the fire: however, it is like that rose which cannot flee. For heavy things cannot be found except by the light ones, and likewise by the contrary.

# The fourth proposition: On grace
## of the graces of nature with nature and sublimation <insert>place here</insert>

**N**ature rejoices with its own nature, for nature is gladdened by nature. Nature conquers nature; nature lives by nature; nature attains nature and embraces it. And this is the fourth word <note>In this context, "word" refers to a specific stage or operation in the alchemical process.</note> of this work, which can be called sublimation and ascension, of which the philosophers say: That liquid matter is made sharp <note>original: "acereta"; likely meaning acidic or penetrating</note> whereas before it was thick and joined with the earth; and this happens by its own occasion, that is, from its own purity. # The seventh proposition: On the reduction of the fixed into the volatile and the volatile into the fixed, and the fusion of the stone

Our blessed stone is multiplied and finished when the volatile sum overcomes the sum of the fixed, and is fixed with it until it melts. And this is the seventh word of this work. Of which the philosophers say: because it is already fixed—that is, the stone—by way of sublimation, you shall make it flying <note>volatile</note>, and the flying fixed, by my subtle and ingenious [way] in the vessel of the philosophers, adjusting by small things so that all may be elevated and that it may be fixed. And move it if you have to add to it a non-fixed quantity, so that the sum of the flying overcomes the sum of the fixed, until it reaches that elevation. For if the sum of the flying overcomes the sum of the fixed, it will fly with it; and if the fixed overcomes, it will be fixed with it. And for the love of this, the thing that shall be elevated, let the sum of it be returned once, and again, and many times, so that by reiterations of sublimations it may all be fixed. And when all shall be fixed, let it be soaked again in the non-fixed part, with the ingenuity known to you, until once again it is all elevated, so that all may be fixed until you give the fulfillment of flow, just as <margin>to be made</margin> it shall be, and raised in the fulfillment of the Sun <note>gold</note> and of the Moon <note>silver</note> for certain. ### Chapter one: for sublimating the spirits; first, regarding mercury <note>original: "agerari," a common alchemical term for argent viu or mercury</note>

Take the water which I will show you how to make later in the chapter on waters. Take as much mercury as you wish and put it in a glass vessel. Take as much of the aforementioned water as the weight <gloss>by weight</gloss> of the mercury, and drop it onto the mercury; it will all turn into a paste at once. Place it in the sun and it will dry, turning shiny like pearls. And if any mercury remains that is not entirely mortified <note>In alchemy, "mortification" refers to the chemical change where a metal loses its outward form or "life," often through oxidation or reaction</note>, separate the "living" from the "mortified," drop more water on it, and do as before. And note

<column-break/>

that when you put the water on top, let the vessel containing the mercury be placed over hot embers; it will work better and with less water. Then take that which is mortified and dry, and mix with it an equal amount of vitriol <note>sulfate minerals</note>, well ground and powdered. Mix with it a tenth part of prepared common salt. Put it all in a shallow bowl <note>original: "salaya"</note> and let it be well incorporated. Moisten it with strong white vinegar made from good wine; the better and stronger it is, the more it is worth. By soaking and drying it in the sun, or over a very gentle fire until it turns to powder, you shall then put it in a luted flask <note>an "ampolla" sealed with "lute," a clay-like paste used to make vessels airtight and heat-resistant</note>. Give it a very gentle fire until the humidity leaves it. Then seal the flask well and increase the fire gently, always increasing it little by little for three hours. Afterward, let it cool and break the flask gently so that you may extract what is inside as cleanly as possible. You will find all the mercury on the sides, gathered around the neck of the flask, very white. Take it and mix it with its dregs <note>original: "feces"</note> that remain with it. Soaking, moistening, and drying in the bowl just as before, put it to sublimate in another flask in the same manner as the first. Do this three times, and it will be well purified.

## Sublimation of arsenic

Take as much arsenic as you wish: and powder it very well: and put it in a new glazed pot and put it over a good charcoal fire. And let it cook until it is all like a tile: and stir it well with a piece of wood until the yellow smoke stops. And when the white smoke comes out: throw it into a bowl of cold water. And when it is cold: take it out of there and dry it in the sun: until it turns to powder. And take an equal amount of filings of Venus <note>copper filings</note>: and mix with it an equal amount of prepared sal ammoniac: incorporate it all by grinding it hard: and then put it in the <term>aludel</term>: and give it a very gentle fire until the humidity is out: and afterwards close the hole: and increase the fire: and sublimate it as you know how. And do this four times. And it will be white.

### Sublimation of Sal Ammoniac

<margin>Prepared rock salt and as much proportioned with it/</margin>
**T**ake as much sal ammoniac <note>Ammonium chloride, a key alchemical reagent used to clean metals.</note> as you wish: and powder it very well and take prepared common salt: by equal weight: these two salts—common salt and rock salt <note>original: "al goma," likely referring to sal gemma or rock salt</note>—should be as much as the sal ammoniac: and put it all in a salt-cellar: and mix it all well together with strong white vinegar: and if you cannot get white vinegar: saturate it with distilled urine. ### Chapter Three: On Calcinating the Bodies: and first of the Moon

**F**irst take as much of the Moon <note>In alchemical terminology, "The Moon" (Luna) refers to Silver.</note> as you wish: and make thin plates of it: or have it filed if you wish: and take prepared common salt: and make a layer of it in your calcining vessel: and put another layer of the said Moon: and put it layer upon layer until it is all in. And do it in such a way that the bottom and the top are of salt. And each of the layers of salt should be half a finger thick: and seal it very well with its cover: and with the "smith's clay" <note>original: "lut del faber," a sealant made of clay, dung, and other binders to airtight vessels</note>: and put it in the calcining furnace: and give it a strong fire <margin>fol. p. 2.</margin> as if you wanted to melt it, but a little gentler, for a whole day and a night: and let it cool: and when it is cold: take it out from there: and you will find all the Moon in one mass. And grind the salt and it all together in a clean copper mortar. And when it is all crushed: put it in a basin of warm fresh water: and stir it so much with your hand until the salt dissolves. And draw it off by a wick <note>A method of siphoning or filtering liquid using capillary action</note>: and wash it two or three times until the salt is gone: and the fresh water is almost clear. And note that every time you pass it through the wick, do so so that the lime <note>The "calx" or powdered oxide of the metal</note> of the Moon does not go away with the water, and if it does, it remains in the wick: and let the water be warm: and afterwards take the said Moon after it is well dissolved. And put it to dry upon the warm ashes. And afterwards return to calcinating it as at first: one layer of salt.

## Sublimation of Saturn

**T**ake as much of Saturn <note>alchemical name for Lead</note> as you wish and make furnaces for smelting. And take a very smooth basin: and fill it with <margin>sweet dregs</margin> and set it in the furnace: and give it a strong fire. And put the Saturn therein and it will melt. And take an iron spatula: and push the dross <note>original: "spuma" (foam/scum)</note> to one side: and keep lifting and skimming it. And keep skimming until all the Saturn is turned into dross. And the fire must not fail, but always be of one intensity: and do not cease so that the Saturn is always molten. And when all has been turned into dross, put it all in the bottom of the basin: and mix it all strongly with the spatula: until it turns into powder: like ashes: and of that same color: and take it out quickly. And let it cool: and take that powder: and common prepared salt and make a bed of the said salt first. And let it be a finger thick: and then another of the powder: and do just as you did with the Moon <note>Silver</note>: layer by layer: and seal it so the salt is on top and below: just as I told you: and let it be put in the calcining furnace for 9 hours. Let it be neither too gentle nor too strong, but let it be given in one manner, and then take it out and let it cool. **A**fterward wash it in the manner I told you for the Moon: and keep it, for you will have need of it later. **A**nd note: that if it is not white enough for you, return it there as many times until it seems white enough to you.

## Chapter four: On making corrosive and sharp waters for dissolving:

**T**ake Roman vitriol <note>Iron(II) sulfate</note>: of which there should be eight pounds, and pulverize it thoroughly: and half <gloss>of half</gloss> a pound of saltpeter: and 4 oz. of euphorbium <note>a caustic plant resin</note>: and 4 oz. of vermilion: and 4 oz. of calcined tartar and 2 oz. of verdigris: and pulverize all these things well and finely: and take 4 oz. of sublimated sal ammoniac: and dissolve it in 4 oz. of strong vinegar. Incorporate all these things in the pan: and soak them with the aforementioned vinegar: and when it is well soaked and well incorporated: put it in a glass cucurbit <note>original: "almyssia" - a vessel used for distillation</note>: in which you can distill it: and then seal it very well with its glass cover, in such a way that no vapor escapes. And put it under horse manure in the greatest heat that you find there: and let it stay there for 19 days. And then take it out: and have a small basin prepared in the calcining furnace with sifted ash: and <gloss>uncover</gloss> unstop the cucurbit very gently: and place its alembic <note>the cap or still-head</note> upon it suitably, in a way that the vapor does not escape: sealing them with its paste and with its cloths, just as it should be: and put the alembic in the basin, in a way that the ash of the basin rises two fingers above the middle. And place its receiver on the alembic, well sealed so that no vapor escapes: and give it gentle fire at the beginning: and a little clear water will come out: and when yellow water begins to come out: remove that receiver: and put another: and guard that white water very well, for with that you can mortify <term>mortify: to chemically alter or "kill" the outward form of a metal, often mercury, to prepare it for further work</term> mercury: and give it fire continuously thereafter, little by little increasing the fire. And place wet cloths over the rest of the alembic: so that the heat of the strong water cannot damage it. And when it comes to the end: increase the fire very strongly. And when all the water has come out: seal the receiver well, where the said corrosive water <note>likely a form of aqua regia or nitric acid</note> will be. And if you have a spirit <note>a volatile substance or metal</note> prepared to dissolve in water according to what your master shall command you: put a well-filed iron into it, and touch it to the tongue, and as soon as you have put it there, the tongue will boil: and immediately pull it out suddenly: and quickly put your spirit into the water. And if you do it thus: it will all turn into water in one hour.

### Another dissolving water

<margin>*</margin>Take one pound of <term>vitriol</term><note>Sulfate minerals, likely green vitriol/ferrous sulfate</note>, half a pound of <term>saltpeter</term><note>Potassium nitrate</note>, and 4 ounces of <term>vermilion</term><note>Cinnabar/mercury sulfide</note>. Pulverize all these ingredients very well and mix them in an <term>alouzia</term><note>A ceramic mixing vessel or gallipot</note>. Place it in the furnace with the grates for distillation, and fit the cap <note>the alembic head</note> well-luted <note>sealed with airtight clay/paste</note> to its receiver. Give it a very gentle fire at first, gradually increasing the heat until the <term>alembic</term><note>The top part of the still</note> appears red. Then give it a stronger fire until the reddish vapor passes into the receiver. Seal it well. Immediately then you can "mortify" <term>azeraui</term><note>Arabic-derived term for quicksilver/mercury</note> as I will tell you above, or dissolve <term>luna</term><note>Silver</note>. This is the water I mentioned above when showing how to calcinate silver and for mortifying mercury for sublimation.

### Chapter five: on dissolving and congealing.

To dissolve means <gloss>when</gloss> the spirits and the <term>calx</term><note>The powdered residue after heating a metal</note> of the bodies are turned into water. There are some who perform dissolution with <term>pigeon droppings</term><note>original: "colomina"</note> moistened with warm water every 3 days, changing the droppings every 9 days. There are others who perform dissolution with <term>quicklime</term><note>calcium oxide</note> and with horse manure, watering the lime so that it generates great heat, whereby the spirits are recovered. It is true that any heat the spirits receive is good, from whatever source, provided they are well-watered. But there are some dissolutions better than others and more natural. Now I will tell them to you without falsehood.

<column-break/>

When you have moved the spirits with the <term>calcina</term><note>The product of calcination</note> and turned them all into water with the corrosive water, make a pit <gloss>deep</gloss> in the earth that is 4 palms deep and 3 palms wide. You shall have your fresh horse manure: one bed in the pit two palms high, and there you shall place your medicine, well-luted and well-sealed, so that in the movement of the spirits no vapor escapes. Hide the flask in the middle and cover it all very gently with that manure and let it stay for 20 days. If it stays longer, it will be better, because the manure takes a good 4 or 5 days to reach its heat once it is separated from the rest; and once it is hot, know for a truth that the heat stays with it for 30 days. This is a good dissolution, and more natural than any of the others.

### Another dissolution you shall make in this way.
<gloss>and properties of a water bath</gloss>

Take a large pot that has many holes, like a <unclear>strainer</unclear> <gloss>or a drain at the bottom</gloss> and fill it halfway with horse manure. Therein you shall place your spirits when they have been turned into waters together with the calx of the body. Fill the pot with very hot and fresh manure so that the flask with the medicine stays in the middle. Seal it very well so that no vapor escapes. Take another pot and set it in a furnace and fill it with water; set the other pot (containing the medicine and manure) on top of the one with the water. Give it fire in such a way that the water above does not boil over.

### Of the Lute of Wisdom, how it is made.

In this manner you shall make the **lute of wisdom** <note>term: "lute of wisdom" (lut de saber) - a specialized airtight sealant used by alchemists to coat glass vessels so they could withstand high heat without cracking or leaking spirits.</note> to seal the vessels when you put them in the ash and to congeal: take sifted wheat flour and take the red part of mastic <note>a resin from the mastic tree</note>, crushed and sifted. ### Chapter six: on making the oils to lock <gloss>salts</gloss> medicines.

Take some **calcined tartar** <note>potassium carbonate produced by burning the crusty deposits from wine barrels</note> and powder it very well. Put it in a flask and plug it very well; put it in **horse manure** <note>used as a steady, gentle heat source for digestion</note> and let it stay there 2, 3, or 4 days, and it will dissolve. Upon the hot wheels <note>likely a reference to a circular furnace or heating apparatus</note> you shall unlock it; in the manure you shall dissolve it. And by the "abebi" <note>unclear alchemical term, likely a specific solvent or process</note> you shall make it extend; and afterwards you shall lock your medicine. As perhaps I will tell you. And if by chance you do not have horse manure, put it under moist earth, and it will dissolve just as in manure.

### Another way to make oil of tartar.

When you have calcined the tartar and powdered it, put it in a small glass jar and cast <gloss>fresh water</gloss> sweet water into it, in such a way that you know that the powder is all dissolved. Afterwards, place it upon the ash furnace, and give it fire in such a way that all the water evaporates; and you will find at the bottom **salt of tartar**, which you shall dissolve again, and it makes a beautiful, clear, and good oil. This oil the philosophers call **rectified oil of tartar**. It is very precious and better than the other. With this and "hartal" oil <note>likely oil of orpiment/arsenic</note> you can lock medicine wherein there is mercury, arsenic, and **realgar** <note>term: "realgar" - a bright red arsenic sulfide mineral used in alchemy and pigments.</note>.

### Chapter sixteen: On "waxing" the medicines

### On the Whitening of Arsenic

Take well-pulverized arsenic <term>arsenich: arsenic trioxide, used in alchemy to whiten copper</term> and twice as much prepared common salt: and put it all in a pan. Incorporate it and soak it with strong white vinegar in such a way that it is all incorporated and made into a paste. And put it all in a glazed pot; and put it in the bread oven. And seal the pot well with the "lute of wisdom" <term>lut del saber: a hermetic sealing clay made of earth, hair, and dung</term> and put it in the greatest heat you can. And let it stay there a day and a night; and then take it out. And grind it and wash it in fresh water that is warm, so that the salt mixes well. And then take as much common salt as you did at first: and put it in the pan: and soak it: and grind it as before: and put it in a new glazed pot that is small, so that it can be well filled with that paste: and seal it with the lute of wisdom: and put it as before in the bread oven in the greatest heat. And you shall do this 8 times, and it becomes very white. In this manner you can whiten realgar <term>rialguar: arsenic sulfide, a ruby-red mineral</term>. But it is necessary that the realgar be raw, for if it were overcooked it would be too hard to grind. For when arsenic is

<column-break/>

overcooked, it is easier to grind. And guard against the great fire of the oven, for if you give it too much fire, it will laugh <note>original: "ria sen"; likely meaning it will vent or sublimate away too violently</note>. And note that you should avoid putting it in an earthen vessel; rather, put it in a glass vessel. And from this spirit thus whitened, you can sublimate with common salt alone, without alums and without filings and without other things. And these natural spirits thus whitened are more noble and more precious: they are of greater labor, but they are worth much more than when they are sublimated raw.

### New Chapter: On Calcining and Moistening the Spirits.

The calcined and moistened spirits are easier to turn into water <note>referring to "liquefaction" or "deliquescence," a key alchemical stage</note>; and know that the calcined spirits are smaller and lighter and more subtle in themselves for turning into water. And they cannot rise <note>sublimate</note>; rather, they are friends of the fire. For the fire has brought them to such a state when they are calcined and moistened that they cannot leave, and they turn more easily into water. And know that this is a great secret that the philosophers hid in their secret [writings] and did not wish to write down. And I want to show it to you, to give understanding of what I said at the beginning of this book: that I would enlighten you, and I do not wish to fail you; rather, I want to show it to you without deceit. For he who wishes to do well for the love of God should not grow weary of it.

### On the calcination of Mercury and the spirits
**T**ake sublimated Mercury <note>original: "Mercuri sublimat"; mercury that has been purified through heating to a vapor and re-solidifying</note>: and pulverize it very well in a mortar: and take a small jar: which you should understand: must be well-filled. And put the powder inside: in such a way that there remain two fingers' width before it is full: and take prepared Roman salt <note>original: "sal romma"; likely a refined rock salt or sal ammoniac</note>: and fill it well: and seal it: and put it in the ash furnace <note>a furnace where the vessel is buried in hot ashes to ensure even, gentle heating</note>. Position it so that the jar is in the middle. And let the ash be a hand's breadth thick on top. and high<gloss>m</gloss> <note>The gloss "m" likely indicates "measure" or "middle"</note> along the sides: and high at the bottom. And give it a gentle fire from above for 8 days. And after the 8 days, remove up to two fingers of the ash from the top: and give it a slightly stronger fire: for another 8 days: and from then on increase the fire a little more for another 8 days: and in this manner you can calcine the other spirits in 24 days.

### On humidifying the calcined spirits
**T**his is how you shall humidify the calcined spirits: take calcined Mercury and grind it: and put it in a small vial in such a way that two fingers' width remains empty: and seal it with two linen cloths: which must be clean: and let there be no other closure. And make a hole in the damp earth. And let it be two palms deep. And cover it with earth: and there it will receive humidity: and water it every 4 days all around: and take care that no water enters inside the vial. And let it stay there for 20 days. And afterwards take it out: and dry it

<column-break/>

above the hot ashes: or in the sun. And in this way you can humidify all the other spirits. And in this way everything can be turned into water <note>liquefied or dissolved</note>: take whichever spirit you wish. and an equal amount of sublimated salt ammoniac: incorporate it all in the mortar. and put it all into a well-washed beaver's gut <note>original: "bodell de castro"; animal intestines were often used as organic membranes for slow steaming or dialysis</note>: and fill it just as if you were filling a blood sausage: and put a cauldron of water over the fire: and hang that intestine above the water in such a way that it does not touch the water. instead let it be a good palm's width above. in such a manner that it receives the steam from the water well. And let it stay there for up to two natural days: and let there always be a fire. And when the water decreases: add more: and if you do this: everything will turn to water: and keep it away from the smoke: so that you may proceed correctly in your tasks.

### How Sal Ammoniac is Made
<note>Sal Ammoniac (ammonium chloride) was essential in alchemy for cleaning metals and creating "strong waters."</note>
Take the soot that forms in the chimney of the kitchen and the sweat <note>likely referring to the condensation or mineral crusts</note> from the baths; mix in a third part of prepared common salt. Moisten it with urine and place it in an aludel <term>aludel: a pear-shaped earthenware pot used as a condenser in sublimation</term>, well pulverized, as one does when sublimating. Let the humidity escape, and then give it fire for an entire day and a night. Cool the fire little by little, ensuring that at the very end the fire is very strong. You shall do this three times: soaking, moistening, and drying. And you will have a sal ammoniac.

### How Alkali Salt is Made
Take soda <note>sossa: likely barilla or plant-ash rich in sodium carbonate</note> and pulverize it. Place it in a pan and add fresh water so that it covers the powder by more than a hand's breadth. Set it to cook over the fire and let it boil until the water is reduced by half or a third. Distill it through a wick <note>a method of filtration where liquid travels along a cord or fabric strip</note> and congeal what distills. Keep it, for it becomes very white. Do this three times, dissolving, distilling by wick, and congealing. You will have a very noble and fusible salt. For this salt has such virtue that if silversmiths <term>argenters: silversmiths or workers in silver</term> knew of it, they would solder with it just as well as with borax <note>original: "armar," likely a corruption of "borax" or "almarcar"</note>. Keep it well. You can prepare all other salts in this way: return them to the fire until they no longer crackle <note>decrepitation</note>,

<column-break/>

dissolve them, distill them by wick, and congeal each one by itself. For they are then prepared to be put into the greatest works.

### Chapter Twelve: On Congealing Mercury
The Philosopher <note>likely referring to Aristotle or Hermes Trismegistus, often cited as "The Philosopher" in alchemical texts</note> commands you to do this for two reasons. The first: when it is congealed <note>solidified or fixed</note>, it is better for keeping, for "mortifying" <note>changing its chemical state to remove its "quickness"</note>, and for sublimating. The second is: because there are medicines of such things and so conditioned that they do not work perfectly upon any other body, nor show their virtue, except upon Mercury. For this reason, he commands it to be congealed; because when one must cast medicine upon "living" <note>liquid</note> mercury, there is no other sign except when the mercury wishes to escape the vessel. But if it is congealed, there is a sign: when one applies fire to the vessel, the mercury returns to life, and that is the time to cast the medicine. Thus, there are two reasons why mercury should be congealed, and there are two ways it should be congealed: one by the vapor of Jupiter <term>Jupiter: alchemical symbol for Tin</term> and Saturn <term>Saturn: alchemical symbol for Lead</term>, and the other with the juice of herbs. I wish to show them to you.

### Of the conjunction of the body and the soul that are found in minerals, how it is done

# Medicine for Venus <note>In alchemy, "Venus" refers to copper.</note>

Now I will show how one can be aided by the "flying spirits" <note>Volatile substances that vaporize when heated.</note> which are for copper. Take one part of sublimated mercury <note>original: "azercuÿ sublimat"</note>; and of arsenic and of realgar <note>Arsenic sulfide</note> take as much as the mercury: and put it in the bowl: and take plume alum <note>A fibrous variety of alum</note>: and sal ammoniac <note>Ammonium chloride</note> in equal weight: and a fourth part of prepared common salt until it equals the weight of the spirits. With the help of the two salts, proceed in the pan, soaking it all with sal ammoniac that has been dissolved in the bladder <note>A vessel used for distillation or steeping</note> until the spirits are well incorporated: and moisten them in the sun until they turn to powder: and put them in a flask: and place it over a good fire and let it be well sealed with clay <note>original: "enlutada"</note>: and do it in that manner which is told in the second chapter on sublimating mercury: and do this four times. And each time increase the heat little by little. And then let it cool. And return and soak it with the aforementioned water of sal ammoniac: because this salt gives conjunction and is like a marriage and creates friendship in such a way among these spirits that they come to perfection. For as Hermes and Aristotle said: that rising to heaven and descending to earth is the way of the work <note>A reference to the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus</note>. And this is understood by sublimation. And by doing this many times the spirits are prepared until they become white plates as if they were made of Saturn <note>In alchemy, "Saturn" refers to lead</note>. And if in this state you can bring the sublimating spirits, the medicine is made and one part will go over 12 parts of Venus. And this should be called a medicine and not an elixir. And if by chance you could not bring the medicine to the state of sublimating plates: pulverize it in a pan: and have filings of copper <note>original: "lima"</note> or of Jupiter <note>In alchemy, "Jupiter" refers to tin</note>: let there be as much as the spirits: incorporate it all <unclear>with...(?)</unclear>: and do it in such a way that it can all enter as a paste into a flask that is well sealed with clay: and prepare it well before you put it to the fire: before the fire. And afterwards put the medicine in: and put it on the sublimating fire: until the humidity is out of it: and then apply an unbridled fire: and from there fire little by little: always strengthening the fire: for up to 12 hours. And then let it cool. And you shall take that which you find in the neck and on the sides of the flask, which are the spirits that descended: and put one part of this over 14 of Venus. And this is called "descension" <note>A process of liquefying or distilling downwards</note>. And if it satisfies you with the joining and the softness. And if not, mix in a 4th part of fine filings: and it will become good and soft. However, note that when you have taken the powder from the flask: soak it with oil of tartar <note>Potassium carbonate solution</note>.

### Work on copper which is called Tarquina.

**T**ake whitened arsenic <note>original: "arsenich dealbat"</note>, sublimated and dissolved in water for 8 days, as you know how. And take purified plates of copper: let them be as thin as paper. Heat them in the fire, and when they are glowing red, quench them in this water. Do this as many times as necessary until it loses its heat. They can be made white in two or three times. Then take an equal amount of fine silver <note>original: "luna"</note> and melt it all into one, and you will make a Tarquina ingot. Note that I tell you the truth: in whatever work where silver is needed for melting, it is called Tarquina. If I wanted another, let it be *haca* <note>likely a term for an alloy of lesser purity</note>, which means "mixed rose" and not "chiseled" <note>referring to hallmarked or pure bullion</note>. And for this reason, there is danger in working it, for when they put it in the cupels <term>cendrades: shallow porous vessels used in assaying to separate precious metals from base metals</term>, its impurity reveals itself. Therefore, it is dangerous to work. However, those who use it do so because they suffer poverty and know no other way.

<margin>Attention to who composed the book</margin>

**T**his book is made to the honor of our Lord God and His beloved saints, and explained by Master **Arnau de Vilanova** <note>A famous 13th-century Catalan physician and alchemist</note>, and given to one of his disciples whom he loved dearly, with this command: that if you work with it, you must share with the poor and the sick, helping them for the love of God. And when he had written it, he kept it

<column-break/>

always in his chest, and would not give it away until he knew his end was near. Then he called him and said: "Because this is one of the greatest sciences in the world, for which the heretics were in prayer and spoke naturally; and from all of them I have extracted the best and the most truthful. You may work it throughout the whole world generally, because I have been able to explain it in this book against all the errors in which the men of this world consume themselves who use this science. For the saints hid it, and I have discovered it to you because I see you are of good character and sound understanding. May you do good for the love of God to the poor. And if you wish to do so, you can, for kings and great lords receive it, as they are all greedy to possess this science. Otherwise, they would fear that you might do harm in all affairs. I would have told you the other work of gold <note>original: "sol"</note>, which is worth much more; if you are inclined to do good, with this you can do much and it will give you fulfillment."

And take care that you do not associate with any man of the world who holds lordship; for when they have seen this work, they would take it from me; their subordinates would grow proud, and great war and great evil could arise from it. Rather, hide it as secretly as you can. And for this reason, do not be proud, nor make a display of it, for evil would overtake you at some time; for God would demand an account of you, sooner or later, as we cannot hide ourselves from God.

### Water of Lead for Gold.
<note>original: "Aqua plumbi ad solem." In alchemy, "Sol" (the Sun) refers to Gold, and "Saturn" refers to Lead.</note>

Take one part of immature Saturn <note>Lead</note> and four parts of the water of vitriol <note>sulfuric acid</note> and saltpeter. Put the aforementioned immature [lead] into this water, and it will dissolve immediately. Distill through a filter and discard the dregs. Afterward, distill through an alembic <note>a chemical still</note> and take the water; keep the red dregs, which are the earth of the vitriol and saltpeter, with an equal amount of dissolved sal ammoniac. Afterward, distill until you finish. Then place it in a glass flask and pour over it the water you distilled from it. Place it in a damp place until it dissolves into a red water like blood. With this water, you shall mix the sublimate <note>mercury sublimate</note> until it drinks as much water as its own weight. Dissolve, distill, and congeal. One part of this tints six parts of Moon <note>Silver</note> into Sun <note>Gold</note>. <margin><image-desc>A small orange-red sun symbol with a central dot and eight rays.</image-desc> folio 135 bottom</margin> Look for such a sign back in the chapter on "Strong Waters" <note>Aqua Fortis / Nitric Acid</note> and the "Golden Finaze," since it was for this work, and it is for Gold and for Silver. And note here that the entire spirit of the strong water is made red, and the sal ammoniac and the sublimated mercury also become reddening agents.

### To make tin into silver

<margin>
The same
from above
folio 76 verso
</margin>

**T**ake 4 lbs. of potash <note>original: "cendres clauellades" - potassium carbonate derived from wood ashes</note> and 7 lbs. of quicklime <note>calcium oxide</note> and make a lye, just as if it were for laundry. Pass it all day through a sleeve <note>a conical fabric filter</note>. Do this as many times as necessary until it can support an egg <note>a traditional test for the density/concentration of a solution</note>. Of that lye, take one lb. and put in 3 oz. of rock alum, 2 oz. of saltpeter, and 2 oz. of white honey. Make it so that everything dissolves; pass it all through felt tongues <note>strips of felt used for capillary filtration</note>. Then put it all into a flask, and put 2 oz. of white arsenic into the flask. Then place it in the ash furnace with its alembic head <note>the top part of a still</note> and its receiver, and distill the water with sufficient fire. Return the water [to the still] and repeat this 4, 5, or 6 times, and the arsenic will be transformed. On the last distillation, stir it a little and then let it cool. Take this water from inside the alembic. Then take one lb. of fine tin and melt it, and quench it in quicklime 4, 5, or 6 times. Wash it with salt and vinegar and pass it through a cloth. Afterward, take the said tin and melt it in a crucible, and heat quicksilver <note>mercury</note> in another crucible. Give it to drink <note>an alchemical term for adding a liquid or molten metal to another</note> and it will all become a hard mass like an amalgam. Then grind it in a stone mortar and wash it again with salt and vinegar until it appears clear and the vinegar is clean, and the tin and quicksilver remain white, clean, and shining. Then melt

<column-break/>

it in a crucible and quench it as many times in the aforementioned water until it turns just like silver. Know that if you pass it through a sieve, it is such that one part of it will turn 10 parts of tin into fine silver, provided it is subtle and passed through quicklime. And truly, here is the best work you can try with tin; this was done by Master Betzer in Avignon.

---

### Secret for congealing the hard [substance] like stone, which is "azeratit"

**T**ake 3 oz. of green olive oil and take 1 oz. of the yellowest sulfur you can find. Grind it well and soak it in the aforementioned oil. Put it in an iron vessel and stir it vigorously with an iron rod so that it is all well mixed. Place it over the fire and boil it a little until the sulfur is dissolved. Then remove it immediately from the fire and let it cool. Add one oz. of well-washed quicksilver, as mentioned, and it will congeal like stone. You shall mix this with the "Work of the Moon" <note>alchemical term for operations involving silver</note>.

# On Rupescissa

### Here begins "The Olive" composed by Brother John of Rupescissa <note>original: "johan de roccatallada"</note> concerning the philosopher's stone, which he wished to show to the elect of God and of the Holy Roman Church.

In the name of God I begin, and of the glorious Virgin Mary and of all the celestial court of Paradise: may they all deign to help me and direct me in this work, so that I may perform it well for their honor and reverence, and that it may be for the profit and salvation of my soul. Amen.

### Here is shown who was the author of the work, and to whom he wished to reveal it.

Notification and revelation of the philosopher's stone <term>philosopher's stone: a legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting eternal life</term> by Brother John of Rupescissa, which he reveals to the Holy Roman Church.

### Here he speaks by way of prophecy of the persecutions <gloss>that</gloss> the Roman Church must endure.

I have considered the tribulations of the elect in the sacrosanct Evangelical Church prophesied by Jesus Christ, especially through the tribulations of the Antichrist; and already he stands approaching the gates of time. There is no doubt that the Holy Church shall be greatly afflicted and shall be a fugitive to the mountains. And certainly, this is to be done by tyrant men and princes, who shall strip her of all temporal riches shortly. Even though the ship of Saint Peter <note>a traditional metaphor for the Catholic Church</note> is tossed in the great waves of the sea of this world, she must nevertheless be delivered in the tribulations

<column-break/>

of those who hold lordship over the people. For this reason, out of love to relieve the great necessity and coming poverty of the holy people chosen by God—to whom it is given to know the mystery and secret of virtue and of truth, without figures—I wish truly to speak and clearly reveal the great stone of the philosophers, for the Moon and for the Sun <note>original: "a luna e a Sol," referring to silver and gold</note>, and for the white and for the red. I shall do this against the custom of the philosophers who were before me, who were touched by such envy that they concealed the truth even from their own. And therefore, it is not my intention to speak by probing or tempting or imputing; but rather, through simple speech of words, I shall inform the sacrosanct general Church of the experiment of truth, <unclear>shining forth</unclear>, ceasing long intentions and moving summarily to the practice; to be brief, I shall draw near.

### Concerning the matter from which the philosopher's stone is made, and where it is found.

<margin>The matter of the stone is of vile price; since it is found free from great concerns.</margin>

The matter truly of the stone is one thing, of vile price, found in every place: because it is a viscous water; but it is quicksilver <note>original: "argent viu," mercury</note>, just as it is drawn from the earth, though it is empty. However, quicksilver willingly engenders in privies <note>latrines</note>. Just as some said that it was found in vile things. And many sons of beasts and of ignorance and of coarseness, not understanding the meaning of the philosophers, [err].

<summary>Brother John of Rupescissa introduces his alchemical treatise, framing the creation of the philosopher's stone as a divine necessity to fund the Church during the coming persecutions of the Antichrist. He identifies the primary material of the stone as mercury (quicksilver), which he claims is common and easily found.</summary>

# The first operation necessary for the composition of the philosopher's stone.

**T**ake Roman vitriol and saltpeter <note>potassium nitrate</note>, as much of one as the other, 2 lbs. each, and grind them finely on a stone or in a hand mortar; and melt it over a slow fire for a bit, so that the water evaporates. Then take 1 lb. of good mercury extracted from ore, and not artificially made; wrap it in a linen cloth and sprinkle it over the aforementioned warm matter so that it spreads through the holes of the cloth; and stir it a little with a stick. And soak them there in the aforementioned matter, so that none of it [the mercury] appears visible. Afterward, put it all in a vessel to
<margin>sublimation of mercury</margin>
sublimate, first over a slow fire until the humidity is gone through the hole at the top of the vessel; you will know this is happening if you place an iron tool or a small wheel over the said hole. And when no moisture appears on the said iron or wheel, close the hole with the "lute of wisdom" <note>a specialized airtight sealing clay</note>; and strengthen the fire for

<gloss>into the council of lords</gloss>

<column-break/>

twelve hours; and at the end, give it a stronger heat so that all the mercury is sublimated, and draw it out white as snow. **I**n this thing you have done two things: first, you have purged it of earthiness and blackness, and you have removed the humidity through which it lived and flowed; and you have congealed it and made it white as a mixer and blender fit for digestion in the closed stove; and you have made it fit to be reduced into water, as will appear from here on.

**S**econdly, you have put into it the invisible sulfur of the philosophers: which is the ore of redness, that is, the spirit of Roman vitriol. And here is a great marvel: that since that spirit is invisible, it has the nature of the ore of redness.

<margin>On the preparation of the stone by sublimation according to Master Arnau de Vilanova in the figurative treatise of the Great Treatise under the figure of our words or terms</margin>
**A**nd for this reason, the mercury congeals in the sublimation into a whiteness the color of snow. And this is why many of the great philosophers suggested that the stone is made of "azure sun" <note>likely referring to a specific purified state of gold or a mineral</note> and sulfur, which is not common sulfur, but the sulfur of the philosophers. And of the aforementioned preparation and sublimation and operation, Master Arnau de Vilanova <note>A famous 13th-century Catalan physician and alchemist</note> spoke in the figurative treatise of the Great Treatise under the figure of words or parables: that is, in the likeness of the Gospel of Jesus Christ. This parable: **Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth** <gloss>that is, is buried</gloss> etc. <note>original: "Nisi granum frumenti cadens in terra"</note>—that is, if the grain of wheat falling into the earth does not die, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. **I** understand by the grain of wheat in the earth the "azure" mixer.

But it should not be revealed <margin>.</margin> except to holy men who are poor in spirit, who fear God, and who love Him with a good <margin>.</margin> heart and good will. And to these, this truth must be revealed, so that they may do good for the reverence of God: to the poor who have need, and to poor maidens <note>original: "poncelles"</note> who have nothing with which to marry, and to poor clerics who have no means to advance themselves in their poverty. For there are many who would be good clerics, but because of poverty they cannot move forward; and for this reason, the secrets that are not revealed to nature are lost, because they have no way to open their understanding. And for the pure love of God, He has wished to reveal it to me so that you may do good to the holy poor for the pure love of God and for the faithful departed. For they shall pray to God that He gives you good guidance through the merit of His holy

Therefore, death and life are in this book, in the hands of the one who uses it wrongly.

**I commend** then this revelation <note>original: "revelament"</note> into the hands of the Crucifix of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom I have received this great mastery <note>referring to the "Magisterium" or the Great Work of alchemy</note>, and to the keeping of the holy angels and the poor evangelists of Jesus Christ, who are not sons of temporal riches but serve their Creator. Saint Paul says to them: "The root of all evils is avarice," which some would desire and thereby wander from the faith. ## The multiplication of the said work

The manner of multiplying our aforementioned elixir <term>elixir: a preparation able to change base metals into gold or silver</term>. Take of living Mercury <note>original: "Mercuri viu"; quicksilver</note> that is very clean, 1 ounce, and of our aforementioned elixir, and put it all in the urinal <note>a glass vessel shaped like a bladder, used in alchemy</note> and seal it well with a cloth. Afterward, place the urinal in the furnace of the philosophers and give it tempered fire as you know how; and let it stay for 15 natural days. Afterward, let it cool and break the urinal, and you will find it all converted into stone. And it will be a perfect elixir to finish; and place 1 part of this over 1,000 <note>a ratio of 1:1000 for transmutation</note>, and thus you can multiply it up to 10 times, so that from 1 pound you can make 10 pounds. Many thanks be given to God now and forever. Amen. :-

## Above all, a true operation for white

Take of the moon <note>original: "luna"; alchemical code for silver</note> dissolved in strong water <term>aygua fort: nitric acid, used for dissolving metals</term> and set it aside. Take vitriol <note>original: "azequizi"; likely a corruption of the Arabic 'al-zaj'</note> dissolved in strong water and let it be aside. Take sal ammoniac <note>ammonium chloride</note> dissolved in strong water and set it aside. And Arsenic <note>original: "Azsenich"</note> dissolved in the said water, 1 ounce. And you must understand that all the aforementioned things must be very well calcined <note>reduced to powder by heat</note> and purged, and well prepared and well sublimated, and well fixed according to the nature of the things.

And afterward, take the dissolved silver and the dissolved vitriol mentioned above, and mix everything together in a small glass vial, well sealed, and keep it aside. And then take the well-dissolved sal ammoniac and the aforementioned dissolved arsenic, and mix them together in a small glass vial, well sealed, and let it be aside. And let it stay thus for 4 days, for thus they will become "pregnant" <note>an alchemical metaphor for the substances beginning to react or combine</note>; and you will have fulfilled the saying of the philosophers.

And after the four days have passed, mix all the aforementioned waters together in one bottle, and when they are mixed, stopper the bottle and let it go under manure <note>decaying manure was used as a source of steady, low heat</note> for 3 days, and there they will make a conjunction. And afterward, take it out of the said manure and put the said bottle in hot ashes with a slow fire. And put on its alembic head <note>the cap of a still</note> to distill; and thus with a very slow fire, you shall distill. Do it in this manner.

To make red vinegar:
First, make the red vinegar, which is made in this way: take one ounce of Roman vitriol <note>Iron(II) sulfate, often used as a source of sulfuric acid</note> and dissolve it in distilled vinegar. However, the vitriol should be sublimated twice beforehand with half an ounce of **sal ammoniac** <note>ammonium chloride</note>; and after you have done this, dissolve it all together with the distilled vinegar. Then, let it sit for 3 days, and afterwards pass it through a filter. Then, inside a glass vessel over ashes, extract it <note>distill it</note>; and after it is extracted, dissolve it again and filter it. Do this three times, and on the third time it remains dissolved. However, evaporate a third part of it, and it should remain like a red oil which congeals in the cold and dissolves in the heat. Set this aside; it is called **red vinegar**.

Next, take one ounce of **vermilion** <note>mercury sulfide</note> and grind it well upon a marble slab. Soak it in the sun with distilled vinegar for 7 days, saturating and drying it. Afterwards, soak the said vermilion for another 7 days with the **red vinegar** mentioned above, saturating and drying it. And then soak it with **sal**

<column-break/>

**ammoniac**, saturating and drying it until it has drunk its own weight, and set it aside. And if you [sublime] it twice and it is sublimated, let it dissolve by itself upon the marble into an oil. Set that oil aside, for it is called **oil of vermilion**.

Furthermore, take one ounce of **Alexandrian Tutty** <note>a form of zinc oxide found in furnace chimneys</note> and make it glowing red in a crucible; quench it 10 times in 8 ounces of vinegar distilled through an **alembic** <note>a classic alchemical still</note>. Then, let the vinegar be reduced by half. Afterwards, let the vinegar rest and pass it through a filter. Then, grind the Tutty upon a marble slab and give it all the said vinegar to drink little by little, saturating and drying it upon the marble until it has drunk it all. Then take that Tutty and put it inside a crucible; cover it and put it in the furnace so that it dries. When it is dry, grind it well upon a marble slab, soaking it with the **oil of vermilion**, saturating and drying it for 7 days in the furnace or in the very hot sun. Afterwards, soak it with water of **sal ammoniac** until it has doubled its weight, and store it aside.

Afterwards, as the gold is dissolved with the "second water": take half an ounce of **sal ammoniac** and three ounces of **saltpeter** <note>potassium nitrate</note>, and make a water <note>an acid</note> from them using an alembic, and store it. Note that all orthodox authors explain the operations of their mastery <term>magisterium: the successful completion of the alchemical process or the "Masterpiece"</term> through generation <insert>and</insert> unfolding, which is always from its own kind. O Venerable Father, I give thanks to God who by His goodness has permitted this science to reach your hands and mine: and the hidden things of the divine.
