The true way they set down through obscure words: and even under figures: so that they could not be understood except by the sons of wisdom. The other way they set down through enigmas and figures so that they might lead men astray. For they know that God will judge this science worthy. He permits this to happen in the world because they desire all others to be ignorant of it. Moreover, the wise have concealed this science lest the impious, receiving it, should be more ready to turn to profane joys: lest the philosophers should have to render an account for their sins. <margin>Note that he seems to speak of these vegetable things—blood, hair, eggs—in those books of which they speak; but rather of that which is quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> and sulfur, from which it is composed in the first mixture in the bowels of the earth, and thus not other things by accident.</margin>

They fall into error, not finding their intended goal. And the cause of their error is this: because it is certain that from a human being nothing is generated except a human being, nor from animals except those similar to themselves.

## Since
therefore all the aforementioned things are utterly foreign to the nature of metals, it is impossible for their generation to occur in metals; for metals are not generated except from their own sperm, just as a human is not except from their own sperm.

## Quicksilver
<note>original: "Argentum vivum"</note> is the sperm of metals and their origin, as the most learned philosophers have said, and even sight teaches us, as I shall declare below.

## Thus
however, the aforementioned things—such as blood, hair, eggs, horn, and vegetable earth—are not composed in metals from quicksilver. Because of this, the perfect generation or transmutation of metals is impossible from them; the philosophers placed them only as an example of my physical stone <note>The "physical stone" refers to the Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the Great Work</note>.

<margin>And these best... mixture... spirits... water... fire</margin>

## There are
also others who took a fourth kind of quicksilver: Arsenic, sulfur, and salt ammoniac <note>term: sal armoniacum; a mineral salt used in alchemy, now known as ammonium chloride</note>, and they say that these flee from fire and fly away in smoke. And they take these in place of the four elements, seeing that the philosophers say in their books that their essence is in the spirits. And they sublimate <note>term: sublimant; the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again</note> these so that they are truly airy; afterwards they fix them so that they are truly earth; then they calcine <note>term: calcinant; heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to powder</note> them so they are truly fiery; finally they dissolve them so they are truly watery. And they compose these according to the books, believing they have the knowledge of them, and they cast the compositions as before upon the metallic bodies; and they find nothing, and thus they are entirely deluded.

## And
the cause of their error is manifold, of which two suffice for the present. One is because, as has been said, metals are not generated except from their own sperm. These things, however, are not the sperm of perfected metals; therefore, etc., generation or transmutation from them is impossible.

<margin>note this writing</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>note this reasoning, for our aforementioned medicine can never be converted from vile bodies, namely urine, blood, hair, and other vile things</margin>

## Likewise
sulfur and arsenic are not consumed in fire; and a stronger fire leaves them as charcoal, which can never withstand the fire. These things—neither by themselves, nor mixed with metallic bodies, nor mixed with elements abstracted from eggs, blood, hair, urine, and other vegetable things—will they admit, just as the stone or our medicine does not. And this is evident through the aforementioned reasons.

## Because
for the generation of a human, there was no admission of any thing except their own seed; nor for the generation of plants except their own seed. Therefore, our mastery <note>term: magisterium; the alchemical process or the "Great Work" itself</note> does not require any extraneous thing.

## Certain people
believe they find knowledge in salts; and they dissolve and calcine them, melt and separate them, and cast them upon imperfect bodies; and they find nothing.

## Others
mix them together as was said, prepare them with the bodies, calcine and dissolve them; and they find nothing.

## And
the cause of their error is the same as the preceding ones.

## And
some believe they can elicit the medicine from the spirits of the bodies; and they prepare them by calcining, dissolving, and congealing; and they cast them upon the bodies; and they are deceived.

## And
the cause of their error is this: that the form of metals is not received from one another, but as it is in its own nature. And from all the aforementioned things, it is clear that our science is not from blood with hair, urine, or herbs, nor vegetables; nor in the aforementioned spirits by themselves, or joined to one another, or in salts, or any other things whatsoever.

**It is asked** from what the lights of the sun <note>gold</note> can be made: why is an imperfect body used? **The answer is** that the work may be completed and the colors which the philosophers <note>the "philosophers" refers to ancient alchemical authorities</note> have established may appear more orderly and according to the sayings of the philosophers.
**It is asked** if all the colors appear in the work of the lights: they do appear, but they do not keep the same order.

**It is asked** if the Sun and Moon <note>gold and silver</note> by themselves, or both together after dissolution has been made, ought to pass through the alembic <note>a distilling apparatus</note>.
**The answer is**: Then the way is better if each passes through by itself. They could, however, pass through together, but with greater difficulty; but whether separately or joined, it is expedient that they pass through the alembic. Because thus one can be certain that the lights are reduced to their first matter, that is, quicksilver.
**Why** is it necessary that it returns to quicksilver?
**The answer is**: Because quicksilver is their first [matter]. And unless they were reduced to their first immediate state, the perfect artificial generation of perfect metals could not occur, nor their multiplication.

**Column 2**

<margin>Note of greatest importance; see above folio 95 column 2</margin>

Take from that and you will not err. If you fear the falsification of the seal, make it pass through the alembic; and if no dregs remain in the bottom of the alembic, it is good and natural. If dregs remain, let it be converted into the body of metals, and according to the species of the metal, the adulteration of the quicksilver shall be recognized.
<margin>Note here the first operation which is in this work <unclear>namely into the appearance of snow</unclear></margin>

Then it ought to be filtered and placed in urinals <note>glass vessels</note> for subliming. And pure, clean, and living water will ascend. And afterwards with vinegar over a slow fire it ought to be stripped. Then it ought to be passed through a horn <note>likely a funnel or specific vessel</note>, and thus it can be placed safely in the mastery.

**For there are two parts of the stone: namely, earth and water.**
**It is asked** for how long the stone must remain in the state of blackness <note>The *nigredo* or "blackness" is the first major stage of alchemy, symbolizing death and decomposition before rebirth.</note>, and what is the sign of the true dissolution of the stone.
**The answer is:** when the blackness appears for the first time, it is a sign of the putrefaction and dissolution of the stone. However, when the blackness has totally vanished, it is a sign of the total putrefaction and dissolution of the stone. These black clouds last in the aforementioned stone for 40 days—sometimes more, and sometimes less. This variation occurs because of the difference in the quantity of the medicine <note>The "medicine" is another term for the alchemical substance being transformed.</note> and also the skill of the operator. Thus, a larger quantity requires more time; a smaller quantity, less. The wisdom of the operator helps through a more careful separation of the ingredients.

**It is asked:** Once the earth is separated, what must be done with the water? **The answer is:** The water must be placed in a urinal <note>term: urinal <explanation>A glass vessel shaped like a bladder, used in alchemical heating and observation.</explanation></note>, and with an alembic <note>term: alembic <explanation>The "cap" or lid of a still used to collect and condense vapors.</explanation></note> placed on top in its receiver as is the custom. Let it be situated in the distillation furnace and distilled with a slow fire. Be so attentive in this distillation that between the drop that falls and the subsequent drop, there are 60 moments. This is measured by a man speaking distinct words with a pause in the middle, saying 1, 2, 3, 4, up to 60 perfect words. This order should be observed in the distillation. That which you find in the bottom is sharply dissolved in new water, in triple or quadruple its amount, or until it is entirely dissolved and the water sprays at the top. Let this be done through distillation so many times until the dregs are utterly removed. And with

the distilled water, you thus have rectified water. <gloss>These are the perfect steps for the rectification of all things <unclear>...</unclear></gloss>
**It is asked** how long the said distillation lasts. **The answer is** that there is no determined time for more or less, but it depends on the greater or lesser quantity of the water, provided the uniformity of the fire is maintained.
**It is asked:** Once the distillation is done, what must be done with the water? **The answer is:** Take the earth which you previously separated and filtered, now pulverized, and place it in the aforementioned glass vessel, having sealed the joints of both. Give it some of the aforementioned distilled water until it floats above the earth. Let it rest with a gentle fire—just as the fire of putrefaction was, or a little stronger—for 4 days, or until the water is dried up with the earth. Then again, add more of the aforementioned water and cook it, and so on, until the earth is white and clear and has "drunk" its water. For just as the earth is putrefied by the power of water, so is it cleansed. If it has been cleansed, by the help of God, the whole mastery <note>original: "magisterium"; the successful completion of the alchemical process.</note> may be directed.
**It is asked** how long this putrefaction and cleansing lasts. **The answer is** 40 days sometimes—more or less—according to the greater or lesser quantity of water.

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for the final stages of the Great Work, specifically the repeated saturation of the material and the subsequent projection (transformation) of base metals into gold or silver.</meta>

The successive <term>imbibitions</term><note>The process of "feeding" a solid material with liquid until it is saturated.</note> and drying processes should be continued until the matter turns red and the earth liquefies. Thus, the medicine for the red work <note>The "Red Work" or Rubedo is the final stage of the alchemical process, resulting in the Philosopher's Stone capable of making gold.</note> will be very powerful.

**Question:** If the entire water of one flask—whether lunar <note>Silver-based or white work.</note> or solar <note>Gold-based or red work.</note>—is to be added, should it be put in all at once in one imbibition?
**Response:** You ought to put only enough water over the matter so that it just covers it, and no more. Then the fire must be continued until it is dry. Nor should the second imbibition be done [until then]; and so on in order until the perfection of the medicine.

**Question:** How is the <term>projection</term><note>The act of casting a small amount of the Philosopher's Stone onto molten base metal to transform it.</note> of this solar and lunar medicine performed?
**Response:** One part is to be cast upon 10 parts of metal recently melted, or upon warm <term>quicksilver</term><note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury.</note>. And then it will be a medicine; and of that medicine, one part is to be placed upon 100 parts. And it will still be a medicine. And of that one medicine, one part is to be placed upon 1,000 parts of an imperfect molten body or warm and clean quicksilver. And it will be bright or splendid gold, according to whether the medicine was prepared for the white or for the red. It will withstand every judgment and examination <note>It will pass the tests of a goldsmith, such as the cupel or touchstone.</note>.

**Question:** How is this white or red medicine multiplied? **Response:** I tell you, you must do this for yourself; I will not tell you in writing. I tell you what none of the philosophers have dared to say. I adjure you by the eternal Creator that you do not reveal this surpassing secret except only to the sons of wisdom and those advanced in the art.

### These aforesaid questions are essen-
### tial to this work. And now

<column-break/>

### Begin the accidental ques-
### tions of this work or the mas-
### tery of the philosopher's stone.

<margin>Note here these very useful and <unclear>necessary</unclear> questions.</margin>
**T**o the accidental questions which you have asked me, I respond to you in order.

**First**, it is asked: how many <term>furnaces</term><note>original: "furnelli".</note> are necessary for the operation? **Response:** One furnace suffices if the seeker is prudent. For one is the furnace of <term>putrefaction</term><note>rotting or breaking down</note> and <term>distillation</term>, of <term>incineration</term><note>original: "cinerationis"; reducing to ashes</note> or calcination, of <term>sublimation</term>, imbibition, and <term>fixation</term><note>making a volatile substance stable under heat</note>, as is shown by the figure described above at the end of the questions.

**Question:** How many vessels are necessary? **Response:** If you have understood this well, look back at the essential questions where this is sufficiently determined.

**Question:** Whether the vessels ought to be closed, and with what? **Response:** The vessels of putrefaction ought to be closed with a linen cloth. Secondly, also those of fixation. The vessels of distillation and incineration ought to be sealed <note>original: "lutari"; sealed with "lute," a specialized alchemical putty.</note> with gypsum and egg white at the joints. The receiver for distillation ought not be sealed to the vessel of the <term>alembic</term><note>the "hood" or cap of the still</note>, but should remain open.

**Question:** How many are the fires of the operation?
**Response:** There are four fires which I understand through these verses:

> **First**, let it be said, is that in which the senses dominate.
> Nature, being faithful, rejoices when the senses are balanced.
> The **third** clings heretically and hurts with violence.
> The **fourth**, the destroyer of the senses, knows not how to spare.

**Question:** How are these fires to be ordered in the operation? **Response:** The first fire is of putrefaction; the second of distillation; the third of fixation; the fourth of incineration, which is sublimation—that is, the end of sublimation.

**Question:** How many colors appear in the work?
**Response:** There are three principal colors appearing in the work: namely: black, white, and red.
But there are many other colors appearing in our work. And they occur in this order. The 1st color is silvery. 2nd black. 3rd violet. 4th lemon-yellow. 5th green. 6th peacock-colored. 7th silvery. 8th perfect white. 9th ash-colored. 10th saffron. 11th perfect red. And there are many other intermediate colors, which need not be a concern.
**Question:** When do the colors appear? **Response:**
<margin>When are blackness and redness seen?</margin>
In the amalgamation, the silvery color appears. In the putrefaction <note>The stage of breaking down the matter, associated with the "nigredo" or blackness.</note>, black appears on the surface. In the reduction of the ferment with the body, it varies through all the colors that can be imagined. In the fixation, it receives firm colors: which are never destroyed by fire when they are projected upon imperfect molten bodies, or upon hot, clean quicksilver <note>original: ar. vi. (argentum vivum)</note>.
**Question:** In what way does the perfect red medicine give the weight of silver <note>original: lune (the Moon/Silver)</note> to bodies not having it? And the perfect white medicine diminishes the weight of lead: and reduces it to the weight of silver. **Response:** The red medicine constricts the parts of silver and other bodies not having the weight of gold <note>original: solis (the Sun/Gold)</note>: until they are measured out to gold in weight: and this is by the power of its specific form: which specific form it attains because of the perfect and long decoction <note>The process of heating or "cooking" the substance.</note> of its ferment. This ferment reaches and converts the imperfect body and the water of life <note>original: aquam vite</note> to its own perfection and nature. The white medicine, however, constricts the parts of tin: and dilates the parts of lead: until they are truly turned to the nature of its specific form, which form it also attains because of the proper decoction of its ferment, which ferment attracts and converts

<column-break/>

the imperfect body and the water of life to its own nature and perfection.
From these sayings, it follows that quicksilver, copper, and tin: when they are converted <margin>Note</margin> into gold by the perfect medium of redness: it restores them in weight according to more or less: and they diminish in quantity—quicksilver and lead do not restore in weight, nor do they diminish in quantity through this medium, but they are tinted only with perfect redness. Lead, however, and quicksilver, when they are converted into silver by the perfect medicine of whiteness, it restores them in quantity, and they diminish in weight. Tin diminishes in quantity and increases in weight. And copper neither restores in quantity nor diminishes in weight, but is whitened only with a perfect whitening to every judgment and examination.
**Question:** How is it possible or even intelligible that one part of this medicine converts thousands of parts of quicksilver or imperfect bodies into a perfect body or silver? **Response:** The entire matter of this medicine, mixed through subtle artifice and ingenuity, is in a spiritual fixed substance: which among the philosophers is called the **Fifth Essence** <note>original: quinta essentia; the pure, incorruptible element beyond the four terrestrial elements.</note>. For in every way it has the nature of incorruptibility and the form of perfection. And therefore, because form has the nature of informing to infinity, if the proper matter is brought near to it: for this reason, if it were possible that all the water of the sea were clean quicksilver, heated, or a molten imperfect body, and a little of this medicine were placed upon it, all that water would be converted into gold or silver: as one part converts another, and so on to infinity. And it would happen as suddenly as illumination occurs, because once the proper matter has the medicine—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of alchemical theory, specifically focusing on the unity of the "Stone" and the reconciliation of seemingly contradictory statements by Aristotle regarding the possibility of transmutation.</meta>

the aptitude for receiving form: and that medicine, which is a fixed formal substance, has the nature of forming, which is therefore necessary. From this, when they are properly brought together and the agents are not hindered in their nature, the effect and action follow.

<margin>Note a. <unclear>tl</unclear> truly noted</margin>
How should that ancient proverb of the philosophers be understood: "One is the stone; one the medicine; one the vessel; one the regimen <note>regimen: the method or process of heat and timing</note>; for the white and for the red, to be performed successively"? Response: It was said above that the matter of all metals is one, namely, quicksilver <note>original: "ar. vi." (argentum vivum)</note> thickened in sulfurous heat in the belly of the earth; and that metals do not differ except by accidental qualities. It was also said that it is necessary to reduce metals to their immediate seed, namely, to quicksilver.

Since, therefore, all the pigments <note>term: pigmentaria (pigments/raw materials) - here referring to the chemical ingredients used in the work</note> of this work are reduced to quicksilver, and the unique thing is one quicksilver, white or red according to a greater or lesser decoction <note>decoction: the process of boiling or heating a substance</note>. Therefore, it is called "one stone," namely quicksilver, which is the immediate seed of metals. "One medicine," namely whitened or reddened. "One vessel," namely of putrefaction, successively one vessel of distillation, and one vessel of fixation. "One regimen" of distillation, one regimen of inceration <note>inceration: a process of softening a substance to a wax-like consistency</note>, one regimen of fixation; for the white and for the red, to be performed successively.

How should that saying of the *Azetheoz* <note>likely a corruption of a title attributed to Aristotle in the Arabic-Latin tradition</note> be understood? Aristotle [says] by means of white sulfur that does not burn, he congeals quicksilver and converts it into silver. And by means of red sulfur that does not burn, he congeals quicksilver and converts it into gold. And this is

<column-break/>

the greatest thing that Alchemists can acquire in this life. Response: In the book *Azetheoz*, Aristotle subtly [shows] in those two the possibility of the art of Alchemy and its truth; and he places the ultimate conclusion of the art of alchemy upon the white—which is the perfect white medicine—and upon the red—which is the perfect red medicine. And if the alchemists have perfect whiteness and redness, they have the perfect stone for the white and for the red; and that is the greatest thing they can acquire in this life through the craftsmanship of this art. And if what he says is true, why does Aristotle say "let the alchemists rejoice [for they know] that one species cannot be transmuted into another"? They can cover the envies of the philosophers <note>a common trope where philosophers hide secrets to prevent the unworthy from succeeding</note> so that it may look like gold, yet it will always be lead; they can tint silver so that it looks like gold, so that men may err in it, yet it will always be silver. Response: In these words, he shows a double mode of alchemical operation: one sophisticated <note>sophysticū: in this context, meaning "imitation" or "fraudulent"</note> and the other true. The sophisticated and false mode is that of those who work according to what was said at the beginning of our work: those who do not reduce the pigments to their immediate seed. And to such people Aristotle speaks, saying that one species of metal is by no means converted into another, except in a false, sophisticated way. And he exemplifies this in the letter; but to those who work according to the true mode, he does not speak in that way, which he includes at the end of the chapter: "unless they are reduced..."

<summary>This page explains the alchemical principle that all metals share a common origin in quicksilver and sulfur, justifying why there is only "one stone" and "one medicine." It also reconciles Aristotle's skepticism toward transmutation by distinguishing between "sophisticated" (fraudulent) surface-level imitation and "true" alchemy that works upon the "seed" of the metal.</summary>

### Concerning the composition of the Philosophers' Stone, first for the White. Then for the Red.

<margin>A brief [recipe] for this stone</margin>

# **The Doctrine on the Composition of the Philosophers' Stone, called the Book of Pheminus.**
## **Chapter 1**

Since, through such a great length of days without ceasing—and not without various anxieties of heart, labors, and expenses—I have not stopped testing in many ways a certain secret <note>original: "archanum," a hidden mystery or profound secret</note> which is sublime in the minds of men but remains deeply hidden. Through this, divine grace can be acquired, and the harsh, stepmother-like poverty of men can be shattered. To you, O King—whom I have judged more worthy than other modern princes for many reasons which I pass over for the present—I shall explain this, God willing, without any cloud or fiction in this little book directed to you, just as I have searched it out even unto this day. Nevertheless, whatever must be worked from that point until the perfection of the experiment, as I have been able to extract it from the secrets of certain expert philosophers, all of this I will subsequently unknot for you without riddles. I beseech, therefore, and with a pure heart humbly implore the name of the Most High—who bestows His wisdom on whom He wills and withdraws it from whom He wills, in whose will and disposition is every creature—that He may aid you in holding your purpose and in concealing the secret, and that He may be our help, and the beginning and end in all my works.

However, most serene Prince, because many vain and presumptuous men

<column-break/>

might think it a folly that I have disposed myself to open this secret to you—which is the best guide before the end—I think it necessary before all things to relate the causes which seem reasonable and which excuse all presumption.

The first cause indeed is this: so that if perhaps you have held some hope in this work, for which I have labored partly for your sake for so long, your Excellence may know that I have received this work upon a true foundation and principle, and have in no way deviated from the right path, nor approached the practice without persistence. For as the wise man remains: he who is ignorant of the principles of an art must necessarily be ignorant of the entire art.

The other cause is this: that if, on account of my faults and sins, I—being unworthy—should be unable to finish this divine and so precious work in time, or if perhaps by some other unexpected accident (which God avert) it should happen that I leave the work itself incomplete, you—whom truth previously noted as worthy—should not remain untaught or despairing.

## **Concerning the necessities regarding the Stone of the Philosophers. Chapter 2 on the same.**

Now indeed, what this secret is; how it is named; of what it consists; how it is worked; how it is projected <note>referring to "projection," the final stage where the medicine transforms base metal into gold</note>; how it is multiplied; and what virtues it possesses; together with certain circumstances of the work itself, you shall see fully contained in the following chapters.

## **Concerning the Secret of Secrets. Chapter 7.**

This secret is the Secret of Secrets of the Most High God, which He revealed by His piety to the holy prophets and ancient philosophers, and which He has hidden from the common people with great vigilance. And as Pythagoras says...

# On the Secrecy of the Art

**Left Column:**

In a certain book of his, God concealed this secret <term>archanum</term> <note>original: "archanum," referring to a profound mystery or hidden secret of nature</note> from the people, lest the world be devastated. For if the secrets of nature, in which the one wisdom of the world lies hidden, were open to the common folk, then study, doctrine, science, and the very name of fortune would cease; and this sublime science would become worthless if it were entirely visible, for no one would wish to learn anything else. Thus, it would either make all living beings equal, or it would cause irreparable damage to the highest order of things. Therefore, it is not without merit that secrets are commanded to be kept. They are more precious when they are discovered through various labors.

Furthermore, Aristotle, in his book called *The Light of Lights* <note>original: "Lumen Luminum," a medieval pseudo-Aristotelian alchemical text</note>, asserts that the ancient philosophers concealed this secret so studiously that few might understand it. For if it were known to the common crowd, there would be no further place for prudence, and the observer of all things would be made equal to the wise.

Again, Aristotle says: the philosophers forbade and concealed this, fearing lest wicked and malevolent men, understanding this, might perform illicit and profane acts, for whose evils the philosophers would have to give an account before God.

Zosimos <note>original: "Rosimus," referring to Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century alchemist</note> the philosopher, also responding to Eutesia, the daughter of a certain King, who questioned him as to why the philosophers so carefully hid this secret, said: "Lest the labor of those inhabiting the lands and streets should perish." They also assert that there will be a judgment of God upon those knowing this science who desire to always keep others in ignorance out of envy; which is clearly the case, since all philosophers, when they wrote anything concerning this secret—

—immediately employed obscure words and riddles, so that one can hardly distinguish the true from the false, unless by the inspiration of the Most High God, or by someone teaching them.

But nevertheless, this secret is sought by many and found by few. And therefore, certain sophists <note>here meaning "false teachers" or "pretenders"</note> who are ignorant of the nature of things and the secrets of philosophy, applying themselves to many great things with labor and expense but finding nothing in the end, ascribe the error of their own unskillfulness to philosophy. They proclaim this work to be not only difficult, but even impossible. Philosophy does not care for this, for she does not invite everyone to her banquet, but only those who are found worthy to recline at this table and be refreshed by such a feast. Therefore, let anyone seeking this science strive not to be a sophist, but a philosopher: that is, one knowing the natures of things, not by meditation alone, but truly by meditation and experience. For without experience, meditation is of no use.

Hence, experience is to be sought more than meditation. For he who has attained the experience of this thing will be a philosopher regarding this matter, and will be worthily numbered among the guests of the aforementioned table. His faculty, which surpasses every price of worldly things, is satisfied with perpetual sweetness and affection.

This aforementioned secret is indeed named by some "the medicine," and by many "alchemy." For it is worthily called "the Stone" <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note>, because when it is perfected, it has the form of a stone; and it is of a very dark color, appearing slightly—

# On the Nature and Names of the Stone

...possessing clarity: and it breaks with a moderate blow. Its appearance gladdens the hearts of men to the highest degree and strengthens them.

**E**lixir is its name in Arabic, a name which is interpreted in Latin as "ferment" <note>original: *fermentum*</note>. And truly it can be called a ferment: for just as the ferment of dough multiplies the dough, so this elixir multiplies itself.

**M**edicine is what it is called for this reason: because just as human medicines heal and cure sick bodies, so this medicine purges and heals "sick" or imperfect metals through projection <note>The act of casting the alchemical powder onto molten base metal to transform it into gold.</note> alone.

**A**lchemy is also its common name, which it takes from a certain philosopher who was called Alchimon, and who was the first to discover this stone by divine grace. Regarding the matter from which the Philosopher's Stone is composed:

**O**ur Adestus <note>Likely a corruption of *Asbestus* or a specific alchemical pseudonym</note> and the aforementioned stone, of which the physicians <note>In this context, "physicians" refers to natural philosophers or alchemists.</note> have spoken so much and so greatly, consists of quicksilver <term>quicksilver: mercury (argentum vivum)</term> alone, with no other foreign thing mixed into it. For if anything foreign were mixed with it in any way, this stone could by no means be made from it.

**A**nd therefore Hermes, the prince of this philosophy, says: "Know that quicksilver and fire are sufficient for you for the great work of composing the Philosopher's Stone."

# Concerning all the diverse things
<margin>from which the stone is composed, chapter 6</margin>

Because, in truth, the ignorant—not understanding the secrets of this science—assert that the **Philosophers' Stone** <note>original: "lapis philosophorum"</note> can be made from many animals: namely from the basilisk, or from the eggs of hens, or from human blood, or from the bee, or the tortoise, or many other things possessing souls; or from many minerals: namely various marcasites, or common sulfur, or orpiment <note>arsenic trisulfide, a yellow pigment</note>, or various alums, or inks, or salts, and similar things. Or even from certain vegetables: namely from wine, or honey, or many herbs and diverse plants—upon which those believing they would find the Philosophers' Stone have labored for long periods in many ways, not without great expense, and finally found nothing. Concerning these people, it is greatly to be wondered at, since natural reason evidently condemns their erroneous opinions. For it is clearly established that any animal generates nothing except its own likeness: as man generates man, the lion a lion, the bird a bird, the fish a fish, and metals generate metal.

¶ However, I do not say that certain medicines cannot be made from some of the aforementioned minerals—but not without **quicksilver** <note>original: "vivum argentum," mercury</note>—which whiten copper in such a way that by mixing it with gold and half of pure silver, it appears to be good silver and remains white after the fire.

<column-break/>

But in the trial <note>the "cupellation" or assaying process</note> performed with lead, it is diminished. And therefore, such a work is considered sophisticated <note>in the sense of "adulterated" or "false"</note> among the philosophers.

¶ For a certain medicine is made from arsenic and silver mixed with fine silver, which sufficiently whitens purged copper and converts it into good silver; and this is done with great labor and expense; and in this, profit is found, but not much.

¶ And such a medicine is not considered sophisticated; however, it is not the **Philosophers' Stone**, nor is it in any way to be compared to it: because it does not have such efficacy or power.

<margin>Note</margin>
¶ Many medicines can also be prepared for the "white" and the "red" <note>the two stages of alchemical transformation: albedo and rubedo</note> from raw arsenic mixed with pure bodies, namely silver and gold, through the mastery of the art; these I judge should be passed over for the present, because they are unsuitable for proceeding to the perfection of the pure matter.

¶ And I say that **quicksilver** is counted among the metals and is homogeneous in nature; therefore, it generates metals. Because of this, our stone, which is metallic, can be generated and prepared from it, as was expressed above, since it is the material of all metals.

¶ That it is indeed the material of all metals is proven: for just as we see ice converted into water by heat, it is therefore established that it was previously water. Similarly, we see all metals converted into quicksilver by the craft; it is established that they were previously quicksilver.

¶ But because this secret depends upon the most subtle craftsmanship, it does not easily reach the royal ear. <note>The text breaks off here, suggesting the "royal ear" refers to the patron, likely King Alexander mentioned earlier.</note>

Again, because there are many mockers present who are unskilled in this secret, they claim it is impossible to transmute the species of **metals** into another species. They cite the text of the 4th book of the *Meteorologica* <note>original: "meteoroz"; Aristotle's work on natural phenomena</note> 
<margin>Aristotle</margin> where he says: "Let all **Alchemists** know: that the species of metals cannot be transmuted." Indeed, they claim lead will always be lead.

One can oppose those who cite the aforementioned text without understanding its reasoning, and determine the truth of their opinions 
<margin>Thomas <note>Likely referring to Thomas Aquinas, who wrote commentaries on Aristotle and alchemy.</note></margin> by showing that the philosopher does not labor to make one body out of another body, nor to make a new or foreign mineral out of another mineral. Rather, he only labors so that he might reduce a corrupted and imperfect mineral to health and perfection.

And he perfectly completes that which nature left imperfect. But because this is deeply hidden, many <note>original: "mt̄"</note> ignorant people consider it impossible. It is not to be wondered at if **metals** are partially transmuted from sickness to health, or from imperfection to perfection. However, it ought not be called **transmutation** <note>The author argues this is "perfection" rather than "transmutation" to bypass religious/philosophical bans.</note> because they are not transmuted from their own species to a foreign species; for it is known that all metals are created from **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum: mercury, considered the "mother" of all metals</term> and each of the metals naturally contains gold and silver within itself. Therefore, they are not transmuted into a foreign species but are only healed and partially perfected, and reduced into gold or silver. For all metals are from one seed or nature. And although nature perfects certain metals and leaves others imperfect, it always tends toward its ultimate per-

<column-break/>

perfection, which is gold.

Therefore, it is known that nature is sometimes aided by art, and is many times changed by the same; all these things are shown more broadly in certain books of **Aristotle** and other philosophers. These suffice for the confusion of the errors of the aforementioned detractors and commend this divine philosophy.

<margin>Chapter 7: On the division of the names by which the ancients called the Stone.</margin>
**O most prudent King**, it is necessary for him who wishes to be introduced into this science—this hidden knowledge—to expel the vice of arrogance from himself, and to be pious, upright, and profoundly fearing God, and neighborly to men. Let him be of a serene countenance, greeting others freely, and a diligent observer of the permanent secrets open to him.

Truly, as has already been touched upon above, the **quicksilver** from which our **Stone** is made has two diverse natures: one indeed dry, the other truly moist.
<margin>There are two things in which <unclear>you proceed</unclear>: the Hot and the Moist; whence some call this Water, Sulfur, and others the Male, others the <unclear>spirit</unclear></margin>
Therefore, if we wish to compose our Stone from it, it is necessary for us to divide it into two parts, which the ancient philosophers called by many and diverse names to deceive the ignorant.
<margin>Note two things</margin>

**Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note>, the highest prince and master of this philosophy, named those parts Heaven and Earth, and also the true Male and Female.

**Moses** indeed called them Earth and Water.

**Solomon** the King, son of David, named them Husband and Wife.

**Aristotle** called them the Fixed and the Moist, and also the Hot and the Cold.

**Avicenna** the philosopher called them **Fire** and **Water** and the Red.

**Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in Islamic alchemy.</note>, the father of Alchemists, called them **Quicksilver** and **Sulfur**, as well as the four elements, and many other things.

In this process, it was necessary for the earth to be extracted by the strongest fire of the aforementioned calcination. For if it had not been extracted from the stone without the compound, the pure matter or tincture of that same stone or <term>elixir</term> would, on account of its own ingredients and impurity, hinder its own entrance <note>into the metal</note>. Regarding the matter of the stone reduced to powder, <margin>what the <unclear>resin</unclear> of this ought to be like</margin> the Soul or the aforementioned earth, about which it is said briefly that it permits itself to be calcined: although it has been led to purification, it lacks fusion and the power of entrance. That is to say, it could neither tinge nor enter any metal upon which it might be cast, and this is on account of the greatest dryness which it possesses. And therefore, by necessity, it is required to restore to it the moisture taken away from it. ### On the method of projection of the stone, Chapter 10

<margin>Chapter 10 above</margin>

**B**ut because it is difficult to melt and project <note>The act of casting the alchemical medicine onto a base metal to transform it.</note> upon a million parts at once—and thus to dye them—you shall perform the projection in this manner. Take one crucible and place in it one hundred ounces of crude mercury, well-washed with salt and vinegar; place said crucible over hot coals. And when the quicksilver <note>original: "argenti vivi"</note> begins to smoke, project upon it one ounce of the said stone or elixir, and cover the crucible with an iron lid. Afterward, allow it to cool. The whole mass will be converted into elixir or medicine.

Again, take one ounce from this last elixir or medicine, and project it upon one hundred ounces of crude mercury, washed as stated above with salt and vinegar, in a crucible heated in the fire, and allow it to cool; the whole will be converted into elixir or medicine.

Then take one ounce of this last congealed mercury, and project it upon one hundred ounces of lead or mercury, and it will be converted into the purest, malleable gold, better than that produced from a mine, according to every test.

And it should be known that this medicine converts any other metal upon which it is projected, whether pure or impure, into pure and truly most perfect gold.

But if you wish to work with the white medicine or ferment,

<column-break/>

do in all things and through all things just as I have taught to be done for the red. When this is done, all imperfect bodies <note>Base metals like lead or tin.</note> or even mercury upon which it is projected in the manner described above, it will convert into the truest silver, better than that produced from a mine.

### On the dignities and operations of the Philosophers' Stone, Chapter 11

**T**hus all experienced philosophers assert and affirm as truth: that when the aforementioned stone is brought to its ultimate perfection described before, it makes glass and renders it malleable <note>A legendary material in alchemy; glass that can be hammered like metal without breaking.</note> if the said stone is projected upon it while melted.

<margin>Malleable glass</margin>

And it also dyes crystal in a similar way when melted, and converts it into a true carbuncle <note>A deep red gemstone, often associated with rubies or garnets.</note>.

<margin>Method of making a carbuncle.</margin>

**N**ow, however, it remains to see briefly and summarily the final and more worthy part of our treatise: namely, concerning a certain most noble efficacy and virtue of our stone. And since man is the most worthy of creatures, for whose sake all things were discovered and to whom they are subject, it can therefore be said that the aforementioned elixir was discovered for his service.

**F**or we see many medicines prepared from many vegetables, and even from animals and other mineral species through various means, with which we see sick human bodies recover and be cured; we see mineral gold and many precious stones ground and rubbed, and placed in electuaries <note>A medicinal paste made with honey or syrup.</note> for nobles and the wealthy, through which it is known that health is restored to them and they are freed from various illnesses. How much better and more perfectly, then, and more healthfully through this most virtuous

->On the generation of metals from quicksilver, Chapter 12<-

It was stated above at the beginning how quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum" (living silver); mercury</note> is generated. Now, indeed, it must be told how it is converted into metal through the very long decoction <note>a process of slow heating or "cooking" within the earth</note> of nature. But because this decoction is not clearly visible to men, there are various opinions of the philosophers concerning this. Some indeed assert that from quicksilver alone—namely, with its own innate sulfurous earth—it is congealed and hardened through the long decoction of nature in the bowels of the earth and becomes metal. Others, however, assert differently: that this quicksilver, besides its aforementioned innate sulfurous earth, encounters another sulfur which it meets while flowing in the bowels of the earth; by the vapor of this sulfur, it is congealed and hardened, and thus through the decoction of nature, it is turned into metal. But however it happens, it is clearly established that quicksilver is the sperm and the matter of metals, and that it is congealed and hardened into metal by tempered heat according to the decoction of nature in the bowels of the earth, by the power of its innate sulfur, or another sulfur it meets, or by a mixture of both.
And because it happens sometimes that two pure parts of quicksilver are mixed together, and sometimes indeed impure parts, we therefore see different metals formed and generated according to the different accidents occurring from above—namely, pure or impure metals. This happens because of the purity or impurity of the two aforementioned things: namely, sulfur and quicksilver. How these metals are generated, whether pure or impure, now follows:

### On the generation and nature of gold, chapter 3

<margin>

folio 53
</margin>

Gold is indeed generated and created from pure, clear quicksilver <note>original: "argento vivo"; mercury</note> and from clean, red, fixed, and clear sulfur. And because it was cooked <note>original: "decoctum"; a process of maturation in the earth's "womb"</note> for a great length of time in the bowels of the earth, its parts were so thoroughly mixed that it became solid, heavy, fixed, and perfect. It has no defect. For this reason, it does not rot under the earth, nor is it changed by water, nor consumed in the air. Neither is burnt gold consumed or diminished in fire. In its "height" <note>the outward or manifest qualities</note> it is ethereal, sanguine, hot and moist, saffron-colored, sweet, fragrant, and masculine. In its "depth" <note>the hidden or internal qualities</note> it is lead or earthy silver, foul-smelling, black, sour, cold, and dry. On one side it is tin or watery quicksilver, phlegmatic, cold and moist, black, tasteless, weak, and feminine. On the other side it is iron or a fiery whetstone, colored, hot, dry, red, bitter, sharp, and masculine; and it is the body that connects all things to one another.

Seeing these things, the philosophers of gems <note>alchemists</note> realized that one thing can be transformed into another. They have proven this by experience. Therefore, they affirm their estimation. For example: silver shall be converted into gold, and vice versa, and so with the rest according to their generation and corruption.

### On the generation and nature of silver, chapter 4

Silver is also generated from clear quicksilver and from white, pure, clear, and almost fixed sulfur. It lacks only a little fixation to reach the ultimate perfection of nature; its color

### On the generation and nature of Copper, chapter 5

Copper is likewise generated from turbid quicksilver and turbid red sulfur, through long cooking and strong heat. Because it was much burnt in the cooking, it is therefore imperfect. In its height it is fiery iron, colored, hot, dry, red, bitter, sharp, and masculine. In its depth it is tin or watery silver, phlegmatic, dry and moist, white, tasteless, weak, and feminine. On one side it is airy, sanguine gold, hot and moist, saffron-colored, sweet, fragrant, and masculine. On the other side it is lead or earthy silver, melancholic, cold, dry, black, sour, foul-smelling, and feminine.

### On the creation and nature of tin, chapter 17

**T**in is also made from clear quicksilver <note>original: "argento vivo," literally living silver</note> mixed with clear white sulfur: but it is cooked for a short time with modest heat. Therefore, if it were cooked for a long time, it would be turned into pure silver. ¶ And in its height <note>its outward appearance</note> it is watery quicksilver, phlegmatic, cold and moist, white, tasteless, weak, and feminine. ¶ And in its depths it is a fungus <note>likely a metaphor for a growth or porous state</note> or is fiery, choleric, hot, dry, red, bitter, sharp, and masculine. ¶ And on one side it is lead or earthy silver, melancholic, cold, dry, black, sour, stinking, and feminine. ¶ And on the other side it is airy gold, sanguine, hot and moist, saffron-colored and fragrant, masculine. ¶ It is therefore easy to convert it into silver or gold: because it is easier to reach the sides of these bodies than their depths.

### On the creation and nature of lead, chapter 18

**L**ead is also generated from thick, corrosive, and foul quicksilver: and from thick white sulfur, partly pure and red: and it lacks fixation <note>the ability to withstand fire without evaporating</note> and ignition: because it is also cooked too little.

<column-break/>

¶ And in its height it is black silver, melancholic, cold, dry, sour, stinking, and feminine. ¶ And in its depths it is gold, sanguine, hot and moist, saffron-colored, sweet, and fragrant. ¶ And on one side it is tin and watery quicksilver, phlegmatic, cold, moist, white, tasteless, weak, and feminine. ¶ And on that side it is iron or is fiery, choleric, red, bitter, sharp, and masculine. ¶ It will therefore convert more easily into silver than into any other body.

### On the nature and creation of quicksilver, chapter 19

**Q**uicksilver <term>Argentum vivum: Mercury</term> is created from white sulfurous earth and from clear, viscous water. And in its height it is watery tin, phlegmatic, white, moist and cold, tasteless, weak, and feminine. ¶ And in its depths it is airy gold, hot and moist, saffron-colored, sweet, fragrant, and masculine. ¶ And on one side it is iron or is fiery, choleric, hot, dry, red, bitter, sharp, and masculine. ¶ And on the other side it is lead or earthy silver, masculine <note>likely a scribe's error for feminine, given the context of lead</note>, cold, dry, black, sour, stinking, and feminine. ¶ And let these words suffice concerning the creation of metals and their nature: and let those things which have been said concerning the nature and composition or fixation of the philosopher's stone be observed.

¶ The golden ring itself, covered with silver, is the philosophers' stone <term>Philosophers' Stone: the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting eternal life</term>, which in its depth is golden and masculine, and in its manifest appearance is silvery and feminine. And these parts, though distinct, are always joined. But the seven chains encircling the book are the seven operations <note>likely referring to the seven stages of alchemy: calcination, dissolution, separation, conjunction, fermentation, distillation, and coagulation</note> which bound, perfect, and involve the entire mastery of the stone.

subtly entering the body itself and reducing it to its simplest minimal parts, draws from it the *azam* <term>Azam: likely a corruption of "Azoth," the universal solvent or mercury of the philosophers</term>; it draws it upward into the air and, elevating it, carries it with itself. ¶ And afterward, it infuses the "Soul" into the body thus prepared—reducing it to the nature of the Fifth Essence <term>Quinta Essentia: the purest, celestial element beyond the four earthly ones</term>, which is a simple thing. The body, embracing the soul, rejoices in it; and the soul, entering with the body, perfects it, just as a living thing perfects the dead. They are never separated from one another, because the dead body, when it rises again, shall live forever. ¶ And this is the stone of philosophy, perceiving its own sweet soul.

## Here begins the Book of the Mountain

<margin>Note: this treatise is addressed to Rolesu(?) <unclear>...</unclear> to the Duke of Burgundy</margin>

Blessed be the name of the Lord who gives wisdom to all who fear Him, and does not reproach them. For He Himself is the height and depth of all sciences, and the treasury of all wisdom; wherefore I shall direct my mind toward the hidden and precious secret pearls to investigate certain things of nature. Therefore, in the very beginning of this [work], I invoke the help of Him who is the fountain and origin of all honors: so that He, by His pious love and goodness, might deign to fill the smallness of my <unclear>most ample</unclear> knowledge and, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, elucidate those things which lie hidden in the earthly vessel: so that the secrets and hidden things of nature may be usefully found, and once found, I may be able to manifest them, through Him who lives in the holy of holies.

Philip, son of the illustrious John, born King of France, Duke and Count of Burgundy, Count of Flanders, etc., desiring and affecting to become a disciple of the philosophers and their secretary: so that you might persist with eyes fixed upon the inheritance in possession of a certain famous, illustrious, and glorious philosophical part; but for the prudent...

...a better approach to the principles of the art, even if ignorance should fall upon his intention. However, very little is actually taken away from him regarding the completion of the work, without which his material cannot be perfected. For Art, in all its works, is not able to follow Nature exactly, but rather imitates her as best it can. Therefore, my son, we shall reveal the secret to you: for in this, craftsmen err, because they desire to imitate Nature in every single difference of her properties. For this reason, labor to study uniquely in these small, captivating volumes, and revolve them very often in your mind, so that you may acquire the true intention from my writings. For in them, you will find the foundations upon which you can and should base your mind, and you will know how to expel errors from yourself, and in what ways you can imitate Nature in the craftsmanship of your work.

Take care, therefore, son, lest this precious secret <note>original: "archanum"</note> should come into the hands of the foolish, such as are the modern Alchemists <note>original: "Alkimiste"; the author distinguishes between true philosophers and "puffers" or greedy pretenders</note> in great multitude, who wish to have the fruits so that they may be more ready to perform profane deeds. They do not seek to know the natures, properties, and differences of the roots, flowers, wood, and leaves of the most excellent tree of philosophy <note>A common alchemical metaphor for the growth and stages of the Great Work</note>. Furthermore, without the study of labor, and with all reason cast aside, they are obstinate in their continuous errors. They carry out operations that are entirely vain, destroyed by the demon of error, and improperly obtained; these lead them into wretchedness and perpetual misery. They do not base their intention under the enigmas

<column-break/>

or figures of the philosophers, but rather under the plain, clear, and manifest series of their words. To those prudent ones laboring in skillful study, the philosophers clearly open this sublime science. To the mediocre, it is shown most profoundly <note>meaning it remains hidden or difficult to grasp</note>, but the foolish and miserable men they exclude entirely. This is so that the wicked man might not usurp such a sublime art as if he were upright, always fostering it, in a way, amidst his sins and evil deeds.

And then, after they have lost their possessions—not attending, as we said, to the warnings of the philosophers which they wrote openly in their books—they say the philosophers have seduced them, and they heap blasphemies upon them in many ways. This they ought to impute to themselves, and to their own ignorance and presumption.

This book is divided into three parts:
In the first part, the investigation of the stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the alchemical quest</note> is treated.
In the second, it speaks partly of theory and partly of practice.
In the third, it sets forth the practice with a certain small and true recapitulation of the entire work.

**Seeing** therefore the hermit shining with excessive brightness, and perceiving the affection and desire of my heart, he wished to satisfy it. First, he desired to reveal his true name, which is **Hope**. I said to him: "Why are you called so?" And he said: "Because hope directs one toward the highest good by looking forward and imitating it."

**Whence Hugh** <note>original: "Vnde hugo"; referring to Hugh of Saint Victor, a 12th-century theologian.</note>
> Hope is the confidence of future goods arising from the grace of God and a good conscience.

**Whence Augustine** <note>original: "Vnde Augustinus"; referring to St. Augustine of Hippo.</note>
> Hope is the certain expectation of future blessedness, coming from the grace of God and preceding merits. Without merits, however, it is not hope, but can be called presumption. And without hope, no one shall come to the desired end, but will rather despair.

**He** spoke again: "And because you have come to us, who are the beginning of the entire secret, we shall sufficiently declare to you the whole intention of the first treatise, which is the key to the entire art."

**Know** therefore that the aforementioned ring, which is golden on top and covered in silver, is the <term>Philosopher's Stone</term> <note>original: "lapis philosophorum"; the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold.</note>, which in its depth is golden and masculine, and in its outward appearance is silver and feminine.

**Know** also that in the said stone there are gold and silver in virtue and power, and also in nature; for if these were not in it, neither gold nor silver could be made from it. And yet they are not common gold or silver, since the gold and silver existing in the stone itself are better than they are in common nature, because the gold and silver of the said stone

<column-break/>

are living, while others—the common ones—are dead in comparison to the gold and silver existing in the said stone. Although the philosophers have named the stone itself "gold and silver," they did so because these are in it potentially, but not visibly. And thus you have it that this composite, or simple substance, is only one thing and of a single nature. In it is everything that is necessary for it, which improves it and completes it.

**Therefore** it is called by the philosophers "every thing," since it has in itself every thing necessary for its perfection. And this is not a composite made of animals or vegetables, but is born pure and clear from its own minerals, which are transmuted through the governance of fire, and it rots, turns black, becomes white, and turns red, and arrives at many other colors.

<margin>
Note that no foreign thing is added to it; <unclear>nothing</unclear> generates its fruit [except] the Lion by similarity.
</margin>
**It is evident** that no foreign thing is added to it, because nothing suits a thing which is not proper to it by its own nature. All things bring forth only what is like themselves, nor do they bear fruit except their own fruits.

**A human** indeed begets a human, a Lion a Lion. Just as each thing generates its own likeness. A mule, however, is not made from nor generates a likeness to its parents. So it is also with two things procreated from different kinds.

**Above** it was shown what the ring signifies; now we must speak of the writing on the circumference itself. And first, concerning the spirit. For this entire writing is marvelous, because it contains within it whatever belongs to the secret of philosophy in a brief compendium.

**For "Spirit"** denotes that which, subtly entering the body itself to the end—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of alchemical principles, specifically the relationship between the spirit, soul, and body in the creation of the Philosopher's Stone.</meta>

...arranging the parts through the smallest particles, it draws the **soul** <note>original: "aia" (anima)</note> from it: and elevating the **spirit** <note>original: "spm" (spiritum)</note> upward toward the ether, it carries it along. And afterward, when the **body** <note>original: "corpori"</note> has been prepared according to the nature of the **Fifth Essence** <term>Quintessence: the purest, fifth element beyond earth, air, fire, and water</term>—which is reduced to a certain simplicity—it pours in the soul, and the body, embracing it, rejoices in it. And when the soul enters the body, it perfects the spirit, just as wine perfects the dead: when it rises again, it lives forever. And this is the **Philosopher's Stone**.

Likewise, whatever the philosophers may say about the **ferment** <term>a substance used to "leaven" or transform base metals into gold</term>, you should know that in the truth of the matter, the Stone itself—according to its whole, and according to the spirit, and according to the soul, and according to the body—is always the same in reality.

And therefore the philosophers say: Divide the stone into two parts, namely into **water** and **earth**. Do this again: and extract the father through the spirit, which is the spreader of the soul's power, and the soul itself, which is hidden in the body.

<margin>Concerning the Soul</margin>
Having shown the spirit, we must speak of the **soul**: Therefore, the soul is that **non-burning sulfur** which congeals **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> into gold or silver, which it draws from the body. And this is the soul: which is the **mediator** between the body and the spirit, and it binds and joins them in an inseparable union. Since the spirit cannot be united with the body except through the soul. This is the golden tincture of the philosophers, for without its power nothing can be perfected or completed. Therefore, regarding these metals, our sulfur is not the common sulfur, which is fatty and combustible; for that would destroy and corrupt everything from above.

Likewise, know that sulfur is the **form**, and quicksilver is the **matter**.

<column-break/>

It is necessary, however, that the same sulfur and the same quicksilver which are subject to the work of nature should also be subject to the place of **art** <note>In alchemy, "Art" refers to the human skill used to accelerate or perfect natural processes</note> and not another; for it should appear similar according to its kind and appearance. Unless these subjects were available to my operations, the art would be entirely impossible. Nevertheless, the method of acting, directing, and forming in art is different from the natural one: and likewise the instrument, or the place and time, because of which nature generates gold from that matter; if however the form of gold is generated, it is by drawing it out from that matter. With which form every metal, since it is matter for it, is changed through smelting into the purest <unclear>vospofuu</unclear>, namely gold.

->Concerning the body<-

Having determined above concerning the soul, which is the medium between the body and the spirit: now we must see what the **body** is.

The body, moreover, denotes the gold itself or the inanimate silver, in which the soul used to rule and remain, just as a form remains in its subject. And this, after the separation of the soul, is called the **dead body**: until, through the introduction of the soul, it is liquefied: and then it is called the **living, immortal, resurrected body**.

It is clear, therefore, through the aforesaid, that our "He" <note>referring to the Stone or the Alchemical Man</note> has, like a human being, a spirit, a soul, and a body. <margin>Spirit, Soul, Body</margin> For its **spirit** is its water. Its **soul** is its tincture. Its **body** is its earth.

The spirit, however, is the carrier of the soul's virtues unto the body. Just as a dye is carried to the middle of a cloth through water.

And the soul is the element of the spirit, just as the body is the vehicle of the soul.

Know that this writing is said to be the first key: the resolution of the stone which is called "phora" <note>likely a corruption of the Greek 'phthora' meaning destruction or decay</note>, putrefaction, or digestion, which occurs over its own proper time in a very tempered fire. For just as food cannot be converted into nourishment except through its own digestion, so neither can the stone be converted into a simple substance, nor can the soul be drawn from the body by the spirit, except by means of its digestion. And this is the key of philosophy. For the closer a thing is brought to a simple state, the more perfect it is. For the moisture or humidity, when it exits the stone, turns the entire composition black; and by continuing the fire, that very blackness within it—which is the moisture—turns into various colors, and finally into whiteness, which humidity is called Air. Let it therefore be hardened in its own earth and with the other elements existing in the stone itself, until they become one thing which is white. Because the aforesaid humidity, which is quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note>, causes it to turn black during the corruption of the stone.

That it is necessary first to turn black is proven by this: that the generation of one thing is the corruption of another. And the corruption of putrefaction does not occur except through heat acting upon moisture. 
And heat acting upon moisture produces blackness. Wherefore it is clear that the beginning of the stone is the "crow's head" <note>original: "caput corvi"; a traditional alchemical term for the black stage or nigredo</note>.
Likewise, it is necessary for it to be putrefied, because nothing was ever animated, nor growing, nor ensouled, except after putrefaction. If indeed it were not putrefied, it could not be melted, nor would it be dissolved. If it were not dissolved, it would be reduced to nothing.

<column-break/>

My putrefaction, therefore, is not filthy or unclean; rather, it is the mixing of earth into water and water into earth, part by part, until the whole becomes one body.
Continue, therefore, a tempered fire upon it until it dissolves into an impalpable water, and the entire tincture emerges in the color of blackness, which is the sign of solution. For heat acting in moisture first generates blackness; in yellow it works whiteness; and in white, citrinity <note>a pale yellow or lemon color</note>. Just as is seen in lead when they make it into minium <note>red lead or cinnabar-colored pigment</note>.
And know that in solution the fire shall always be light; in sublimation, moderate; in the coagulation of the spirit, continuous; and in the reddening <note>rubification</note>, strong. Therefore, beware of a great fire, lest you burn the solution before the necessary time. For intense heat destroys the compound, and cold puts it to flight, but gentle heat nourishes and preserves it.

The first chain being loosened, and desiring to loosen the second, I ascend by the rib of the mountain and find the second gate, which was guarded by a beautiful maiden called Prudence. I asked her why she was called by that name. She replied: "Because Prudence, as Augustine says, consists in guarding against snares." 
Tullius <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> says: "Prudence is the discernment of good and evil things." 
Seneca says: "The prudent man does not wish to deceive, nor can he be deceived." 
It is the mark of the prudent to examine the spirit's counsel, lest by easy credulity one slips into falsehoods.
"And because you have come to me, I shall loosen [the chain]..."

Join together, therefore, the two operative virtues: namely, **water** and **fire**, and the **Mastery** <note>magisterium: the successful completion of the alchemical process</note> will be fulfilled. The red, however, is rotated on four wheels; that which is the completed **elixir** is carried along, and the firm **tincture** <note>a concentrated essence or colorant</note> is submerged in its own oil and fixed by its own lime <note>calce: a powdered residue</note>. And then the body is the cause of retaining the water, and the water the oil (which is not burned over the fire), and the oil is the cause of retaining the tincture, and the tincture is the cause of making the color appear. And the color is the cause of demonstrating the whiteness. And the whiteness is the cause of retaining every **volatile** <note>substances that easily evaporate</note> from flight. For the body which has been whitened does not permit the spirit to flee, nor allows it to appear further.

And therefore, he who does not liquefy and cleanse errs in many ways. For he who blackens the earth in a white fire dissolves and coagulates it, until it is in color like a sword stripped of darkness. And he who, once the whitening is complete, brings the soul into it, and then after it has liquefied...

<meta>This page continues the alchemical discourse on the dissolution of bodies and introduces the famous Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus. The handwriting is a late 15th-century Gothic book hand.</meta>

<margin>
Dissolve [...]

You should know that the dissolution of bodies <note>In alchemy, "bodies" usually refers to metals like gold or silver</note> aids their sublimation. The reason is that then the earthly body is sublimated into the air, that is, into heaven. Wherefore you should know that when we dissolve, at the same time—without any interval of time or space—we sublimate, calcify, cleanse, dissolve, wash, join, compose, and separate.

Hence Haly <note>Likely referring to the Arabic alchemist Khalid ibn Yazid or Haly Abenragel</note> says in his *Secret of Secrets* that between the dissolution and the composition—or the marriage and conjunction of bodies—no space of time intervenes. The reason is because when the body is dissolved, in the very act of dissolving it is joined with the spirit. And therefore he says that dissolution is not [merely] conjunction. 

Wherefore this is the order of my operation: which happens all at once in a single hour. For when our body is placed for dissolving, it is then immediately blackened, and immediately separated into its smallest parts, and immediately calcified; and then immediately it is dissolved and sublimated, and by sublimating and dissolving it is joined with the spirit.

And if there should be anything foreign mixed into the body, that part is not dissolved, but remains at the bottom of the vessel used for dissolving. And thus it is cleansed of the foreign matter, if any was in it. However, one must not wait to purge it until it is dissolved. Nevertheless, dissolution effects it in a certain way; yet it is not held as clear as is fitting.

### The Testament of Hermes
### on the composition of the Stone
### of the philosophers

**T**he philosopher said: It is true, without falsehood, certain and most true. That which is above is like that which is below. And that which is below is like that which is above. To perform the wonders of the one thing. Just as all things were from one by the meditation of the one; and just as all things were born from one thing by a single adaptation. Its father is the Sun; its mother is the Moon; the wind carried it in its belly. Its nurse is the Earth. 

He is the father of every <term>talisman</term> <note>original: "telesmi", referring to the completion or perfection of the work</note> of the whole world. Here its power is complete in the earth 
<margin>subtle / dense</margin> 
if it be turned into earth <gloss>gently</gloss>. You shall separate the earth from the fire, the subtle from the dense, gently and with great ingenuity. It ascends from the earth into heaven and again descends into the earth, and it shall receive the power of the superiors and the inferiors. And so you shall have the glory of the clarity of the whole world. Therefore all obscurity shall flee from you. This is the strength of all strength, because it overcomes every subtle thing and shall penetrate every solid thing. 

Just as the world was created, from this shall be wonderful adaptations, the manner of which is here. Therefore I am called Hermes, having three parts of the <term>wisdom</term> <note>original: "sapie"</note> or <term>philosophy</term> <note>original: "phie"</note> of the whole world. That which we have said concerning the operation of the Sun is completed.

# The Commentary of Ortulanus on the Testament of Hermes regarding the Investigation of the Philosophers' Stone

**True**—that is, it is true that a portion of this work is given without falsehood; he says this to distinguish it from those who say the art is a lie. **Certain**—that is, proven, because what has been experienced is certain. **Most true**—that is, that the Sun <note>original: "Sole"; here referring to alchemical Gold</note> procreates most truly. He uses the superlative degree, "most true," because the generated Sun exceeds the natural sun in its modes and properties, both medicinal and otherwise. Consequently, he touches upon the operation of the Stone, saying: **That which is above is like that which is below.** Here he says that the Stone is divided into two <margin>The Stone, the element of the Sun and Moon, is reduced to that which is in its <unclear>substance</unclear> through the fission and solution of fire, where the spirit and soul remain fixed in the bottom of the vessel, as is seen better in harmony through the spirit by virtue.</margin> principal parts through the mastery <term>magisterium: the technical process of alchemical perfection</term>: into a superior part which ascends upward, and into an inferior part which remains fixed and clear. And indeed these two parts agree together in virtue. And therefore he says: **that which is above is like that which is below,** and vice versa. And know for certain that this division is <margin>The earth indeed <unclear>nourishes</unclear> the <unclear>substance</unclear> <unclear>with which</unclear> blood, in the <unclear>manner</unclear> of an animal, <insert>namely</insert> through a soul of this kind; the <unclear>hidden</unclear> soul of the earth <unclear>and</unclear> from the earth is <unclear>nourished</unclear>.</margin> necessary to perform the miracles of the one thing—namely, the Stone—because the inferior part is the earth, which is called the Nurse, and the superior part is the soul, which vivifies the whole Stone and rises up; whence, once the separation is made and the conjunction of the Stone is celebrated, many miracles are performed.

<column-break/>

**Just as all things were from one by the meditation of one.** Here he gives an example, saying: **Just as all things were from one**—namely, from one confused globe or confused mass—by the meditation, that is, the creation, of one: namely, Almighty God. And just as all things were born, things issued forth from one confused mass **by one adaptation**—that is, by the sole command of God and by miracle. Similarly, our Stone is born and issues from one confused mass containing within itself all the elements which were created by God; and by His miracle alone, our Stone is <unclear>born from there</unclear>. <note>A small ink sketch of a human profile facing left appears in the margin adjacent to this paragraph.</note> And just as we see nature generate from one animal many others similar to itself, so artificially the Sun generates the Sun with multiplication in the virtue of the aforesaid Stone.

**The second part follows:**

**Its father is the Sun.** That is, gold. But because in every natural generation there must be a suitable receptacle for the seed, harmonizing with it <margin>father</margin> with a certain consonance and <unclear>likeness</unclear> to the gold itself—and that is silver. Therefore it follows:

**Its mother is the Moon.** That is, silver. <margin>mother</margin>

And it must be noted most diligently that <margin>that is, if you wish to <unclear>choose</unclear> toward the white, the matter becomes where the Moon is; toward the red, gold, just as the sun of the sun toward the red gold becomes the matter of the <unclear>firmament</unclear></margin> the conjunction of these two bodies is necessary in this art—namely, for the "white" and for the "red" <note>The white and red stages of the alchemical Great Work</note>. And there are two reasons: one of which is that gold, although it is the noblest among metals and more complete, perfect, and fixed, nevertheless, if it is dissolved so that its smallest parts are separated, it will be spiritual and will fly away from the fire like Mercury <note>original: "Mercurius"; Quicksilver</note>, which is a marvel; and this by reason of [...]

It identifies the "Sun" as gold and the "Moon" as silver, emphasizing their necessary conjunction for the alchemical Great Work.</summary>
