Likewise, there is another reason why the joining of these two bodies is necessary: because while gold by itself and silver by itself are most difficult to dissolve, yet if they are joined together, they flow and melt easily. Goldsmiths know this when making solders for gold. Hence, if in my Stone there were only one of these two, the medicine would never flow easily through any mastery of the art, nor would it give a tincture, nor would it tinge except as much as it is itself, because it would not be a receptacle for the tincture. And then the final secret is to have a medicine that flows before the flight of quicksilver <note>original: "mercurij viui" - liquid mercury, which evaporates or "flies" when heated.</note>. Therefore, the joining of these two is necessary. Because when the two have received each other in the joining of the Stone, the Stone is impregnated in the belly of the wind. And this is what the Philosopher <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus.</note> said: **The wind carried it in its belly.** It is clear that the wind is air, and air is life, and life is the soul. And I have spoken of the soul which vivifies the whole Stone. And so it must be: that the wind carries it and brings it back, and opens it through the mastery of the art. And then it follows that it receives nourishment from its nurse, namely the earth. And therefore he says: **Its nurse**

**is the earth.** Because just as a fetus nourished without food never reaches maturity, so our Stone without the fermentation of its earth will never reach its effect. This fermentation is called nourishment. For just as one is generated from a father with the joining of a mother and the nourishment of the mother, so the "sons" are similar; those who have lacked long devotion will be like the mother in whiteness, and will reflect the weight of the father.

### It follows: The father of all perfection of the whole world.
<margin>
Perfection <note>original: "Telesis" - from the Greek 'telesmos', meaning completion or ritual perfection.</note>
</margin>
That is to say: although there are many operations of the Stone, there is one final and master operation. The Philosopher calls it the father of all perfection <term>telesmus: a Latinized Greek term for the completion or "consecration" of the Great Work</term>, and of all preciousness, and of all the treasure of the whole world; and it is in every living stone in this world. This is as if he were to say, "Behold, I lead you to its possession." **Its force is entire if it be turned into earth.** "Its force"—namely, that of the Stone—is entire, that is, perfect and complete, "if it be turned into earth." That is, if the soul of the Stone itself (of which we made mention above, because the soul is called the wind and the oil in which the entire force of the Stone resides) has been turned into earth and is fixed in the stone, so that the whole substance of the Stone is nourished or fermented by the matrix, namely the earth. Thus the whole Stone is converted into ferment; just as in the making of bread, a little ferment <note>leaven or yeast</note> nourishes and ferments a large or very great quantity of bread, and likewise the whole substance of the dough is converted into ferment. <margin>When the dough is brought to our earth... multiplied...</margin> In this way, the Philosopher wishes that our Stone be fermented for the multiplication of the Stone, just like leaven. Consequently, he sets forth how it ought to be multiplied; but first he sets forth the cleansing of the Stone and the separation of its parts.

<margin>

Of the Earth

saying: **"You shall separate the earth from the fire: the subtle from the gross: gently with great ingenuity."** <note>This is a core precept of the Emerald Tablet, attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</note> That is to say, gently and little by little: not through violence, but with great ingenuity; for this is done by the slowest fire of the philosophical furnace. "You shall separate," that is, you shall dissolve. Because dissolution is the separation of parts: the earth from the fire. "The subtle from the gross": that is, the dregs and impurities. "The gross": that is, the air and water from the whole substance of the stone: so that the stone remains there most pure, without filth. Once prepared in this way, the stone is suitable for multiplication. <note>Multiplication is the alchemical process of increasing the quantity or potency of the transmuting agent.</note> And thus he posits multiplication and its easy liquefaction through its power of penetration, both in hard bodies and in soft ones, saying thus: **"It ascends from the earth to the heaven: and again it descends to the earth."** This is very much to be noted. Because when our stone is divided in the first operation into four parts—which are the four elements—as was said above: and these are the principal parts. Namely, one which ascends above, which is called "not fixed" <note>Volatile</note>. The other is that which remains below, fixed: which is called the "ferment" or the "earth" which nourishes and ferments the whole stone, as has been said. From that part which is not fixed, it is necessary to have a good quantity and give it to the stone, which has been made most pure without filth, to absorb it so many times through the mastery <note>The "Magisterium" or Great Work</note>: until it carries the whole stone upward by the power of its non-fixed nature through sublimation. And this is what he means by "it ascends from the earth to heaven" after the stone itself has been thus exalted.

<column-break/>

It is necessary that it be macerated upon marble with the element extracted from the stone itself in the first operation: that is, with the "water of the stone": and to roast it so many times by subliming: until, by the power of the fermentation of the earth exalted with the bodies, the whole stone again descends into the earth and remains fixed and flowing. And this is what he means: "it descends again into the earth." And thus it receives the superior force by ascending and the inferior force by descending. That is: that which is corporeal is made spiritual by ascending. And that which is spiritual is made corporeal by descending. **"And so you have the glory of the clarity of the whole world."** That is, he says that with this stone thus composed, you shall possess the glory of this world. **"Therefore all obscurity shall flee from you."** That is, all poverty and sickness: because the stone thus composed is curative of every sickness. **"This is the strong fortitude of all fortitude, because it will overcome every subtle thing: and penetrate every solid thing."** That is, it overcomes even by overcoming and changing quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> into its own likeness, and it will penetrate other hard and solid bodies. **It follows:** **"Just as the world was created."** So was this stone made. Because at first the whole world and whatever is in the world was in one confused mass, as was said above: afterwards, by the craftsmanship of the Supreme Creator, that mass was divided into the four elements, wonderfully rectified and separated: through which separation...

From this, there will be wonderful adaptations. That is, if you separate the elements, they are wonderful things composed for my work in the composition of my stone: rectifying them through the joining of the elements.

The method for these wonders is adapted to this purpose—here, the first method of operating is given. Here, he is certainly called **Hermes** <note>Refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> because the master philosopher gave the composition of the stone. First, he notes himself, so that his sons <note>A traditional term for students or initiates of alchemy.</note> arriving at this science may remember his name. Concerning these, whether joined or divided, the philosopher had true knowledge in the operation of the **Sun** <note>original: "Solis"; in alchemy, this often refers to Gold or the masculine principle.</note>. And these parts are contained in a single stone, according to **Mercury** <note>original: "mercurio"</note>. And therefore this stone is called "perfect," because it has the nature of minerals, vegetables, and

animals. For it is a pure and single stone, having four colors, namely the elements: which, unless it has died in hope, remains alone. And if it has died in the ways mentioned above, being now joined, it brings forth much fruit; namely, when the aforementioned operations are completed.

O dearest reader: know that regarding the operation of the stone, I have told you the truth. And if you have found the said operation, there is nothing more for you to complete, but that which has been said is finished: concerning the operation of the stone of three natures and four colors, existing as was said in a single thing, according to the operation of the Sun alone.

Therefore, let it be a **vegetable stone** for me who speaks: because from the juices of three herbs joined together by sailors <note>The Latin "nautis" (sailors) may be a scribal error or a specific technical metaphor.</note>, which were noted below, after they had stood in dung for 40 days, I saw a worm emerge. In finding its [nature], there was no difference from the other. Therefore, the stone is from vegetables.

from quicksilver <note>original: "mercurio vivo"</note>: it grows to the size of a toad, the form of which is terrifying. And this is an animal substance. By itself, it is an elixir <term>elixir: a medicinal or transformative substance</term> acting upon lead. Therefore, it is an "animal stone." That it is also a mineral is evident because a projection <term>projection: the act of casting a small amount of the Stone onto base metal to transform it</term> is made upon it, and it converts into metal. No one, therefore, doubts that this Mercury is the Stone itself: which kills itself, rises again, and gives life; and it converts itself into gold.

And because of this, Alphidius <note>original: "aluiphs," likely referring to the 10th-century Arabic alchemist Alphidius</note> says: One stone, one medicine: to which nothing foreign is added, so that it must be converted into gold or silver.

Afterward, there are two helpers through whom the work is easily fulfilled. One is a destroyer, who kills the entire operation unless it is removed.

<margin><unclear>Beware, for whoever has gold [...] of reduced oil [...] is his</unclear></margin>

The helpers, however, are those which are prepared. One is a white sulfur of reduced oil. Its property is to congeal Mercury and to complete the repetition. As Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in alchemy</note> testifies: by using it, it congeals Mercury; take it up, and it gives life to itself. The property of Mercury, however, is to thicken the whole Stone and to give it life, if it is prepared in the proper manner. It is also called "good air" and "incombustible oil." Therefore, he who neglects the oil from Mercury should take prepared Mercury in its place. And the destroyer of the Stone is sal ammoniac <term>sal armoniacum: ammonium chloride, used as a flux</term> which is found for sale. But where the philosopher speaks of sal ammoniac joining the marriage between the body and the spirit, he is speaking of the oil

<column-break/>

extracted from Mercury, as has been said. There are also many other collateral things very suitable in the preparation <note>original: "brayatione," likely a variant of preparation or grinding</note> of the work, such as salts, vitriols <note>original: "atrementa"</note>, and alums; and certain other things, both of alum and also of vegetables. For certain waters are made from these which immediately dissolve bodies such as gold and silver; and then, after this, the water of gold and silver is mixed with the Stone (which was first well-purified from everything foreign), and then it strengthens the work in one day, which in another way would be done in three months.

Likewise, a water is made from animals which immediately makes an oil out of sublimated Mercury.

Likewise, a water is made from vegetables which immediately takes away the burning and scorching of Mercury, and it will remain white and incombustible. And so there are so many wonderful things created that are suitable for the composition of my Stone. Thus, there are many things here tending toward one end. And let these things suffice regarding the composing of the Philosopher's Stone.

May the name of the Lord be blessed forever and ever. Amen.

<meta>This page marks the beginning of the "Book of Morienus," a foundational text in the history of alchemy. It establishes the lineage of the legendary Hermes Trismegistus and introduces the translator, Robert of Chester (Castrensis), who is credited with the first translation of an alchemical work from Arabic into Latin in 1144.</meta>

# Here begins the book which Morienus edited for Khalid, the King of the Egyptians, which Robert of Chester translated from Arabic into Latin.

Robert of Chester said: We read in the histories of the ancient divines that there were three philosophers, each of whom was called Hermes. The first of them was Enoch, who was called Hermes by another name, and by yet another name <unclear>azenaing</unclear> <note>likely a corruption of a Hebrew or Arabic name for Enoch</note>.
The second was Noah, who similarly was called Hermes by another name, and was named <unclear>meraurias</unclear> <note>likely a corruption of "Mercurius"</note> by another.
The third of them was the Hermes who reigned in Egypt after the Flood, and held his kingdom for a long time.
This man was called "the Triple" <note>original: "triplex," referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note> by my predecessors because of three virtues collectively attributed to him by the Lord God.
For he was a King, a Philosopher, and a Prophet.
This was the Hermes who, after the Flood, was the first inventor of all arts and disciplines, both the liberal and the mechanical.
For all who came after him strove to walk in his path and to follow in his footsteps. Why say more? It would be long and difficult to bring back to memory at present the virtues and teachings of such a great and mighty man, especially since we have not undertaken this task in the translation of this divine book, nor—

<column-break/>

<margin>Note on the first inventor of Alchemy</margin>
—is this that book. This is the book which is titled *On the Composition of Alchemy*. And since my Latin world <note>original: "latinitas," referring to the Latin-speaking scholarly community of Europe</note> has not yet known what alchemy is and what its composition is, I shall clarify this helpful term in the present discourse under a definition, lest anyone be ignorant of it. Hermes and the other philosophers who lived previously defined this term thus. For it is said in the book on the <unclear>iutatiuo</unclear> state: Alchemy is a corporeal substance composed from one and by one body, joining together more precious things by mixing and effect, and naturally converting them by that same natural mixing into a better kind.

<margin>
Against the Alexandrians first [...] [...] [...] [...] [...] [...]
</margin>
In the following parts, we shall explain what we have said, where its proposition will be fully treated. But although our intellect is <unclear>slender</unclear> and our Latinity modest, we have undertaken this so great and so large a work to translate from Arabic into Latin. Wherefore, for the singular grace conferred upon us by our modern God, we return thanks to that highest God, who exists as three and one.
However, I did not make my name clear at the beginning of the prologue, lest someone should take this labor of ours for himself, and even claim its praise and merit as if it were his own. Furthermore, I observe this omen for myself, lest anyone waste away with envy <note>original: "liuore," literally 'blueness' or 'bruising,' used here for spite</note> toward my name, which is often accustomed to happen by many.
May God be Almighty, to whom He may confer His grace, and with whom grace proceeds, and where and—

He inspires whomsoever he wills. Therefore, we ought to rejoice in our actions: because the creator and founder of all things—I speak as if of a specific part—shows his own divinity, so that it might not remain entirely hidden from us.

<margin>Hermes, the first inventor and constructor of the art of Alchemy <note>original: "Alchimie"</note></margin>
**M**orienus said of him: The divine mind of Hermes fully grasped all parts of philosophy. ¶ Moreover, when he had studied for many years in the discovery and publication of the higher mastery <note>The "Magisterium" or the completion of the Philosopher's Stone</note>, he was the first to find and publish this great secret. He composed a book about it, which he kept with him, and after his death, he left it as an inheritance to his disciples. After his death, he distributed it, and they studied in this book and all its precepts for a long time so that they might be able to achieve its effect.

¶ Therefore, after they attained their desire, they gave various and innumerable instructions concerning it. They did this so that those who came after them might not be deceived by a brotherly cause, as if they had revealed a common thing to the foolish. Truly, a long time after the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, there arose a certain man brought forth from a spiritual and divine house, who had studied in divinity for a long time; among the divine books, he found this book.

<margin>Adfar of Alexandria was the first among the Christians to learn the composition of the stones of the philosophers <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note> from the Book of Hermes</margin>
Now this man was a native of Alexandria, from which he took his name, Adfar of Alexandria. ¶ After he found the aforementioned book, he did not cease to study it with a watchful mind and great industry. After he had studied it for a long time, he fully attained its effect and knowledge.

¶ From this knowledge, therefore, this divine man gave many various and wonderful instructions. When these were promulgated under his name and became known in those parts of the region, at the time when I was staying in the city of Rome, the name and fame of this man reached me as if

<column-break/>

flying. For in his time, I was settled in Rome, where I was born; I was then a young man, whose first downy beard had not yet worthily covered his face. I had been made a prudent and learned Christian from the earliest stage of life by both parents, and to whom all Latinity <note>The Latin-speaking world or Latin learning</note> had already directed itself. ¶ Therefore, I heard the name and fame of this man, and I hastily abandoned my parents and my homeland at once; I set out on the journey I had conceived in my mind until I arrived at Alexandria. ¶ Having entered the city, I walked for a long time through the streets and lanes as a new guest, until I found the house of this man. ¶ At last, I found that one house and entered it. When I had entered, I found this man sitting in his oratory <note>A private room for prayer or study</note>, studying over his books. ¶ But after he fixed his eyes upon me, he said, "You have found me, friend; come here." ¶ I approached him and sat down near him upon a certain instrument <note>likely a stool or a piece of laboratory equipment</note> that had been placed there. ¶ He was a man already decrepit with great age, but still bearing a [strong] countenance, and graceful in health and stature of body. For his face revealed to those looking closely at him the things that lay hidden in his mind. After he was ready to talk with individuals, he asked by what name I was called, where I was born, and what cause had led me on my journey. ¶ And I answered him and said: "I am called Morienus, a Roman by nation, whom even the name and fame of you could not fail to draw away from parents and homeland."

¶ And he added: "And what is your faith? Are you a worshiper of the gods?"

¶ **The King.** O Morienus: now explain clearly the quality of this arrangement. For God will now be in the reasoning.

¶ **Morienus.** I shall tell it to you according to what has been handed down to me by the ancients. For you ask well. In the direction of this preparation, therefore, you should rationally establish the parts of the arrangement in their proper order, and omit them in no way.

¶ The first of these is **intercourse** <note>original: "coytus"</note>; the second is **conception**; the third is **pregnancy**. The fourth is **birth**. The fifth is **nourishment**. If, therefore, there is no intercourse, there will be no conception. And if there is no conception, there will be no pregnancy. And if there is no pregnancy, birth follows in no way.

¶ This is the direction of this arrangement: which is likened to the **creation of man**. For the Almighty, the Most High and Great Creator,

<column-break/>

whose name be forever blessed, created man not from pre-assembled parts—as is a house, which is known to be constructed from its various components.

¶ For there is no single thing that constitutes a man [in that way]; a house, however, consists of its established parts: such as the wall, the roof, and the foundation. These are the parts of a house, and the things are spoken of in relation to one another. But man does not consist in this way, because he is a creature. For man, from the moment his essence is changed, is seen to pass from one state to a better state. And thus man always persists in a creation which seems very different from things joined together.

¶ And so it proceeds from day to day and from month to month, until the Great and Most High Creator completes His creature in the perfected time and in the defined days. And because those things would first have been created according to their being in an unformed state, God placed a defined time in which He might complete what was already finished in the mind. Such is the strength and wisdom of the Most High God. It is also fitting for you to know, O good King, that this **Mastery** is nothing other than the **arcanum** <note>A profound secret or mystery.</note> and the **secret of secrets** of the Great and Most High God. For He Himself entrusted this secret Mastery to His prophets, whose souls He has placed in His paradise. If, however, the wise men who came after them had not discovered their expositions concerning the quality of the **vessel** in which it is prepared, they would never have reached the perfection of this Mastery, nor could they have reached it. Therefore, commit these things to your memory. I have shown above that this Mastery does not differ much from the creation of man. Now also...

### A confection of marvelous operation which restores and clears the sight; it comforts the stomach, purges a person of superfluous humors, cleanses the kidneys, breaks stones, expels wind, and is especially powerful for the restoration and clearing of the eyesight.

Take of **Fennel** seeds: 2 lbs; **Mountain Parsley**: 1 lb; **Wall Germander**: 1/2 lb; **Greater Celandine** root, juice, or its seeds: 1/2 lb; **Eyebright**, **Anise** seeds, **Celery**, **Parsley**: 3 drams of each; **Long Pepper**: 3 drams; **Ginger**, **Cinnamon**: 2 drams of each; **Pennyroyal**, **Dill**, **Rue**, **Hyssop**, **Southernwood** flowers, **Juniper** berries, **Saxifrage**: 3 drams of each. When all these are pulverized, prepare them with cooked and skimmed honey. Take it in the morning and evening, taking as much as the size of a walnut at a time.

### Gaius Plinius Secundus, in Book 22, Chapter 14 of the *Natural History*, speaks concerning the virtue of Almond Oil.

**Almond oil** purges and softens bodies; it dries the skin and commends its brightness. With honey, it removes spots from the face. It is also beneficial for the ears with rose oil and honey, and a decoction of pomegranate buds. It kills worms in the hands <note>likely referring to skin parasites</note>, and disperses heaviness of hearing, phantom sounds, and ringing; likewise, it heals pains of the head and eyes. It cures boils, and when mixed with wax, it heals sunburn. It cleanses running ulcers <gloss>and fistulas</gloss> and sores when used with wine, and treats swellings when mixed with washed honey. Applied by itself to the head, it induces sleep.

### A marvelous plaster against ulcers of the shins, even if they should be fistulated.

Take of common oil and very strong vinegar: 4 lbs <gloss>of each</gloss>.
Iron: 6 drams; Red Vitriol: 2 drams; <gloss>of each</gloss> Burnt Copper leaf: 1 1/3 drams; Steel filings: 1 1/3 drams; Verdigris: 1 1/3 drams. Let all the aforesaid be very finely pulverized, each by itself. Take the oil and vinegar and let them boil for one boil; then remove from the fire and place in it **Litharge** <note>lead monoxide</note> <gloss>---</gloss> 2 lbs. Then return it to the fire and let it boil until it thickens, stirring it continually with a stick. Then let the other materials be added and cook until it is converted into a red color. Finally, remove from the fire and let a plaster be made.

I had this from **Salvatore Rossell**, for it has been tested.

**Recipe.** Take a double-sized flask of butter <note>likely a vessel shaped like a butter-pot or used for clarified butter</note> and place inside four pounds of oil; the older the oil is, the better. Then take a handful of the perforated herb <note>original: "perforata herba"; likely St. John's Wort, *Hypericum perforatum*</note> and its seeds. Cut it up small so that it can enter the said flask, and then put it in the flask. Seal it very well with a stopper on top, and place it in a cauldron full of water to the <unclear>brim</unclear>. Let it boil for the space of two hours, but tie the said flask to the chain <note>the pot-hook chain over the hearth</note> so that the boiling does not break it. After it has boiled, draw out the said oil and squeeze the said herb very well with a cloth, and throw the herb away. Then put in more of the herb and do as was said above; and you shall do this three times, and you will have boiled it for six hours in total. Then take the said oil, purified very well with the said cloth, and put it back in the flask with the following roots, very well pulverized: four ounces of rhatany <note>original: "radina"</note>, four ounces of tormentil <note>original: "trementilla"</note>, and four ounces of white dittany <note>original: "dittamo bianco"</note>. You shall boil it for four <insert>two</insert> hours with the said powders, and always let it stay in the said flask. Place it in the sun for the space of one month; afterwards, use it for whatever you wish, and it will be most perfect.

I obtained this prescribed recipe from the Reverend Lord Martino, of the Order of Canons Regular

<column-break/>

of Saint Augustine, an elegant preacher. He reported that by the benefit of this oil, given to a certain infant in the measure of one beaker, and after eight hours following the oil—the same infant being bound to a table—the same infant was freed from a certain great serpent <note>original: "serpentem"; likely a large intestinal parasite or tapeworm interpreted as a serpent</note> which they said he had nourished in his body. The head was extracted through the anus with iron pincers <note>original: "tenaculis ferreis"</note> by a hermit who had composed this oil and had given it to this infant to drink. The creature that was extracted was of marvelous magnitude, length, and thickness. Nor had there been any physician who recognized the cause of such sickness, weakness, and poor color in this infant except for this hermit; nevertheless, the infant consumed food and drink more voraciously than anything else. The said hermit freed him from the said serpent for free and for the love of God, although the father of the infant, being rich and wealthy, offered him a hundred gold coins <note>original: "centu aureos"</note>, and indeed half of all his goods, since he was his only son. And he reported that this truly happened.

And because this oil has virtue against worms and all poisons when drunk and fortified, I have therefore noted it here on the 16th day of September, 1481.

And Lord Johannes Brung de Salsa, Doctor of Arts and Medicine, added that this same ointment, rubbed along the spine, heals those suffering from quartan fever <note>original: "quartanarios"; a fever associated with malaria where paroxysms occur every fourth day</note>, provided they are purged first; he has experienced this many times. October 10, 1489.

## Against the Evil of Cancer
<note>original: "Contra malu Canorĩ" - likely a misspelling of "Cancri"</note>
Take a piece of linen cloth and make a hole in it as large as the sore; place it over the sore. Then take another piece of the same size to cover the sore and soak it in fresh water. Take some arsenic <note>original: "resegallo" (realgar), a toxic arsenic sulfide used in medieval medicine to cauterize tumors</note> well-pulverized, and place it upon the said soaked cloth, and apply it to the sore. Let it stay for the space of twelve hours, and then remove it and clean the said sore well. You will see a white rim around it. Then take some rose ointment and apply it to the said sore, keeping some fine threads in the said rim; change the said ointment twice a day, provided that the ailment has not exceeded sixteen months.

## A Miraculous Medicine for Diverse Ailments and Infirmities and for Many Other Things as Mixed.

Take nutmeg, <gloss>10</gloss> cloves, <gloss>10</gloss> galangal <note>a root similar to ginger</note>, <gloss>10</gloss> cardamom, <gloss>10</gloss> agaric <note>a medicinal mushroom</note>, <gloss>10</gloss> cubeb <note>tailed pepper</note>, <gloss>10</gloss> of each half an ounce. <gloss>10</gloss> Grains of paradise, <gloss>10</gloss> ginger, <gloss>10</gloss> cinnamon, <gloss>10</gloss> of each one ounce. <gloss>10</gloss> Pulverize all these together very well and afterwards place them in the best white wine; the thicker the material, the better it is. Place it in an alembic <note>a distilling apparatus</note> and distill it over a slow fire. This water takes the place of balsam. It gives entry to the spirit in the body and fixes that which is not fixed <note>an alchemical reference to stabilizing volatile substances</note>. It deletes corruption and preserves everything it touches in good condition. It is effective in all "cold" ailments <note>referring to the humoral theory where illnesses were classified as hot, cold, moist, or dry</note>.

Likewise, it draws to itself the virtues of herbs and spices. <margin><image-desc>A small sketch of a human eye</image-desc></margin> It clears blurred vision. It heals abscesses <note>original: "apostema"</note> both internal and external. Likewise, it removes spots from the eyes, as well as redness and heat. It restrains tears. Given as a drink to epileptics, it cures them, as well as every "gout" <note>a general term for joint pain or fluid imbalances</note> caused by cold, and paralysis if the areas are anointed. It cures sciatica, those with podagra <note>gout of the foot</note>, and those with dropsy <note>edema</note> caused by cold. It makes new wine taste old. It puts poison to flight. It cleanses, sweetens, softens, and makes every metal malleable.

## To make merchant silver.

You shall take a fish that they call *moque* <note>original: "moque" or "moqua"; likely a small, non-commercial fish or sea slug</note> or *fertolaga*: which is a fish that comes out in the nets when the fishermen are fishing, and they throw it away as it is good for nothing. And having taken the said fish, split them and place them on a board to dry. And once dried, grind them as much as you can, and once ground, put them in a flask and add enough lemon juice so that it covers the said *moque* by the thickness of a knife-back or a finger. And this being done, seal the mouth of the flask well with cloths and **lute it** <term>enlutal: to seal a vessel with a paste of clay or dung to make it airtight</term> or seal the mouth of the flask well so that it cannot breathe. And this being done, put the said flask in the sun for 8 days. And this being done, take it away; and shake it twice a day during those 8 days, and let the said flask stay well sealed. Afterwards, you shall take white lead <note>original: "blanquet"; basic lead carbonate used as a pigment and in alchemy</note> of the kind that the apothecaries sell in cakes, and grind it; and once ground, put it in a flask. And let the white lead be only the third part of the weight of the dry *moque*. So, if the *moque* is one pound, the white lead must be 4 ounces. And having ground the said white lead and put it in the flask, you shall add enough distilled vinegar to cover the white lead by one finger; and let it stay in the sun for 8 days, shaking it once every day. And this being done, you shall **store** <term>estugaras: to set aside or preserve</term> the flask. Afterwards, you shall take a marble slab and take sublimated quicksilver <note>mercury sublimate</note>, a third part of the *moque*; and rock alum, a third part of the weight of the *moque*. For if the *moque* is one pound, you shall take 4 ounces of sublimated quicksilver and 4 ounces of rock alum. For the white lead, the sublimated quicksilver, and the rock alum

<column-break/>

all three materials together must weigh as much as the *moque* does. And you shall grind the sublimated quicksilver and the rock alum well upon the marble slab, and while grinding, moisten it little by little with the distilled vinegar that you had put in the flask with the white lead, in such a way that it remains thick like a sauce. And put this same ointment to distill in a glass **alembic** <term>alembi: a distilling apparatus consisting of a gourd-shaped vessel and a cap</term>; and once the water or vinegar is drawn off, set aside the said water, for it is not good for the work. You shall take the dregs that remain in the said alembic or flask, and on a marble slab, moisten those dregs with the water from the *moque* that you had stored in the flask. And you shall make it so that the said dregs and the water of the *moque* remain like a clear sauce. And this being done, you shall put it in a glass alembic to distill, and the water that comes out, store it well in a well-sealed flask. For this water performs a marvelous work. And this being done, you shall take purged and prepared **iron** <term>ferret: literally "little iron," referring here to iron filings or purified iron</term> as you know how; and make filings of it. And you shall put the said filings in a pan or **crucible** <term>crejol: a vessel used for melting metals at high temperatures</term>, and you shall put in some of the said water that you have stored so that it covers the filings. And let it boil there for one hour; and ensure that the water always covers the filings while boiling for one hour. Remove the said filings and melt them in a melting crucible; and once melted, cast in **arsenic** <term>arsemch: arsenic oil or arsenic compound used to whiten copper or iron</term> oil into the crucible, a third part of the weight of the iron filings. And having added the oil and stirred it while it boils, cast the said filings, thus melted with the oil, into the water of the said *moque* which you will have placed ready in a pan. And having quenched the said iron, return it to the crucible.

### To make oil of arsenic

You shall take white tartar <note>term: "tartar" (potassium bitartrate crystals from wine barrels)</note>: and you shall put it in a wet cloth: and you shall put the <margin>to do it many times</margin> said cloth with the tartar amidst the coals for an hour or two to calcine. And once calcined, you shall grind it: and once ground, you shall take its weight of calcined pulverized tartar and you shall put it in a glass vessel over water: and there let it stay until it be made into oil. And the said oil of arsenic is made. And this such oil you shall put into the work of the "under-layer" for the silver that is mentioned back on the other page.

# Sonnet of Brother Elias on the Philosopher's Stone

->Sonnets of Brother Elias on the Philosopher's Stone<-
->which is said to have been fashioned by Saint Francis of Assisi<-

It delights me to speak briefly
of all the secrets of the happy art <note>The "Happy Art" or "Sacred Art" is a common synonym for Alchemy</note>
from the smoke to the root
I have been contemplating from the midst of my mind.
Therefore I pray to the Supreme Clemency
that He grant me the grace to open
and to tell every secret
of those who have spoken in this science.
Whoever wishes to follow such a leader
must not twist the art away from nature.
Sun and Moon and Mercury <note>note: original "Sol e luna et mercurio," referring to Gold, Silver, and Quicksilver</note> are enough for you
to make the good paste,
and do not put various seeds within,
for nature does not desire the contrary.
My fathers, by diverse ways,
have all come to one effect:
that every imperfect body
they have healed of various maladies.
From the soul they have divided the elements:
the water from the air, and that of the fire <note>original: "som," likely referring to the Greek *pyr* or the "summit" of fire</note>,
and then little by little,
rectifying them, they have made them shining.
Then they have joined them together in one essence;
one sublimes, another calms and dissolves,
and iterating, revolves,
then congealing, they achieve fixation <note>term: "fixatione" (the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat)</note>.
But the first work is putrefaction <note>term: "putrefactione" (the "black stage" or *nigredo* where the matter decomposes)</note>.
But note well, lest you be in error,
that it is one single thing from which have issued
the aforesaid elements:
the soul, the body, the spirit, and the moisture.
Furthermore, in it are four, three, and one:
the quintessence <note>term: "quinta essentia" (the fifth element or purest essence)</note> treads with ferment,
mercury, gold, and silver,
nourished together, yet each divided.
As in the egg, the white with the yellow,
the skin, the shell, and the seed of the rooster;
a clearer example I cannot give you.
Therefore you must note
to what you set your hand, and then practice,
so that your mind does not go wandering.

<summary>This page provides a practical recipe for "oil of arsenic" used in silver-making and transitions into an alchemical sonnet attributed to Brother Elias. The poem uses the metaphor of an egg to explain the unity of the four elements and the "quintessence" required for the Great Work.</summary>

When you compose, do not let it slip from your mind
that to make a dough that is good and fine
one requires water and flour
and leaven <note>ferment</note> to bring the dough together.
Similarly, if without leaven
you work, or without water or flour,
in our medicine <note>the alchemical substance</note>
you will find your hands full of wind.
And to turn every darkness into brilliance,
our practice is not that of the common people.

And not from a dead rose, but from a living one
is this divine and holy medicine completed,
which restores <margin>4</margin> every imperfect body to true light.
Now take the fresh stone
and without making any other division,
place it in a vessel
well sealed with a "burning seal" <note>hermetically sealed, likely with wax or fused glass</note>.
Then place it in its sweet bed,
for here it stays until it is perfect;
but take note of the small cask <note>the furnace or container</note>,
for the whole effect lies in the fire <note>original: "vulcano"</note>.
And they perform the whole art in one vessel
with a slow fire <note>literally "slow hole," referring to the furnace vent</note> and in a single furnace.
Here it sublimates, dissolves, and distills;
the water descends and humbles,
because it causes putrefaction, calcination, and fusion.
<margin>5</margin> Where it waves and rises and falls.

<margin>Here is the first stone / then the work, which is 9 months</margin>
My stone is of a beloved rose,
precious, sweet, and gentle,
yet vile in its price <note>a common alchemical trope: the secret ingredient is cheap and overlooked by the ignorant</note>
when considering its hidden virtue.
I do not waste time, because I do not fear
the time in which many are deceived,
and also others are ruined,
who make their works sad and slow.
The shortest time is nine months,
as the courtly philosophers <note>the great alchemical authorities</note> attest.
Furthermore, it shows many colors,
like a meadow of flowers;
but after every color, it plants itself in black,
and near the end, it shows itself as white.

<column-break/>

Then, by a more distant transformation,
it becomes entirely the color of gold,
with such a beautiful labor
that it gives joy to every healthy mind.
Another sign also manifests
if your devotion is finished:
it is not if it smokes or bubbles,
but if it stays still without any other disturbance.

Furthermore, I direct its proportion,
which causes many people to fail:
after it no longer smokes and makes no more movement,
ensure it is joined and well-cooked.
And take good care that no medicine
is tested directly upon the Sun or Moon <note>gold or silver</note>.
<margin>7</margin> But so that one weight goes upon a thousand,
and even more if your elixir is perfect,
ensure that you are wise of intellect.
And do not hold what I say as vile:
take one dram <term>drachma: a small unit of weight</term> of the medicine
and ten drams of pure mercury,
and put it in the deep place
of the burning furnace inside the mold.
And after the heat begins to flee,
quickly put in the elixir,
and everything is converted into medicine
 of gold, perfect and fine.
Of which, throw one weight upon the remainder,
and you will find yourself content with the work.

Our ancestors, to hide this art,
have spread it across diverse volumes;
some call it "gums,"
and some "molten mercury," Jupiter, or Mars.
Some call it by the name of every metal,
some call it by the name of the planets,
and each weaves it with different nets
and different names up to the "tregallo" <note>likely a corruption of a technical term for the final stage</note>.
Now "hair," "mineral stone,"
"it must be," "herbal stone,"
arsenic, orpiment, and "dzacho" <note>likely zaffre or a salt</note>,
and sal ammoniac,
and copperas, basilisk, and blood,
<margin>9</margin> Laton <note>an alloy resembling brass</note>, ezoch <note>mercury</note>, eznech <note>antimony or similar</note>, kibrith <note>sulfur</note>, and the serpent.

# Knowledge of Marcasite:

According to the philosophers <note>original: "phi." - likely referring to alchemists or natural philosophers</note>, there are as many species of marcasite <note>term: Marcasite - in historical metallurgy, this referred generally to iron pyrites or other shiny metallic ores, not just the modern mineral FeS2</note> as there are species of metals. That is: golden, silvery, blood-red, leaden, coppery, and irony. Each one of these species is identified by the touchstone <note>term: Touchstone (paragone) - a dark stone used to test the purity of precious metals by the color of the streak they leave</note>. The golden variety shows the color of gold; the silvery shows the color of silver. And so all the others in their species. And this is the
<margin>1</margin> first proof.
The second proof is this: place a little bit of it upon the coals and blow [with bellows]. If it melts quickly, it is leaden or blood-red. If it is difficult to melt and holds its own, and maintains its proper color, it is good.
<margin>1</margin> The third proof: take some of the whole marcasite, a small piece, and wash it and dry it. Have an ash-cup <note>term: Incinario - a vessel or cupel made of ashes used in assaying</note> ready and take a bead of lead and place it in the said ash-cup in the furnace hole, covering it with charcoal as one does for cupellation. And when the ash-cup is red-hot, place the said lead inside, and as it is melted, place the said marcasite in powder inside it. The lead will consume it; the lead will boil and go off in smoke, and the marcasite will remain at the bottom in its proper color. Then remove the ash-cup from the hole, blowing over it as it comes out of the hole to keep it clean. Take the said marcasite and test it upon the touchstone; if it turns out golden or indeed silvery according to its grade, it is good. And thus the philosophers [say] that if it does not stand up to this comparison, it is worth nothing.

<column-break/>

The said species of marcasite are: one is a very hard rocky lump, and the other is a rounded mineral, and this [latter] one is good.
When you wish to melt marcasite, first take it and wash it and dry it. Then take one part of marcasite, take three parts of saltpeter <note>term: Saltpeter - potassium nitrate, used as a flux</note> and a good amount of soap. Knead everything together and place it in a crucible <note>original: "crudo"</note> to melt slowly. And when it is melted, pour it into a channel filled with oil, and it will return to a bead. It will break under the hammer and will show its proper
<margin>1</margin> color on the touchstone.
Good marcasites, which have their sulfur digested <note>note: "digested" here means chemically matured or refined by nature</note> within them, do not smoke when placed in the furnace hole and do not give off a smell of sulfur. They maintain their proper color, and when you break them, they shine inside like gold or silver, and they break softly on the touchstone, etc.
<margin>S</margin> If it is difficult to melt: some of them have minute veins and tiny grains like silver filings, and the result is powdery and hard to break.
<margin>S</margin> There are other marcasites which are not so perfectly golden or silvery. The golden one will turn out high on the touchstone, at 20 or 22 carats <note>original: "h xx . et xxy . hante"</note>, and among other things, these are good. The lesser ones do not yield fruit <note>note: "fruit" refers to the metal yield</note> and lose much of their heat in the furnace and will stink of sulfur.
<margin>S</margin> Similarly, there are rare silvery marcasites which will turn out on the touchstone in a good silver whiteness, at 10 leagues <note>note: likely a measure of purity or alloy grade</note>, and these...

<summary>This page details three diagnostic tests for identifying types of marcasite and provides a recipe for melting and refining the ore using saltpeter and soap. It distinguishes between high-quality "digested" ores and inferior, sulfurous varieties based on their reaction to heat and their appearance on a touchstone.</summary>

Similarly, they are good through sublimation <note>original: "sullimatione"</note>, white and pure, and also through the removal of sulfur <note>original: "desulfuro"</note> and the washing of sulfur:

This is a general mixture <note>original: "bragula"</note>, and as much as we remove the stench of sulfur, they become more beautiful in appearance and remain higher in gold or silver content; and they return much from the sulfur. These are the best, whether by the art of white or red <note>original: "fene cana bonfusto"</note>, for fixing cinnabar <term>Cinnabar: a bright red mineral consisting of mercury sulfide, the primary ore of mercury</term> and for making the small metallic seeds <note>original: "metexini"</note> that fall by projection onto copper and <unclear>hupia</unclear> steel, and they form gold and silver according to their operation.

Know this remaining part: it will be a good <note>original: "Petronanglo"</note> for the depth of the light <note>original: "deluminare"</note>, and it is made in the manner of a crust. It has with it its own digested sulfur, which burns and is called the "sea of light." And the deeper it is sought, the better it is. ## Work which is done with silver Marcasite, which converts cinnabar into silver.
<note>Marcasite here likely refers to iron pyrites or a similar metallic sulfide used as a reagent.</note>

Take silver Marcasite, well purified; which, having been ground, you shall place in layers <note>original: "solaze"</note> in an iron vessel. This vessel

<column-break/>

ought to be like a small pan <note>original: "capria"</note>, not very high, with its cover well sealed. Then you shall make layer upon layer of the Marcasite and of cinnabar prepared thus: namely, let the cinnabar boil in vinegar for eight hours in a cup with a cover of some earthenware lid, so that the vinegar does not evaporate. And let the said cinnabar become the color of lead. This cinnabar ought to be in pieces in the manner of dice or small beans. And so, place it in the said pan in the said prepared marcasite, layer upon layer, so that the first and the last layer is of marcasite. And let it be well sealed with clay <note>original: "opitirata cum luto"</note> so that it does not evaporate. Let it be placed in the fire among the ashes for two natural days. Then allow it to cool and open the vessel; and you will find the cinnabar converted into silver, in such an amount as there was quicksilver <term>Quicksilver: Mercury</term> in the said cinnabar. Take.

# Here begins the little book on the composition of the philosopher's stone, which is titled The Lily

<margin>
Edition 3, Volume 3 of General Law 4.

**F**or those striving to exalt nature concerning the Sun <note>Gold</note> and the Moon <note>Silver</note> and the other planets <note>Metals</note>, as well as medicine: at least in this work, they may find the true and perfect doctrine of that most sacred scripture concerning the one cleansing agent. This is so that anyone engaged in the highest labors might not emit fruitless and varied efforts through different persons. In this book, nothing is placed without mystery, and nothing else will be found than the decree from the sayings of the philosophers. Let this please individuals elsewhere, even in those specific points repeated many times in other places; where perhaps something was more obscure in the beginning, or imperfectly uttered, they may find it more fully subjected to this little book in the following parts.

<margin>
See... folio 211, column 2...
folio 209, column 3.

**T**he title of this work is *The Lily*, as if plucked from among thorns. And lest it leave any doubt in the author: to one wishing to ask about the order of the things to be treated—why the more worthy things like medicine and the Sun do not come first, but rather the Moon first, the Sun second, and afterwards certain other extraordinary things as will appear below, and thirdly the medicine—let their doubt be satisfied in this way: Either because the end is more worthy than the beginning, or, more truly and better, because the things that whiten are not the same as those that redden. Nor can the red be made unless the white precedes it. As Senon says: "Know that unless you whiten this stone, you cannot make it red." It is through the red that the other planets are dyed. Nor can the third thing, namely the medicine, proceed except from that same red. And therefore, by necessity, the order had to be such that the white is placed first.

<column-break/>

Whether it be the Moon: it makes the elixir <note>original: "vpm ixir"</note>, which, when placed in whiteness, makes white or "Moon" out of the bodies; through which white, one arrives at the red. Concerning this, hear the philosopher saying:

**A**ll investigators of this art, seeing that appearing whiteness remaining on the base, be few <note>i.e., be rare/careful</note>, because the hidden essence is in that whiteness. And then you must not extract it, but rather cook it until the whole becomes red. And thus, deservedly, the second part follows concerning the Sun or from the red: from which, or from whose perfection, proceeds the retreat of the planets and even the perfection of the medicine itself. And hence it is that not without reason—by the three and the one preceding the medicine—they proceed by gradual perfection in the shortest time. Just as it is said: In the Father from whom the Son proceeds, and from both of them the Holy Spirit.

philosopher [?]
</margin>

# On the Unity of the Substance

They call this thing by many names, which **Azage** <note>original: "ayage"; likely a corruption of the Arabic *al-zaj* (vitriol) or *azoth*</note> says as does **Bonellus**, because the philosophers multiplied the names of this thing in order to deceive those who come after: As **Hermogenes** says:

<margin>⸗</margin>And again, they have called it by all names; yet for each thing there is only one true and proper name, as **Pythagoras** says. Nevertheless, they never call the thing itself by its names because of the excellence of its nature. Or otherwise, as it says below: however much the nicknames are diversified, the end is always in one thing alone and the same.

For **Luchas** <note>likely Lucas, a common authority in the *Turba Philosophorum*</note> says: You do not have need of many things, but only one. <margin>⸗</margin> And the foundation of this art, for which many have perished, is indeed one.

And the venerable **Diomedes** says: Use nature, for nature is not improved except in its own nature, by which names you introduce a foreign thing; neither powder, nor any other thing.

And **Bacten** says: Beware lest you introduce anything foreign.

And the **Prophets** <note>original: "phietas"; likely referring to the "Philosophers" or "Sages"</note> say: Abandon the plurality of dark names. For Nature is one, which overcomes all things. <gloss>Azage, that is, one water which contains all things as one</gloss>

And **Bonellus** says: The whole work and the regimen is not made except from water. When they say the thing you seek is one; and unless there is in that thing that which improves itself, that which they seek will not happen.

And **Saichos**: Seek the metal <note>original: "es"; usually *aes* meaning copper or bronze, but here used for the alchemical "body"</note> which is one for the work by means of fire.

And **Senon**: I signify to those who follow: that a certain round thing <note>likely the alchemical vessel or the "orb" of the work</note> converts the spirit and vapor into the four foundations; it is from one thing.

And **Astanus**: Nature is one, according to which it overcomes all things.

And **Ayandus**: Therefore it is called **Azage**, because it shall be made one. For different natures do not

<column-break/>

improve that thing. For Nature is one: which makes itself to germinate.

For **Luchas** says: Roast this white metal until it makes itself germinate, because **Magnesia** <note>a technical term for the crude mineral body of the Stone</note> does not whiten if it permits the spirit to flee.

And **Aristeus** said: Thus let this composition be in the four elements. Likewise the same **Aristeus**: This thing extracts from itself the life which it has, both soul and generation. If, therefore, this metal is roasted until it makes itself germinate, and different things do not improve that thing: and this composition is perfected in all four elements. So that it may extract from itself the life which it has, both soul and generation: from which it follows that this thing is one in the end and not diverse.

But they say this thing is composed of three: namely, **Soul, Spirit, and Body**. For this metal is like a man; it has a body and the spirit of a man, and its breathing is exact, which after God is life to it. Likewise, the metal breathes in moisture: which, receiving power, multiplies and increases. That metal is like other things. Therefore the philosophers say: that the metal is disturbed <note>likely referring to the "corruption" or blackening stage</note> and again it becomes many times better than it was before, as **Bonellus** says.

Likewise **Hermogenes** says: This thing is like a man; it has a body and a soul.

Wherefore the philosophers said: that a body does not penetrate a body, but <gloss>that is, the tincture</gloss> a subtle nature, which is the soul, which penetrates and tints the body.

But they speak of the **Sulfurs** which were hidden in the four bodies. But it is called four bodies. The Male or masculine, which is properly called the male, is the liquefaction or water <gloss>that is, produced from water</gloss> and let it not go out <gloss>that is, from the vessel</gloss> as **Arisleus** says, saying: Imbibe this milk with its own water, which shall go out from it: which is the **Permanent Water** <note>original: "aqua pmanens"; the central solvent of alchemy that does not wet the hands</note>.

<summary>This page argues for the fundamental unity of the alchemical substance, asserting that despite many confusing names used by ancient sages, the "Stone" is a single nature composed of body, soul, and spirit. It emphasizes that the work must be done using only the substance's own internal "water" and "nature" without foreign additions.</summary>

# The Separation and Union of Elements

The <term>elements</term> <note>The four classical elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</note> are separated by their own governance. And as he composes them, he brings them back into one. Regarding this water, the <term>Philosopher</term> <note>Likely referring to Hermes Trismegistus or a generic authority in the alchemical tradition</note> says: "O nature, she who always turns the body into <term>spirit</term>. O how wonderful is this nature which hangs over all things and overcomes all things." And it is the sharpest vinegar which made pure gold into spirit, without which vinegar neither whiteness, nor blackness, nor redness, nor rust can be made. And know that when it is mixed with bodies and becomes one with them, it turns the body into spirit; indeed, by a spiritual fire, it dyes with an unchangeable <term>tincture</term> <note>A permanent color or essence</note> that cannot be destroyed.

Listen also to **Ortolanus** <note>A 14th-century alchemist known for his commentary on the Emerald Tablet</note> saying: "Know that in the beginning of the mixing, it is necessary that the raw, pleasant, and sincere elements—being themselves upright—be mixed over a gentle fire. Beware of increasing the fire, so that the elements may join together by shaking, follow one another, and be embraced." And it is completed when it burns away little by little until they are dried out in that gentle fire.

And know that one (that is, the <term>soul</term>) burns, and another (that is, the spirit) is spoken of, and one (the body) strengthens, and one allows the other to fight against the fire. For the elements, diligently cooked, rejoice and are carried into foreign natures; that is, the soul is turned into the body, and the body is turned into the soul. Because of this, that which was melted (the body) becomes solid. The moist becomes thick, and they are body and spirit: and the spirit joining the solution fights against the fire. Wherefore the Philosopher says: "Convert the elements, and you will find what you seek." To convert, however, is to make the earth moist and dry, and the dry moist, and the fleeing <note>volatile</note> fixed. And that which is composed germinates itself; it compels itself.

Many know the gum of this investigation; some of them have found certain applications which cannot endure the punishments of the fire, for they are diminished by it.

<column-break/>

But our <term>elixir</term> and the applications made from the gum and from our honorable <term>stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note>—because it naturally contains the tincture within itself—sustains the punishments of the fire itself. Indeed, it is never diminished by it, because it is made in the power of the fire. And shall the mother kill the son whom she nourished? Certainly not.

And understand that I place "gum" here for "generation" or "the generator"—that is, for the water making both whiteness and redness. For these are the same things which whiten and redden internally and externally, with a gentle first cooking moving them.
<margin>
Gum in the spirit which is fourfold.
</margin>

For the sign of the goodness of the first cooking is the extraction of its redness; otherwise, that first cooking is not made well, as the "Flower of Flowers" <note>A common title for alchemical treatises</note> says.
<margin>
Know that it is not some dung in... <unclear>midrodwim</unclear>...
</margin>

For when you see it already black, know that the whiteness of the mind <note>original: "mentis"</note> is hidden in the belly, appearing first as hidden. And then it behooves you to draw out that whiteness from that blackness by a most subtle fire. But seeing that whiteness standing out in the vessel, be certain that redness is hidden in that whiteness. And then you must not extract it, but rather cook it until the whole red becomes the whitest.
<margin>
It should be noted that the body is given in the mixed water in which...
</margin>

Nor should anyone wonder that you will find diverse sayings of the Philosophers regarding the aforementioned things—namely, the names of the body, our spirit, and the components being diversified. For sometimes it is called "dregs," and sometimes "the womb," for from the same thing they proceed. Sometimes it is called "not-fire," and not without reason; for sometimes it is said to **act**, and sometimes to **suffer** <note>To be acted upon</note>.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the union of body and spirit in the alchemical process, following the previous page's focus on the philosophical marriage of elements. It cites various authorities to validate the necessity of liquefaction and the "permanent water."</meta>

It carries [the influence] and thus acts in turn: and sometimes it suffers <note>original: "agit et patitur" - a common alchemical concept where one substance acts as the active agent and the other as the passive recipient</note>.
Likewise, they are named from the spirit: and are of an indivisible nature of society. For truly one is never separated from the other, although they may seem segregated to the sight, or superficially; indeed, one cannot exist without the other. For their spirits are separated through the way of nature perfectly, so that they are not separated from one another, as **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the famous 8th-century Islamic polymath and "father of chemistry"</note> says in the same book.
Understand this according to the saying of **Bonellus** <note>A frequent authority cited in the *Turba Philosophorum*</note>: namely, that without heat nothing is ever generated. And a bath intense in heat is preferred. If indeed it be cold: it puts [the work] to flight. Let the temperament, however, be a smooth and suitable body.
Sometimes these three are called spirits, and not without cause. For also their earth or thickness in the earth is called thus an airy and subtle persuasion: which all consist in the same thing without a middle generator. Because it is also a body: or from bodies. That it is indeed a body, **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the Persian physician whose works were foundational to medieval alchemy</note> says, saying: Take the body which I have demonstrated to you and fit it into thin plates.
Likewise **Bonellus**: it is better that there be made from metals a certain heart of the sun: this is gold and the sun.
Likewise **Zimon** says: And know that the body is that in which the gold is.
Likewise the **Physician**: And know that it is in the water if it is diligently ground. If however you say how water may become powder:
<margin>The resolution of the body into water</margin> It should be noted that the intention of the philosophers is: that the body which was not water is sent into water: and water is mixed with water, and they are made into one water together. It must be understood, therefore, that unless everything is turned into water,

<column-break/>

it does not arrive at the work. It is necessary, therefore, for the body to be compared to the flame of fire: so that it may be destroyed: and become weak in all water; <margin>Note above a. n. mąq...</margin> because that is it, until the whole becomes water.
But those beginning, hearing "water," think it to be the water of a cloud <note>i.e., common rainwater</note>. If however they had read the books, they would know it to be the **permanent water** <note>term: *aqua permanens* - a specialized alchemical solvent, often mercury or a "philosophical" water that does not wet the hands</note>: which cannot be permanent without its own body in which it is dissolved: and they are made one.
Likewise **Exustus** says: Take the stone of gold: and mix it with the moisture which is the permanent water: and place it upon its own base over a slow fire: or a gentle heat: and so let it be done. For that which is the standing earth receives the **tincture** <note>term: *tinctura* - the transformative essence that changes the color and nature of a metal</note>, namely from the spirit lurking in it.
Of which **Hermogenes** says: Look upon the lurking spirit, and do not despise it: because in it remains a great secret. He says this has greater power than its parts, namely the soul and spirit. This happens through the tincture which it received: after the companions were joined by a dowry, namely after the **whitening** <note>term: *dealbatio* - the "albedo" stage of the Great Work, where the matter is purified to a white state</note>. For in that whitening, being joined, they sound in one way and of all.
And that which first acted, namely the "wild" <note>original: "sera" - likely referring to the wild/untamed sulfur</note>: then begins to suffer from the "sea" <note>original: "a mare" - likely referring to the mercurial sea</note>. And that which first drew, namely the said wild thing or sulfur: is now drawn by the sea: or by **mercury** <note>original: "ar. vi." - abbreviation for *argentum vivum*</note>. And that which first dominated: then is transferred into the dominated.
For the male, who first allowed himself to be drawn: receives the stinging spirit from the wild thing first drawing or dominating. Namely, when the male himself draws the wild thing from himself: which wild thing is called the prior power of my honorable stone.
It is also called the sharpest **vinegar**. Whence that saying: grind it with the sharpest vinegar, and cook it until it thickens. And beware lest the vinegar turns into smoke and perishes.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the philosophical union of body, soul, and spirit in the alchemical process, specifically focusing on the internal perfection of the Stone.</meta>

It seems to be separated from them: from the body and the soul. Yet it will not be so. For the spirit, as has been said, never dies, because there is nothing that can separate or occupy it; rather, it gives life to the body and the soul.

**A**nd thus we must understand what was said by the philosophers: *Nature rejoices in nature* <note>original: "Natura natura letat"</note>, that is, in its own continuation. And nature itself overcomes nature by mortifying the body and giving it life; for from itself it is made, and into itself it is turned. It is increased and multiplied, and we say that many are extracted from one, which requires nothing else when it lacks guidance, and returns to the genus in which it may be cleansed.

**S**imilarly, when it is cooked further, it becomes water. Then, when it is cooked more, it thickens so much until it becomes a stone, which the world then calls the "stone imminent in the metal" <note>A reference to the potentiality of the Philosopher's Stone existing within base metals</note>.

**A**fterward, it is broken and soaked, and it is cooked with a fire more intense than the first, until it becomes like dew or scorched blood. Then it is placed into bodies, and it tinges them into gold, as Bonellus <note>An authority often cited in alchemical florilegia, likely referring to a figure from the "Turba Philosophorum"</note> says.

<margin>namely</margin>
**A**nd as I said above: this stone is contained within two very thin liquids or clear fluids: the soul and the spirit. Thus, it is not necessary for anything external to be introduced or added. For from it, as if from a root, it is taken; it flourishes in the structure which contains these things, as has been said, and all things are founded upon that root.

**B**ecause, however, this foundation of the work has a primary root, and because the power does not abound equally in these roots—just as neither the splendor of the Sun nor the planets are known without patience and delay:

**A**nd therefore Zmon <note>Likely a corruption of "Zosimos" or "Agmon," common names in medieval alchemical texts</note> says: If anyone introduced to this art knew its nature, he would endure the lengthiness of the cooking,

<column-break/>

until he might extract the purpose by the will of God.
**F**or this [stone] extracts from itself all the riches which it holds in its soul from its generation; it is not from another or from others, but from them the flowers are truly drawn out. It makes itself germinate, and that which is inside it sends outside, and that which is outside it sends inside. Thus, the external cleanses the internal until the red—that is, the "born red" <note>original: "natē rubeū"</note> hidden in the body—is turned into white. In the first part of the work, the white is turned into red, not hidden as before, but appearing in every part of the work; and thus they cleanse each other in turn.

**A**nd this is what Bonellus said: "And unless there be in that thing that which cleanses it, how shall it be done?"

**I**ndeed, there is in it that which cleanses it, unless you drive it away with too much fire or haste.

**F**or this reason, Zmon said what was stated before: If anyone introduced to this art knew the natures, he would endure the lengthiness of the cooking until he might extract the purpose by the will of God.

<margin>folio 209</margin>
**I**t should also be noted that the body without the earth—which, standing firm, receives the <term>tincture</term> <note>The transformative "dye" or essence that changes the metal's properties</note>—is said to have a greater union with its offspring: namely, the soul and the spirit, as has been said. For the matter which is placed upon it turns into its own color.

**A**nd as I said before, it is the carrier of the virtues of the soul through the body. And thus the son is said to cleanse the father, first by mortifying him, then by giving him life. And this spirit is called "liquefaction," or the soaking or infusion of water, as I said before.

**A**ccording to the allegory of the wise: Fire is that which stands and tinges; Air is that which confirms and takes possession; Water is that which whitens and, entering, expels from the bodies; Earth is that which, standing firm, receives the tincture.

**And** it must be known, as was said before, that the spirit and soul do not unite with a good body except in the white color. For then all the colors that can be seen in the world today appear; and then they roar <note>original: "fremant", perhaps suggesting a chemical reaction or bubbling</note> and come together into a good odor, namely that of <term>whiteness</term> <note>original: "albedinis"</note>.

**Whitening** <note>original: "dealbatio"</note> is truly the beginning and the foundation of the whole work. From then on, it does not vary into different colors—that is, through others—except into red, in which is the end of the color.

**Yellowness** <note>original: "citerano", referring to citrination</note> which occurs between white and red is not called a "color" <note>i.e., not a primary stage</note>. In the boiling after the whitening, you cannot err. For by increasing the governance of the fire after the whiteness, you will arrive at the yellowing before the visible redness.

**It must be noted** also that the ancients called this aforementioned water—which produces the blackness, whiteness, yellowness, and redness—the "poison of the fire." For without it, why? Because the battle of the fire is won by it. For it is that through which the body

<column-break/>

Column 2:
is turned into spirit. For many spirits overcome bodies, even those born of bodily lack, until they die and their soul is extracted, which is the staining spirit. You can by no means stain a body with it, nor is a body stained unless it is [first] stained [itself]. Nor does a body penetrate a body; truly it is the substance of nature, which is the soul, that penetrates and stains the body.

**When** the body has been liquefied, the spirit returns to its generator. This generator—that is, <term>magnesia</term> <note>In alchemy, not the modern element, but a mysterious "primitive matter" or mineral complex</note>—becomes airy and subtle from its offspring, namely from the spirit or water, without liquefaction, which happens only after the whitening. Wherefore the fleeing power—that is, the soul and spirit—is turned into that which does not flee—that is, into the earth—and makes it spiritual, and clean from its earthliness—that is, airy and subtle. Immediately thereafter, the spirit may rejoice in the altered body, it having been made incorruptible.

**Lest** I seem to have omitted anything in this work, leading to error: it must be known that in this operation the composition first becomes black, as was said; then red; then yellow. And many times yellow, and many times red, because many times they are dried and liquefied; and these are the paths before the whitening.

**Hold this** in your mind: that you should not care about those colors which appear before the whitening, for they are not true colors. And whatever happens regarding the colors, the whitening must be waited for, which, as said before, is the foundation, beginning, and establishment of the whole work; nor does it vary thereafter.

**From** the things previously mentioned and well understood, it appears that our composition consists of, or our work will be, a composite.

Under such a system of governance <note>Latin: *regimine*; refers to the controlled heating of the alchemical vessel</note>, consistency cannot be maintained except by those who, having granted certain premises, follow them to false applications. And the philosophers note such things as were said before: by which these men are deservedly called counterfeiters. And let those who see the work of my hands being made from the dust of the winged basilisk <note>The basilisk is a mythical serpent; in alchemy, it often symbolizes a volatile or poisonous stage of the matter</note> remain silent because of the reasons aforesaid: that nothing is born except from its own nature, just as only a human is born from a human. And nature is not improved except within its own nature. In this, they are perhaps not deceived when they say the scent of the stone of the philosophers is like the scent of graves. And for that reason, they perhaps believe it to be of the basilisk, which is a most foul-smelling animal.

If you find that this matter ought to be nourished like an infant in the womb, as certain philosophers say: you should draw it and its "son" out for a certain quantity of time, but with a gentleness of decoction <note>Slow boiling or heating</note>. So that the matter may be moderated even by the heat of the Sun. And Hermes <note>original: *Am̄* likely referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note> says this matter is like a nourisher of eggs.

**W**hence what Rosinus <note>An Arabic alchemical author, often identified with Zosimos of Panopolis</note> said to Eufenia, when she was inquiring about this operation; he replied: "We begin," for in this operation we begin from the moist. Consider that there are four seasons of the year: namely Winter, Spring, Summer, and Autumn. So that you may understand what occurs in these four seasons or principles. We begin this operation, therefore, from Winter, which is moist. We begin from the moist, proceeding by extracting the work through gentle decoction. Like the gentleness of heat in Spring. Afterward, through greater heat, reaching the whitening <note>Latin: *dealbationem*; the Albedo stage</note> and then the waxing <note>Latin: *incirationem*; making the matter supple like wax</note>; just as in Summer the heat is increased; until finally reaching the redness <note>Latin: *rubedinem*; the Rubedo or final stage</note>. After repeating

<column-break/>

this through greater heat, just as in Autumn the fruits ripen through greater heat and are gathered from the trees.

**A**nother text <note>original: *littera*</note> says: reaching Spring through the "budding," that is, the opening of the roses, which is done with gentle devotion <note>or "boiling," likely a scribe's play on *decoctio*</note> as in Spring. **T**hen reaching Summer, that is, the waxing, through a greater intensity of fire as in Summer. **F**inally proceeding to Autumn, in which the fruits ripen with greater heat so that we may reach the reddening <note>Latin: *rubificationem*</note>.

**N**or is it necessary to consider in this work anything except its own pledge <note>or "pigment"</note> or the lead of the philosophers <note>A symbolic "lead," not the common metal</note>, although it is found written otherwise in some places. For all things that are written in this art are written to hide it, not as other sciences are written for our instruction. Wherefore the philosopher said: "Do not cloud the composition with a plurality of things, nor those things which the philosophers have placed in their books; for my truth is one." In this truth is the spirit we seek, with which we tinge the body as often as necessary, and we lead any of them naturally from a state of diminution to a natural completion. And also, in this tinging spirit, we may make malleable glass <note>A legendary material that bends rather than breaks</note> or unbreakable glass, as it seems, and make a carbuncle <note>A deep red gemstone, often associated with the Philosopher's Stone</note> out of crystal.

**A** single small quantity of our matter—as in the operation of the mixing of the planets—once the medicine is mixed, is one part over 82 pounds; and one part responds to 43. And if there were a thousand times a thousand, it would flow through each from a thousand to a thousand, until the whole world is filled.

**I**t remains now to speak of the final and most worthy part of our treatise...
