# On Medicine, Briefly and Summarily

Since man is the most noble of all creatures, for whose sake all things were created and to whom all things are subject—and since his body is beyond all valuation, as both divine and human law testify—it is only right that his health and youth be preserved. This is achieved by driving away weaknesses and turning aside approaching ailments with the greatest diligence, a pursuit to be valued above any amount of riches. This work of ours surpasses the medicines of Galen, Hippocrates, Avicenna, and all other philosophers, whether they be potions or any other compositions, such that it may even drive away leprosy. <note>The author claims his alchemical "elixir" is superior to the traditional Greek and Arabic medical authorities.</note>

The reasoning for the aforementioned is this: we declare that this is the spirit which is generated in any body, and thus it becomes an antidote and medicine for its own bodies, by scouring and purging them. This must be done by means of natural fire, just as it is in the bodies of metals. If this occurs in the bodies of the infirm, it is much stronger in human bodies, which possess within themselves natural heat and motion, ready and assigned to expel every superfluity and repel any weakness. This medicine, applied gradually in concentrated form, will protect the body so that no disease shall come to it in the future.

For in this way, everyone is mindful of what is common among the nations: that they seek to preserve their health and youth by applying a magnet <note>original: "Magnetē"</note> to gold <note>original: "auzo," a variant of "auro." The magnet was thought to draw out the "soul" of the gold.</note> in prepared filings. How much more, then, ought this to be possible through gold that has been extracted in the middle and decocted?

<column-break/>

This flows out with the medicine; the more subtle the substances are, the better they are. What more can be said? How much more effective is it through this gold which was hidden in the body of the magnet, but is now purged, airy, and made spiritual? The more subtle a medicine is, the more effective it is, as can be seen in the practice of any physician; for they all strive for the refinement, grinding, visitation, or decoction of their medicines, or any other method of preparation.

What more shall I say? These things which I have faithfully inscribed on parchment for memory, I heard and learned. I saw them performed with my own eyes by a practitioner working with total faith, and afterwards, I found them to be true myself. When I began to perform these prophetic works, terrible things occurred through my servants. Standing among these troubles and despairing of the work itself due to the complications, I left the work imperfect and gave it to a certain friend <unclear>friend</unclear> who seemed to me to be most worthy of this matter of the Stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone.</note>. I explained its operation most diligently with all details and by word of mouth.

May He deign to grant this, who with the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, God, forever and ever. Amen.

The Master under whom this work was performed completed this task in 80 days.

**Here ends the book which is called the Lily.** <note>original: "liliū." The Lily was a common title for alchemical texts, symbolizing purity or the white stage of the work.</note> Thanks be to God.

Arnold of Brussels <note>A famous scribe and early printer active in Naples.</note>
</insert>

## Here begins the little book of the philosopher's stone which is called the Abridged Lily

**O**ur gold <note>original: "Aurum est nostrum"; referring to the "philosophical gold," not common bullion</note> consists of three things: namely, body, soul, and spirit. For from the elements, nothing useful is made without proportion and governance.
¶ It is proper, therefore, that the body be imbued, so that from it unity and growth may be received, as well as the eternal breath of life.
¶ This is called the water of quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note>: which is not obtained except from the liquefied body.
¶ Moreover, the body is liquefied in the decoction <note>term: decoctionis; the process of heating a substance in a liquid to extract its essence</note> when the blackness appears like water.
¶ And the sign of the first decoction being dominant is the extraction of its own abundance and its conversion into blackness.
¶ In the belly of our blackness that first appears, the whiteness <note>term: albedo; the second major stage of the alchemical process, signifying purification</note> is hidden; therefore it is necessary to extract that whiteness from its blackness.
¶ When, however, we see that whiteness in the vessel, we are <unclear>blessed</unclear>; the [redness] is hidden within that whiteness. It is not necessary that it be extracted then, but it must be cooked for so long until the whole becomes red.
¶ For when it is mixed with the body and becomes one with it, it turns the body into spirit: and with spiritual fire, it colors it with an invariable tincture <note>a permanent dye or essence</note> that cannot be erased.
¶ For our spirit is a poison overcoming the struggle of fire, through which the body is turned into spirit.
¶ When the body is also carefully ground with water. And unless the body, which was not water, flows in water, and that water is mixed with other water
¶ So that it is one water and many together, and everything is turned into water, the work is not achieved.
¶ It is necessary, therefore, that the body, by the flame of fire

<column-break/>

occupied, be drained and become weak.
¶ With the water in which it is, until the whole becomes [liquid]. ¶ Not indeed the water of the common people, but the permanent water: which, however, cannot be permanent without its own body in which it is dissolved and made one.
¶ Therefore, let the stone of gold be taken, which is the permanent water: and let it be mixed with moisture: and let it be placed on its base over a slow fire: and let it become earth: which <term>substance</term> <note>original: "fra," likely an abbreviation for "frater" or "forma," here interpreted as the material substance</note> being constant, receives the tincture from the spirit lurking within it.
¶ When, however, the liquefied body is [prepared], it turns toward its generator. For the generator, that is, the <note>original: "aganesia," likely a corruption of "magnesia"</note> becomes airy and subtle from its offspring: namely, from the spirit or water. From the liquefaction which happens only after the whitening. For then both fleeing things—that is, the soul and the spirit—are turned into a fleeing thing—that is, into the <term>substance</term>—and make it equal and clean from its earthiness, that is, airy and subtle. So that thereafter, the spirit being altered by the body, it may rejoice in it in the manner of a finished work. ¶ Without heat, much [life] is generated.
¶ Inasmuch as the body, so that the elements may return pleasant and synthesized and upright, let them be mixed over a slow fire. But through tempering, the body becomes gentle.

¶ Therefore, one must beware of excessive fire, since it is an enemy to cold and to seeds. For first, its moisture is cold. Therefore, let it be cooked with the sharpest vinegar until it thickens.

# On the Liquefaction and Tempering of the Stone

God indeed restores to it <note>the body or the stone</note> its soul. This **liquefaction** <note>melting or softening</note> in that gentle fire must be repeated continually until the **blackness** <note>the *nigredo* stage, representing decay and the first step of transformation</note> which appears at the first stage of the work is destroyed.

The more the bodies are mixed and ground, the more the body is dissolved; **quicksilver** <note>original: *argentum vivum* (mercury)</note> thins it by the power of fire.

Therefore, cook the "entering thing" or the "cloud" with its body, because that smoke is white and whitens all things. For by it, whatever is destined to be whitened is indeed whitened.

Therefore, mix its smoke until it congeals and becomes exceedingly white. Also, roast the **white flower** until it causes itself to germinate. For then the **magnesia** <note>a term for the crude alchemical material or "mother" of the stone</note> whitens; it does not permit the spirit to flee, nor the shadow of the copper to appear. For now, nature contains nature.

For **tin** <note>original: *stannum*</note> [transforms] all things that are mixed with it and converts them into its own color; it is the bearer of the virtues of the soul, the spirit, and the copper. **Lead** is said to improve the father, but first it mortifies <note>kills or chemically breaks down</note> him.

But these things properly concern the lifting of the lye or the infusion of water: an **action**. According to the allegory of the wise: **Fire** is dry and touching. **Air** truly confirms and matures. **Water** whitens and enters, removing the vapors. **Earth** also stands firm and receives the tincture.

And it must be known that **quicksilver** is a fire that burns, mortifies, and preserves under a single regime.

It must be known, however, that the body cannot tint unless it is tinted.

And unless its spirit, hidden in its belly, is extracted and becomes a body and also

<column-break/>

without spirit—which is a spiritual nature—from which the colors will appear.

It must be known that in the end, the mixture is made, because all that receives the spirit. Let them be imbued again with a more intense moisture and fire, until it becomes fresh, or like red blood, or the spirit assumes the color of a **pomegranate**.

For let it be known that sperm is not generated from blood unless it is diligently cooked in the liver and has an intense color; and then, with no addition of sperm, nothing is finished.

Similarly, let our copper become spiritual sperm through **putrefaction** <note>the process of rotting or breaking down the matter</note> and "supra-refaction."

The philosophers have divided the "potable water" used in the washing of the vapor into two parts.

For the water stands—that is, it is united—by the struggle of the fire through the long duration of cooking, rotting, and thickening.

For the thing is congealed by the heat of the sun—that is, by gentle devotion—on account of which the tempered composite ought to be introduced into a **bath** or a **cinder-pot** <note>original: *cinerarium*; a vessel filled with ashes to provide indirect, even heat</note>.

Afterwards, with the Dragon <term>Dragon: a symbol for mercury or the raw mineral matter</term> having been placed in the vessel without a sepulcher, let a fire of three breaths <note>referring to the intensity of the bellows or air flow</note> and subtle heat be kindled in the pit of the furnace. Let this burn continually, and let it not be increased, until the diversity of colors begins to appear.

The Philosophers <note>the "Philosophers" refers to the ancient alchemical authorities like Hermes or Geber</note> however, have placed a similar position in these matters of man and of roasting in the end. And this perhaps because of the diversity of the moisture of the place. For in a flowery and moist place, the work congeals more quickly; but in a dry place, it congeals more slowly. Whence they are held to use the cooking until a suitable change is seen by sight. So that the change may certify us and...

Some, however, state that the completion of this work happens in 180 days. Others in 150. Some even assert the whole work is converted into earth in 40 days. And some bring forth the whole work in such a time, but they have received it from the [raw] material.

For the stone does not contain in itself the royal tincture <note>the "tincture" is the power to transform metals</note>. For in the body of <term>Magnesia: a term for the "mother" of the stone, often associated with lead or antimony</term>, it is created perfectly; yet it does not have motion by itself, unless it is perfected by the art and operation. Just as is seen in an Infant, who as far as creation is concerned is born perfect, but is imperfect as far as working is concerned, unless he is first nourished with a little milk, then with more, and then with stronger food.

For this, therefore, our work is necessary to us, so that the tincture of the philosopher may be improved, which is in its own nature / and also that it may be made 65 <note>possibly a numerical code or degree of heat</note> according to the allegory of the wise, to prepare a compound from the clearest species of seasoned antidote.

<summary>This page describes the allegorical "burial" of the dragon and the woman (mercury and sulfur) and provides technical instructions for the gradual heating of the alchemical furnace. It emphasizes the need for a slow, controlled fire to achieve the "tincture" and compares the development of the Stone to the growth of an infant.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the alchemical "elixir" or "medicine," transitioning from its power to transform metals to its supreme medicinal value for the human body.</meta>

and the medium for curing, purging, and transforming all bodies into the true light.
**F**or as much as it is written: "Son, extract from the ray its shadow," <note>original: "fili extrahe a radio suam umbram"</note> that is, its earthiness, which they used to hide in the body of **magnesia**.
**M**agnesia is so named because a **great secret** <note>original: "magnum archanum"</note> lies hidden within it.
**N**or is it necessary in this work to consider the course of the signs or the planets, although it may be found in some writings. For all things written in this art or science were written to hide it, and were not composed in the same speech as our teaching.
**W**herefore the Philosopher says: "Do not swear by the composition of plurality, nor those things which they have placed in their books." For the Truth is one, and it is that which we seek; which is ready at any time. And by its distribution, things are led to their natural completion; and even with this spirit, a rigid power becomes malleable, yet unbreakable. And from crystal, a carbuncle <note>A deep red gemstone, often associated with the Philosopher's Stone</note> is made.
**A** small quantity of this our **elixir**, mixed into the work of the planets <note>The "planets" here refer to the seven base metals (e.g., Lead/Saturn, Iron/Mars)</note>, one part—namely, in a thousand parts—converts every metal into the truest gold, until it completes the number.
**I**t remains now to look at the final and most worthy part of our treatise: namely, concerning medicine, briefly and summarily.
**S**ince this is the most worthy of creatures, discovered by divine grace, and so subject to it; and indeed it does not receive destruction by the elements, remaining by divine or human right. Because it gives strength in health and youth, by driving away lingering weaknesses from the years.

<column-break/>

averting those things that come upon us, it must be sought with the greatest diligence above any divine things. For this our **elixir** works above all the medicines of **Hippocrates, Galen, and Avicenna** <note>The three most authoritative figures in medieval medicine</note> and all the potions or concoctions of other philosophers; it drives away both the wasting disease and leprosy.
**A**nd the reason is as stated: because a divine power is in this spirit which we seek, with which we tinge every body. If indeed it is the cleansing and the medicine for curing and purging all bodies. <unclear>And these things are to be done in the fire...</unclear> <unclear>...in the infusions of metals...</unclear> <unclear>...much...</unclear> <unclear>...for indeed in itself...</unclear> having in itself and driving away every superfluous weakness; and by bestowing the nourishment and medicine little by little, it will protect the highest part, lest any disease should take hold in the future.

Here ends the book of the Abb... <note>The text cuts off, likely "Abbot" or a specific name like "Albertus"</note>

The procedure hereafter regarding marcasite <note>a mineral often confused with pyrite or "fool's gold"</note> was practiced by my D. H.; it was found to be very good <unclear>... keep</unclear> out of 10 in perfect grade.

Take 10 pounds of roasted marcasite in a mortar and make of it the finest powder that can be made; then put it into cupels or iron plates having the full width and roundness of the <term>vessel</term> <note>the crucible or container</note> and make several layers in the manner of those iron boxes at the bottom of the <term>casket</term> <note>a small furnace or chest</note> containing inside and upon it the height of a finger's breadth to place it upon that first cupel, above which, once the other is thus placed upon the said one, you will place others. You will apply about the thickness of a finger of the aforementioned powder mixed with a fourth part of the said powder of <term>Borax</term> <note>used as a flux to lower the melting point</note> and thus from level to level you will place and cover the said cupels in the manner described above until they reach the top, and then make everything melt together in strong heat.

When everything is melted, it is necessary <gloss>at this time</gloss> to draw the said <term>vessel</term> from the fire and let it cool and clean it better; then put it into a <term>matrass</term> <note>a long-necked glass flask</note> in such a way that they can break and leave them until they are consumed in the <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>nitric acid</note> which will be in the said <term>matrass</term>. This being done, empty the water into a strong cauldron of a metal other than the <term>vessel</term> which cannot be destroyed; put the <unclear>precipitate</unclear> there and by this means the said <term>vessel</term> which is of gold will remain at the bottom of the cauldron, which can in no way evaporate by making it purified with sand that you find good, having washed it well, etc. It is thus that one can use the base of some iron to melt <unclear>... of silver</unclear> <unclear>... the ointment</unclear> of a <term>vessel</term> of gold.
